articles.summary: Denmark and Greenland assure sovereignty in US military deal, aiming to enhance Arctic security while respecting self-determination amidst Trump's controversial claims.

blocks.text: DENMARK. Denmark's Minister of Defense Jeppe Bruus, along with Greenland's Minister for Foreign Affairs Mute B. Egede, visits the NATO military exercise Arctic Shield 2026 in Narsarsuaq, Greenland, on Wednesday, September 9, 2026
Photo from Ritzau Scanpix/Mads Claus Rasmussenvia/Reuters
Denmark and Greenland assure sovereignty in US military deal, aiming to enhance Arctic security while respecting self-determination amidst Trump's controversial claims.

items: Denmark and Greenland reaffirmed that any agreement with the United States will not compromise Greenland's sovereignty, despite President Trump's claims of 'permanent control' over the island's security.

A new agreement is set to allow the US to establish a significant military presence in Greenland while preventing adversaries from building bases there, with details about the extent of this presence still unclear.

Both Denmark and Greenland expressed optimism that the upcoming deal, expected to be signed during the UN General Assembly, will enhance security in the Arctic while respecting the sovereignty of the Danish kingdom.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

COPENHAGEN, Denmark – Denmark and Greenland on Saturday said any agreement with the United States would not compromise Greenland’s sovereignty, after President Donald Trump said the deal would give Washington “permanent control” over the Arctic island’s security, leaving its precise scope unclear.

The United States, Denmark and Greenland said late on Friday they had entered into an agreement for the US to ‌develop a significant military presence on Greenland, while prohibiting US adversaries from building their own bases on the island.

Key details of the agreement have not been made public, including the degree of US military presence in the self-governed ⁠Danish territory and whether any formal power over foreign policy and resources would be ceded to Washington.

Denmark and Greenland expressed hope that a deal, which is expected to be signed during the UN General Assembly next week, would end months of uncertainty triggered by Trump’s threats to seize control of Greenland.
“Next week could be a good week – for Greenland, Denmark, and the United States,” Denmark’s Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said in a statement posted on Facebook on Saturday.

“A time of uncertainty will hopefully give way to a binding agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic, and thereby our shared security within NATO and Europe — while respecting the (Danish) Kingdom’s red lines,” he said.
Denmark and Greenland have repeatedly insisted that Washington respect the sovereignty of the Danish kingdom and accept that Greenland is not for sale.

Trump said on Truth Social late on Friday that under a deal, “the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America.”

The deal “gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland,” Trump said, adding that no adversary would ever be permitted to have a base or military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments there, without Washington’s express written approval.
Trump made the announcement after Reuters exclusively reported that the US and Denmark were closing in on a deal.

“I am pleased on Greenland’s behalf that we are nearing the conclusion of an agreement — an agreement that benefits not only our collective security but also the continued development of this country,” Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said on Saturday in a post on Facebook.
“The agreement recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of our Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination,” he added.
Trump’s threats, which peaked in January, triggered a diplomatic crisis that strained relations within NATO and pushed Denmark and Greenland into negotiations aimed at defusing the pressure.
A NATO spokesperson on Saturday said the alliance welcomed the agreement, which would “help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Thousands protest Kennedy Center demolition fears
articles.summary: Protesters took part in a "Hands Around the Kennedy Center" human chain. The demonstration comes amid fears the Trump administration could tear the arts hub down.

image.caption: Protesters joined hands to form a human chain around the venueImage: J. Scott Applewhite/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Thousands of people have demonstrated at the Kennedy Center in Washington D.C. amid fears President Donald Trump's administration could demolish the arts hub.
Crowds of people gathered in the Foggy Bottom area of the US capital city, many carrying signs as they joined in "Hands Around the Kennedy Center."
Some of those gathered held hands and formed a human chain around the center.
Protesters waved placards reading "hands off Kennedy Center" and sang songs close to where workers removed Trump's name from the building in June following a court order.

blocks.caption: Actor Lynda Carter, a vocal Trump critics, addressed the rally on FridayImage: Jose Luis Magana/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Protesters, residents condemn move to demolish Kennedy Center
"It makes me sick to my stomach," the AFP news agency quoted Neal Racioppo, a Washington resident who runs marketing and communications for a theatre, as saying.
Trump "can't get his name on this cherished building, so he is depriving the world of what it could be."
"He does not have a right to decide that an institution, a living memorial to a past president, can be demolished," another protester told AFP.
"The Kennedy Center is vital to the arts in Washington. We need it. We need this,” said local arts community member Bud Wilkinson.
"This is not just about putting the president's name on the Kennedy Center. It's about censoring the performances and the programming," Wilkinson said.
Trump and the Kennedy Center
The Kennedy Center — inaugurated in 1971 following the assassination of US President John F. Kennedy — has been a focal point of Trump's plans for Washington since 2025.
Trump has been pushing for major renovations and claims the building was left in a severe state of disrepair by those previously in control.
Trump's handpicked Kennedy Center board voted last year to rename the institution the Trump-Kennedy Center.
In May, a judge ruled that his name was illegally added and ordered it removed.

blocks.caption: The Kennedy Center board voted last year to rename the institution the Trump-Kennedy CenterImage: Cliff Owen/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What has Trump said about the Kennedy Center?
On Wednesday, Trump appeared to imply that the Kennedy Center could be torn down if his administration did not receive "recognition."

"For the Trump administration, for me to get involved and to take that on long term and to carry it or to raise money to carry it, I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition, because frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close," Trump said.
"It'll end up being ripped down. It's in very, very bad shape, very dangerous shape," Trump told reporters.

articles.title: Students scramble for accommodation after provider goes bust in Dundee
articles.summary: Case highlights severe financial strain on sector across UK as string of university housing schemes fail

blocks.text: Nearly 70 students in Dundee have been left scrambling to find accommodation for this academic year after the latest in a string of university housing schemes went bust amid severe financial strain on the sector.

Students in the city have been forced to find alternative housing and rapidly move their possessions as term begins this month after the collapse of the owner of Marketgait Apartments, a city centre block.
The company filed for administration in mid-July with 68 rooms let. Just weeks earlier it had been urging students to quickly secure its “perfect homes” in online marketing.
It is further evidence of a crisis in the UK student housing sector, with companies going bust or disposing of properties owing to to a combination of poor demand or oversupply in different regions.

Accommodation providers are grappling with falling international student numbers, down for a third year; a cost of living squeeze; and higher borrowing and build costs, exacerbated by the Iran war, affecting upgrades at older properties.
While domestic student numbers are at a record high, a growing proportion live at home, mostly because of the cost of renting, in what has been called “the rise of the commuter student”.

blocks.caption: Marketgait is less than a 10-minute walk from the University of Dundee. Photograph: Jeremy Sutton-Hibbert/Alamy

blocks.text: A boom in new-build student housing in recent years led to too many tower blocks in places such as Coventry, Leeds and Nottingham. Glasgow, Bristol and London still face shortages, with a general lack of affordable rooms.

Modern, purpose-built housing tends to command higher rents than student halls on campus or private rooms, and is out of reach for many domestic students, with wealthier overseas students the main occupants.
Three weeks before the then owners filed for administration, Marketgait Apartments in Dundee was still being promoted to students.

The 116-room building, less than 10-minute walk from Abertay and Dundee universities, had a concierge and a shared lounge with a pool table. The weekly rent was pitched at £199 for a studio and £165 for an en suite room.

“Looking for your perfect student home in Dundee?” the operator, Prestige Student Living, wrote on Facebook on 23 June. “Marketgait Apartments still have rooms available – but not for long! Secure your spot today and avoid missing out on a prime location, modern living, and everything you need right on your doorstep. Book now before it’s gone!”

On 15 July, however, partners from FRP Advisory were appointed to the Jersey-based special purpose vehicle that owns the redbrick block after its owners, the real estate manager 90 North and Kuwaiti investment company Rasameel, failed to repay a £5.7m loan against the property.

Falling student numbers at the building led to financial losses, leaving the company unable to fund essential fire safety remedial works. The building remains closed while its new owner, ATK Property, carries out the work.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: James Elliot says students at at Margetgait had contracts for a year, but now have to leave within a month.

blocks.text: James Elliot, 21, who recently graduated from Dundee university, said he knew people living in Margetgait who had to move out and were “anxious, stressed and shocked”.

“A lot of the students had contracts to stay there next year, but they were just told they had to leave in a month, you need to be out, you need to move your things out.” Students were helped to book alternative accommodation.

Elliot, a housing activist and member of Scotland’s tenants’ and community union Living Rent, added: “Because so many international students were away back home, they couldn’t do that in person. They had all of their belongings there for next year, clothes, pots and pans, everything they needed for uni. So they had to pay a fee for a third party to store their things for them.”

Prestige said the lets in place when Marketgait went into administration included 27 students who had renewed their contracts for the 2026-27 academic year. Of those, 17 had already moved out for the summer. Six others asked Prestige for details of a moving company and paid for it themselves.

A Prestige spokesperson said the decision and subsequent closure was beyond the managing agent’s control. “Our team took immediate action to notify students, help them secure alternative accommodation in Dundee and return all payments made to us. We deeply sympathise with the students affected by the news and will continue to do all we can to support them.”

This is the latest failure in the sector. Amare Students, which ran a 64-room student accommodation block in Birmingham, went into administration in January. Alma Place, a 393-room block in Belfast, was acquired by London-based investors the same month, just over a year after going into receivership.

Several struggling housing providers have sought planning permission to open up their buildings to non-students, including a 91-room block in Coventry that is in receivership. Receivers want to let 50 rooms to city workers instead of students.

Unite Group, the UK’s largest developer and manager of student accommodation, is accelerating a programme of selling off unwanted blocks, with 15,000 to 20,000 beds earmarked for sale, after it slumped to a £418m loss in the first half of the year. Its portfolio will slim down to 55,000-60,000 beds in 20 cities, compared with 29 at present, “to increase alignment to the UK’s strongest universities, where student demand is robust and growing”.

articles.title: The US air force admitted to deploying weapons in space. Don’t expect the White House to explain why
articles.summary:
The revelation ‘left experts scratching their heads at exactly what Donald Trump has in his cosmic arsenal’

In Hollywood at least, space weapons are a relatively simple concept. The good…

blocks.text: In Hollywood at least, space weapons are a relatively simple concept. The good guys, from Captain Kirk and his crew in Star Trek, to Luke Skywalker’s rebel alliance in Star Wars, battle intergalactic villains with an array of colorful lasers and particle-beam cannons, then the bad guys get dispatched in a spectacular, explosive finale.
The messaging coming out of the White House on the subject, by contrast, could not be more vague.

This week’s attention-grabbing revelation by air force secretary Troy Meink – that the US has deployed some kind of weapons in space – carried nothing in the way of context or detail, and left experts scratching their heads at exactly what Donald Trump has in his cosmic arsenal. And, equally importantly, what he intends to do with it.

“You can count the words, and the disclosure, on one hand, so there’s not much there to work with, and we really don’t know what kind of weapons he was talking about,” Clayton Swope, deputy director of the aerospace security project and a senior fellow in the defense and security department at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), said of Meink’s announcement.
“The US is looking for another tool to deter what it sees as concerning Russian and Chinese behaviors in space, so my guess is that revealing it has on-orbit weapons would be your way to do that.

“[But] that level of detail needed to make this disclosure effective as a deterrent isn’t there. It could just be a building block, and the US is going to lay out more later with that. To me that would make logical sense, if that was the plan.”
What the plan actually is has never been made clear, and Meink, in his announcement, stressed it was unlikely ever to be.

“Me talking about the details of what we’re doing would actually not benefit deterrence, so we’re not going to talk about the specifics of what we’re doing, whether we’ve tested it, not tested it, or anything else,” he said.

blocks.caption: A solider during a ceremony for US Air Force airmen transitioning to US Space Force guardian designations at Travis air force base in California on 12 February 2021.  Photograph: Noah Berger/AP

blocks.text: But as Russia and China, both US adversaries, have advanced their own aggressive outer space ambitions and agendas, Trump has responded by placing an ever-increasing focus on militarizing the heavens.

During his first term of office, he created Space Force, the first new, separate branch of the US military in more than seven decades. Last month, he signed an executive order designating the first US Space Academy, a proposed joint civilian-military institution modeled on the army and navy training academies at West Point and Annapolis, to be sited at an as-yet unnamed location.
This week, Military Times reported plans to recruit and train 10,000 new guardians, as Space Force service members are known, to join uniformed ranks within the next five years.

Gen Dan Caine, who as chair of the joint chiefs of staff is the country’s most senior military leader, told the Air, Space and Cyber Conference in Maryland this week, that the armed forces including Space Force must be “prepared to fight, endure and win … from the seabed to cislunar space”.

Added to a number of other maneuvers and bold pronouncements Trump has made concerning space in recent weeks and months, it is hard not to see the space weapons reveal by Meink – who holds a civilian position reporting to the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth – as a further blending of the traditionally separate military and non-military roles of US space policy.

blocks.caption: The chairman of the joint chiefs of staff general, Dan Caine, holds a briefing at the Pentagon on 24 April 2026 on the US-Israel war on Iran. Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/Reuters

blocks.text: In August, the White House unveiled a national space transportation policy that gives Hegseth, as head of the defense department, new responsibility and authority to determine with the chief of Nasa, Jared Isaacman, who manages all US space launches, and sets an ambitious, expansive federal target of more than 1,000 launch and reentry operations by 2030.

The president, meanwhile, has made no secret of his desire for US astronauts to beat China and land on the moon before he leaves office in January 2029; and in March laid out plans, arguably rooted more in optimism than expectation, to invest $20bn (£15bn) on a moonbase to secure for the US the first permanent foothold on the lunar surface.

Some analysts see an almost sea change in the way the Trump administration has approached space in pursuit of its geopolitical goals, compared to previous presidents who upheld decades of separation between the government’s civilian and military needs.

“The way that the US has structured it since Nasa was established in the late 1950s was we have a civil space organization focused on civil exploration, on science, and then we have the Pentagon,” Swope said.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump signs an order to create the US Space Academy as Kevin Hassett, director of the National Economic Council, and Nasa administrator Jared Isaacman watch on 28 August 2026 at Nasa’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas.  Photograph: Karen Warren/AP

blocks.text: He continued: “There seems to be a tendency to pull them together more than we’ve seen in the past [and] the creation of the Space Academy is just another data point that suggests that at least within the eyes of this administration, the missions are very not just complementary, but very, very similar.
“The civilian space agency and Pentagon, [it’s] not just that they complement each other, but that they’re essentially doing the same mission.”

Certainly, Trump has become more visible in space circles since inviting Isaacman, at the second time of asking, to lead Nasa. Seen as an ally of Elon Musk, the billionaire SpaceX chief and former political acolyte of the president, Isaacman has proven a staunch Trump loyalist in social media posts and in public appearances.

It was the “experience of a lifetime”, Isaacman gushed on X, to accompany Trump on Air Force One to the Johnson Space Center in Houston last month, where the academy announcement was staged before rows of Nasa’s civilian astronaut corps bedecked in their blue flight suits.

In a separate, lengthier post, Isaacman defended the need for a space academy with military theming, arguing that US ambitions necessitated “a bright new generation educated and prepared for this environment”.
He wrote: “If you understand the increasingly important and contested environment above us, then [the academy] is as timely and necessary today as the Space Force has already proven to be.”

blocks.caption: Isaacman looks on during an Artemis Accords signing ceremony for Turkey at Nasa headquarters in Washington DC on 31 August 2026. Photograph: Jim Watson/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The argument that the academy blurs the line between peaceful applications in space and the military, he said, “may be the weakest argument I have seen”, before chronicling a succession of previous Nasa missions and operations that were classified and defense department-based, and noting the agency’s early rockets were modified and evolved from military ballistic missiles.

“Nasa’s mission is as peaceful as it is patriotic,” he said. “We explore for the benefit of all humankind, but we go there under our flag. That mission would be impossible without the Guardians standing watch over the domain as we venture outward.”

Lori Garver, a former deputy administrator of Nasa during the Biden administration, said that while she saw the academy as potentially helpful to the US space program and its future workforce, she was concerned it conflated the agency’s mission for peaceful, civil space exploration with Space Force’s military goals.

“Nasa’s charter and legal foundation calls for a civilian agency separate from the military,” she told the science publication Ars Technica. “Structuring a feeder college along the lines of a military academy strikes me as ill-conceived.”

Others say it is difficult, or impossible, for the US to remain committed to the 1967 Outer Space treaty that mandated, among other regulations, that all nations use space for peaceful, non-militarized ends when some countries are blatantly defying it.

US intelligence agencies said in 2024 they were monitoring the development of a new Russian space weapon with the capability of shooting down satellites in Earth’s orbit. Lt Gen Gregory Gagnon, head of the Space Force combat forces command, told reporters at the Maryland conference that China was “actively pursuing activities in the system, in parts of space”, which the country has denied.

A Space Force “threat fact sheet” details how Russia and China are both “testing and fielding sophisticated counterspace capabilities with the intent to disrupt and degrade US space-enabled capabilities”.

So, to Swope, the CSIS analyst who worked for the Central Intelligence Agency’s directorate of science and technology for more than a decade, the US’s declaration that it had deployed space weapons of its own was more significant than the absence of detail.
“It’s this idea of space superiority, ‘I want to use space, I don’t want my adversary to’,” he said. “That’s just where we are today.

“Is more of that happening in space? I don’t think this announcement is determining that, or even accelerating that. It may be more just a recognition that the US has woken up to it, and we may just not know it because it’s not public.”

Another question, he said, is what kind of weapons the US may have. “It has talked previously about systems that operate in the electromagnetic spectrum, for jamming or interference with radio signals, that’s what we know publicly about what is in the US counter-space arsenal,” he said.
“War is really bad whether it is confined to Earth or orbit, and maybe we need to have a better thought not just on how we could limit specific types of weapons, but that we want to avoid generally.
“You can’t just walk into a quote-unquote space war and expect that not to be ugly.”

articles.title: Kevin Warsh may be the adult in the room. But can he calm the US economy?
articles.summary:
Fed chair presided over unanimous decision to raise interest rates despite intense campaign from White House

In the end, Kevin Warsh’s Federal Reserve acquitted itself well. For all the…

blocks.text: In the end, Kevin Warsh’s Federal Reserve acquitted itself well. For all the uncertainty he had sparked at the previous meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee, when he refused to provide any indication of what he was prepared to do to tame stubborn inflation, the chair on Wednesday presided over a unanimous decision to raise interest rates for the first time in three years.

“Today’s action starts to show that we’re serious about this,” he said at the press conference after the meeting, with “this” meaning inflation in excess of the Fed’s 2% target for over five years. Welcome though it was, his embrace of economic orthodoxy nonetheless did little to dispel the Keystone Cops quality of governance in Donald Trump’s US.

Warsh’s resolve – raising rates just a few weeks before elections that will determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress – appeared even more resolute in the face of a veiled threat from White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett, who pointed out to his chums on Fox that “if you want an independent Fed, then one thing the Fed does is it stays out of the way of elections”.

The central bankers’ parsimonious comments in the press conference following the meeting made a sharp contrast with the more unhinged commentary from other members of the administration, including the president himself, who earlier this month celebrated the resilience of the labor market with a mind-boggling threat to “STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT” unless the Fed cut interest rates.

Trump has yet to turn on Warsh in the way he did on his predecessor, Jerome “numbskull” Powell. But the signs are ominous. After the rate hike, Trump went ballistic – spewing more of the random, incoherent thoughts that have become his trademark. “Interest Rates in the United States should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World,” he wrote on social media, despite recalcitrant inflation and a budget deficit that is likely to exceed $2tn this year. He again demanded the powers that be to “LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!”

Yet more significant than the contrast between Warsh’s words and the incongruent economic rhetoric from the White House is the tension between the Fed’s decision on Wednesday and pretty much every other initiative from the administration, from the volley of tariffs against imports from everywhere to the war in Iran to Trump’s “promise” of $5,000 a head if he wins the midterms to treasury secretary Scott Bessent’s desperate efforts to pull interest rates down even as the Fed is raising them.

All things considered, financial markets reacted relatively calmly to the day’s events. For sure, the S&P 500 index took a nosedive on Wednesday afternoon, closing some 0.4% lower at the thought that the Fed would likely now raise rates again in December and twice in 2027. The yield on the 10-year bond rose sharply, again surpassing 5%. But investors appear to have bought – for now at least – that whatever deranged policies may emerge from the rest of the administration, monetary policy will remain comparatively sane.

Investors should probably remain on their toes, though. A rational Trump would probably thank Warsh for his hawkishness. There might be a plausible argument to keep rates where they were because inflation is driven by temporary forces, like a war. Yet had the Fed staid its hand, or – goodness forbid – cut rates as the president has demanded, the bloodbath in the treasury market would have been gruesome, as investors were forced to accept that the chair of the central bank would not stand up to the nut who appointed him.

By contrast, by raising rates and demonstrating he is serious about curbing inflation, the Fed is likely to calm market jitters and reduce long-term inflation expectations, which will ultimately redound in lower yields on treasury bonds, allowing for lower interest rates on mortgages and other long-term loans that matter to businesses and consumers.

More clown cars are likely on the way. In his fury on Wednesday, Trump again threatened to stop trading with countries that have a surplus with the US – a proposition so devoid of sense that it is hard to comprehend, let alone critique. The war in Iran is likely to continue throughout the administration, bringing more volatility to energy markets.

Even Bessent seems to be losing his hold on reality. Vexed over rising treasury yields – which are raising the cost of servicing the government’s Brobdingnagian debts – the man whom markets believed would play the role of adult in the Oval Office on matters of economic policy has started to emulate the desperate government officials he once pummelled into submission.

Bessent built a reputation in financial circles in 1996 as part of the team built by George Soros and Stanley Druckenmiller that pushed the British pound out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism. They made a tidy profit by teaching hapless British ministers that however many pounds they bought to defend the exchange rate, they could never overcome a market determined to sell. Today, Bessent has taken the losing side of that trade, betting that he can buy enough treasuries to bring long-term interest rates down.

The Fed on Wednesday likely helped Bessent’s cause. Still, the peculiar image of a central bank raising interest rates while the treasury secretary resorts to gunslinger tactics to lower them won’t restore trust in the creditworthiness of the United States. (“I am the house,” he proclaimed, hoping to achieve a steely gaze, rhetorically twirling and reholstering his revolver. “You can bet against me if you want.”)
Can an unexpectedly solid Fed chair stabilize the ship of an American economy discombobulated by slapstick policymaking? Here’s hoping. But holding one’s breath may be a bad idea.
Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter Being There on Substack

articles.title: Unease in ‘newly independent’ Piddington as world media and Danny Tommo descend
articles.summary:
As villagers take stock following symbolic vote, some fear far-right weaponisation of asylum dispute and influx of ‘masked people like in Dover’

The first significant event in the newly…

blocks.text: The first significant event in the newly independent principality of Piddington was a decision to select the newt as the national animal, reflecting optimism that the amphibian’s endangered status might help block plans to open a centre for 1,250 asylum seekers on neighbouring land.

The choice was announced on Thursday morning, the day after Piddington announced that villagers had voted overwhelmingly to leave the UK. Parish councillors were also thinking about asking local children to design a flag and considering whether the new principality’s national sport should be cricket or football.

The second noteworthy event was the arrival of Daniel Thomas, who prefers to be called Danny Tommo, the leader of the new balaclava-wearing anti-migrant movement Patriot Platform, with an offer to rally his masked supporters, if the site is opened, “to protect women and children” locally.

By the end of the week, some residents of this pretty Oxfordshire village were still struggling to interpret Tuesday’s symbolic ballot of 358 villagers, and the announcement on Wednesday that Piddington had voted to “secede from the UK and pursue self-determination” by a margin of 285 to 26, in protest at plans to convert a former military base near the village into housing for asylum seekers.

blocks.caption: After expressing unease over the vote on Newsnight, Rachel Marsh, a Piddington resident for 20 years, said she’d received ‘violent threats online from a lot of very toxic keyboard warriors. I’ve never encountered anything like this before.’ Photograph: Alicia Canter/The Guardian

blocks.text: For many, the vote was a demonstration of plucky British eccentricity in the face of adversity, with Ealing comedy Passport to Pimlico vibes. The day after the independence vote there was still a summer fete atmosphere: Battle for Britain bunting was hanging over the doorway to the village hall, “I Am Spartacus” placards stood by the roadside alongside new signs telling drivers that they were entering the Principality of Piddington, “The Village That Roars”. Journalists from Japan, Norway and Ireland arrived, puzzled by the lack of public transport and functional wifi; they scrutinised the community noticeboard in search of clues to explain the village mindset (“Tortoise Found”, “Harvest Coffee Morning”, “Pilates for All Abilities”).

For others, the week’s events have more troubling outcomes. Chef Rachel Marsh, who used to run a livery yard in the village where she has lived for 20 years, was meeting police officers on Friday to discuss her safety. She received death threats and her family was targeted with racist abuse online after she expressed unease in a Newsnight interview that fear was being used as means to “rally and activate people” locally.
The determined jollity of the village independence movement left a sour taste, she said, in the light of the backlash she had received both from local residents and online activists.

“Given that their aim is to protect women and children it is quite ironic that they are using aggression like this towards me for speaking up against racism,” she said. Originally from New Zealand, Marsh has lived in the UK for 40 years; her husband’s parents were Windrush generation arrivals from Jamaica. Messages posted online this week suggested that she and her husband should leave Britain. “We’ve had violent threats online from a lot of very toxic keyboard warriors. I’ve never encountered anything like this before.”

blocks.caption: A sign near the MOD base in Piddington where the government plans to house more than 1,000 asylum seekers. Villagers’ reasons for opposing these plans range from concerns over environmental risks and treatment of asylum seekers to hostility towards immigrants.   Photograph: Alicia Canter/The Guar…

blocks.text: Marsh, like everyone else in Piddington, opposes the government’s asylum housing plan, announced in June. Residents were particularly dismayed at the government’s decision to submit a fast-tracked ‘Urgent Crown Development’ application, designed for projects deemed to be of national importance, allowing ministers to bypass local authority planning processes, as they race to meet a commitment to shut down asylum hotels entirely “in this parliament”.

But village harmony has fractured in places, over disagreements over how best to oppose the decision. Some locals back a Wrong Plan, Wrong Site campaign, primarily focused on the legalities, cost and environmental risks of the proposed housing. Other activists have highlighted the perceived risk to local women of the site. One local, asking not to be named, said the rhetoric in the village had become markedly “more hostile to asylum seekers” over the summer. “The tenor has changed,” he said.

The leader of the parish council, Tim McNally, who led the independence movement, said he was happy that the village had “sent a message to the political jugular”, adding that he was now talking to other village leaders elsewhere in Britain, sharing a blueprint with advice on how to object to unpopular decisions imposed by central government.

In interviews earlier this week he said he would consider renaming the village Trumpington if the Donald Trump agreed to adopt the principality as the 51st US state. Since June he has been filming video appeals for support, speaking direct to the camera as he walks around the village on his @piddingtonroars X account. The campaign has attracted Elon Musk’s attention, prompting the SpaceX CEO to tweet to his 241.6 million followers: “Soon, this will happen to your town”, above a description of the plans for housing for asylum seekers in Oxfordshire. McNally responded: “Thank you, Elon, for helping our little village roar around the world.”

blocks.caption: Local parish councillor Joe Marshall, who said that a meeting was being held with the far-right group Patriot Platform ‘so we can open a dialogue’.  Photograph: Alicia Canter/The Guardian

blocks.text: On Thursday, parish councillor Joe Marshall was cheerful about the ballot result, if still wrestling with the practicalities of independence. The village would continue to view King Charles as their monarch, he said. Councillors were wondering if “someone’s son’s under-11 cricket team” might agree to represent the principality. “Ultimately we’re not going to be culturally any different from Britain,” he said.

He saw nothing problematic about the swift visit from a nationalist activist leader, stressing that all politicians, environmental campaigners and political figures were welcome to visit. “We’ve not written to these people to invite them but with the high profile of what we’re doing right now, these people will want to come. Our responsibility as a parish is to ensure the safety and the security of the village,” he said, adding that a private meeting with Patriot Platform was being held “so we can open dialogue”.

“I assume that their intent is to offer protection, which right now we don’t need because there is no one on this site,” he said. “We’d rather engage with people, walk them around the village, have a cup of tea and a chat, rather than say: ‘We don’t want you here’.” Villagers were disappointed, he said, that there had not been any similar visits from Home Office ministers or government officials. “They haven’t sent a representative even to have a private conversation with the parish council.”

Thomas arrived without an entourage of men in balaclavas on Thursday afternoon. On Friday morning he posted a video of himself outside the gates to the Site A military base, standing outside the village hall, on the village green and interviewing two villagers.

blocks.caption: Robin Smith, who lives near to Piddington, says the asylum seekers who would be housed at the MOD site ‘are humans. This camp is not the right place for them.’ Photograph: Alicia Canter/The Guardian

blocks.text: Robin Smith, who runs an IT consultancy in Bicester, was sorry to have missed him on the whistlestop tour. “I would have liked to have met him and to have heard him explain his manifesto. The people who are coming over are humans. This camp is not the right place for them.” Andrew Smith, a Network Rail employee from Bicester, was less upbeat: “We don’t want to see masked people like there were in Dover – that’s not really the view of the local people; we are concerned to do the right thing. These people have got to go somewhere, but it has to be properly resourced with the proper facilities.”

The Liberal Democrat leader of Oxfordshire County Council, Tim Bearder, said it “was disgraceful the way the far right are weaponising” the dispute. But he was encouraged by a Wednesday evening planning committee meeting, where district council officials were critical of the government’s proposed plans for the new site. “It was considered in 2005 and rejected. There is no electricity, no water, and no footpath. There have been two fatalities on the nearby road. It’s not in the best interests of local residents or the asylum seekers,” he said.

Calum Miller, Lib Dem MP for Bicester and Woodstock, said the interference of external groups was not welcomed by the majority of people in the local area. “The events of this week have shown the power of local opposition to this proposal,” he said. “Local councillors, local people, and a local legal challenge are taking the government to task for this proposal.”

Rachel Marsh was one of the 26 people who opposed the independence vote. “This is just a publicity stunt. It’s complete theatre,” she said. She was uneasy at the arrival of Patriot Platform’s leader in the village. “My feelings about the appropriateness and suitability of Site A are exactly the same as the rest of village – I object, like everyone else – but you don’t need to base objection on a fear-based rhetoric.”

articles.title: Following Carlos Yulo at Asian Games? How to keep track of his scores
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines–Unless you’re a true-blue gymnastics fan, it can be both tedious and puzzling to follow Carlos Yulo as he guns for glory in international tournaments. Here’s how to simplify…

articles.title: Jim Ratcliffe says the UK is a country ‘on the slide’
articles.summary:
Co-owner of Manchester United says Britain is in decline because of high taxes and immigration

The co-owner of Manchester United Sir Jim Ratcliffe has described the UK as being a country “on…

blocks.text: The co-owner of Manchester United Sir Jim Ratcliffe has described the UK as being a country “on the slide” from the days when it had “the greatest empire in the world.”
Ratcliffe, who founded petrochemicals giant Ineos, and has resided in Monaco, which has a relaxed tax regime, since 2020, said Britain is in decline because of high taxes and immigration.

Ratcliffe’s latest attack on the UK comes seven months after he told Sky News that the country was being “colonised by immigrants”. He subsequently said he was sorry if those remarks had “offended some people”.
The billionaire told the BBC’s Big Boss Interview he believed the UK was in decline from the days when, he said, “we were a great people.”

He said: “We had the greatest empire in the world. We were a great people. We won two world wars. We’re good, honest folk. But unfortunately, at the moment, I think the UK is on the slide. It’s quite difficult to see how we arrest it.”
Ratcliffe also said the UK had “a bit of a green eye towards wealth at the moment”, “encouraging” the wealthiest to relocate.
He told the podcast: “In America, they applaud people who create wealth.

“And the good thing about those people who create wealth is that they then spend that wealth in the economy in which they’re resident. And, unfortunately, with the things that they’ve been doing, they’ve been encouraging the people who have created wealth to leave the UK because it’s just become uncomfortable for them for tax reasons or whatever.

While the UK’s tax burden has risen to its highest level since the second world war at about 35.3% of GDP, the Office for Budget Responsibility says it remains well below the average of 14 western European economies.

Ratcliffe has also been at odds with Manchester United fans over the summer after the club embarked on a major ticket-touting crackdown that ultimately revoked 685 season tickets, prompting protests from United supporter groups like the 1958.
The businessman was already fiercely unpopular among the Old Trafford faithful, ever since he decided to hike ticket prices and sack 450 club employees.

The billionaire also took aim at the government’s decision not to invest further in North Sea resources by granting licences for the Jackdaw and Rosebank oil and gasfields, which he said amounted to “insanity”, and warned the UK’s reliance on energy imports meant the country could “run out of gas” if there was a cold spell this winter.
after newsletter promotion

He said: “The risk you’ve got this winter is that we run out of gas. If we have a really sharp cold spell, then there is conceivably the possibility that we’ll run out of gas and have to switch the industry off.”
In response to the billionaire’s criticism, the government said it was working to deliver growth and that business investment had increased in the last two years.
A spokesperson told the BBC that they did not foresee any problems with gas supply: “We have a diverse energy mix and are confident in our security of supply.”
Asked if he was planning on returning to the UK, Ratcliffe said: “Not at the moment, no. I don’t see growth being tackled.
“Two things: we need politicians who are tough enough to deal with some very difficult problems, and we know what the problems are.
“And we need politicians who will make decisions which are good for the country, not good for themselves and their party. And we haven’t had one of those for a long time.”

articles.title: Hundreds evacuated after fire breaks out at seaside hotel in Kent
articles.summary:
Emergency services called to Grand Burstin hotel in Folkestone, where a fire is believed to have started in the basement

Hundreds of people have been evacuated from a hotel in Folkestone…

blocks.text: Hundreds of people have been evacuated from a hotel in Folkestone after a large fire broke out overnight.

Just after 1am on Saturday, emergency services were called to the Grand Burstin hotel in The Harbour, Folkestone, where a fire is believed to have started in the basement, Kent fire and rescue service said.

About 280 people were taken to safety and a welfare centre was set up by Folkestone and Hythe district council. No injuries relating to the fire have been reported and the cause of the blaze is not yet known.
The fire caused 26 fire engines to be dispatched to the seafront hotel, the fire service said. According to the Britannia hotels website, the hotel overlooks Folkestone’s harbour and has 550 rooms.
Folkestone and Hythe district council posted on X, saying: “A fire is currently ongoing at the Folkestone Grand Burstin hotel.
“We are operating a welfare centre at Three Hills Sports Park for people being evacuated from the site, where we are providing support to those affected.
“We are supporting all emergency services involved in the response and their efforts to get people to safety.

“Our advice to residents living nearby is to: close all windows and doors; avoid the area and do not attempt to approach the hotel; follow the instructions of emergency services; keep roads clear to allow emergency vehicles to access the area”.
Kent fire and rescue service said in an update: “Ten fire engines remain at the scene of a fire at the Grand Burstin hotel in The Harbour, Folkestone.
“Crews wearing breathing apparatus have worked hard to bring the fire under control and are now dampening down any remaining hotspots.
“It’s believed the fire started in the basement of the property, but the cause is not yet known.
“Around 280 people evacuated the building, and a welfare centre has been organised by Folkestone and Hythe district council. No fire-related injuries have been reported.
A spokesperson for Kent police said: “Kent police was called at around 1.20am on Saturday 19 September 2026 to reports of a fire at a hotel on Marine Parade, Folkestone.
“Officers remain in attendance to assist traffic flow while our Kent fire and rescue service colleagues work to tackle the fire.”

articles.title: Millions without power as Cuba hit by latest major blackout
articles.summary: Widespread power outages have become increasingly common due to fuel shortages made worse by a US blockade.

blocks.text: Millions in Cuba were left without power on Friday as the country was plunged into yet another major blackout.
The country's entire electricity grid suffered "total disconnection" that triggered a nationwide outage, Cuba's energy ministry said.
Power was restored to some priority areas by late evening, including those near hospitals and water pumping stations in the capital Havana, grid operator UNE said.

It is at least the sixth partial or total blackout to hit Cuba this year, where ageing electricity infrastructure and chronic fuel shortages have been placed under further strain by a US blockade on oil shipments to the communist-run nation.
UNE said the outage started just before 14:00 local time on Friday (18:00 GMT) due to a transmission fault coupled with poor weather conditions in central Cuba.
Protocols to begin the "gradual restoration" of power were activated, the operator's national load dispatch director Felix Estrada said, with the process ongoing on Saturday.
Cuba relies heavily on fuel imports, meaning tight US sanctions and an oil blockade since the start of the year have exacerbated existing shortages.
Food and medicine have also become more scarce, with hospitals struggling to function normally and schools and government offices having to close.
"Lately, it's becoming a habit," Havana resident Frank Lorenzo told news agency Reuters on Friday.
"Before it happened less frequently - once a month… just yesterday we were 24 hours without electricity, they turned it on for just an hour and it went down again."
"It's one thing after another: no water, no gas for cooking, no electricity," 36-year-old schoolteacher Lidia Fernandez told news agency AFP. "Honestly, I don't know how we haven't gone crazy."
Francisco Rodriguez, 78, said his home had already gone without power for 28 hours on Friday and feared he would not have light "for several days".
The repeated blackouts have prompted rare protests in Cuba, where unauthorised demonstrations are illegal and those who defy the ban risk being jailed.

Havana has blamed its fuel crisis on the Trump administration and denounced all of its sanctions - including a new round announced in August - which are part of a wider pressure campaign against the Caribbean island's leadership.

Cuba's regional ally Venezuela was believed to have sent it around 35,000 barrels of oil a day - about half of its oil needs - until Venezuela's own supplies were cut off following the US seizure of its President Nicolás Maduro in January.
US President Donald Trump has threatened tariffs on countries shipping oil to Havana, and a number of such shipments have been seized by the US.

Washington meanwhile attributes Cuba's energy crisis to poor internal management and has accused it of posing a "national security threat". Trump has openly discussed toppling its leadership, including threatening a "friendly takeover" in March this year.

articles.title: Boying Remulla eyes revival of investment ombudsman
articles.summary: Ombudsman Jesus Crispin "Boying" Remulla said Saturday his office was planning to establish an investment ombudsman tasked to address concerns of business leaders.

blocks.text: Published September 19, 2026 6:02pm
Ombudsman Jesus Crispin "Boying" Remulla said Saturday his office was planning to establish an investment ombudsman tasked to address concerns of business leaders.
Speaking on his weekly radio program, Remulla discussed with his co-hosts the various ways how government processes burden different stakeholders.
The discussion raised that many business leaders and groups were hesitant to invest because of political instability—so whatever businesses are already operating should have fewer requirements.
Remulla called for the lessening the requirements for businesses, saying this may lead to more jobs for Filipinos.
"Magtatayo kami ng… investment ombudsman (We will establish an investment ombudsman)," Remulla said on radio station dzRH.
With such a government position in place, entrepreneurs would be able to go to the investment ombudsman if they have complaints at the barangay level or higher.
The investment ombudsman is an old post, with multiple administrations attempting to revive the post to curb corruption in the procurement of business permits from the government.
In 2007, then-Trade secretary Peter Favila attempted to place an investment ombudsman within the Department of Trade and Industry.
Remulla said efforts were already underway to hire more lawyers for the effort.
"We're hiring 61 more lawyers ngayon hanggang December, then next year, we will hire 100 or 200 more," Remulla said.
(We're hiring 61 more lawyers now until December, then next year, we will hire 100 or 200 more.)
Remulla admitted that there were issues with agencies such as the Anti-Red Tape Authority and the Philippine Competition Commission, but did not elaborate. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Trump ally Stephen Miller leads sweeping push to accelerate removal of migrant children
articles.summary:
Exclusive: key White House loyalist orchestrating multi-agency effort condemned by critics as cruel and racist

Stephen Miller is leading an unprecedented and intense White House drive across…

blocks.text: Stephen Miller is leading an unprecedented and intense White House drive across a host of government departments to accelerate the removal of undocumented immigrant children from the US, using tactics that critics say are cruel and racist and, in some cases, flout federal law, the Guardian has learned.
As deputy chief of staff at the White House, focused on immigration policy, Miller is seen as the mastermind and enforcer behind Donald Trump’s hardline anti-immigration agenda.

He is directing a whole-of-government approach that has been ramping up throughout Trump’s second term and is targeting a vulnerable population of undocumented children. Many abruptly find themselves denied access to legal immigration pathways in the US, with their applications fast-tracked and then rejected before being forced out of the country.

Almost 200,000 children have been ordered removed from the US by immigration judges since Trump returned to the White House, a doubling of such court orders since January 2025, according to analysis of data from the Department of Justice’s executive office for immigration review (EOIR) conducted by the California-based advocacy Mobile Pathways and shared with the Guardian. The advocacy group has focused its numbers on children appearing in immigration court, regardless of whether they arrived in the US alone or with family, and believes the total to be an undercount.

Miller has harnessed personnel and power for his task from at least five cabinet-level government departments, as described to the Guardian by several sources briefed on various initiatives, many of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation. The departments include Health and Human Services (HHS), which oversees the care of migrant children who are in the country without a parent or guardian; the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), where Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) are based; and the Department of Justice (DoJ), which houses the immigration courts – with the state department and the Department of Defense playing more subsidiary roles.

blocks.caption: The six-year-old son of a pregnant woman in Denver whose family was planning to return to Venezuela. The boy’s father was deported earlier. Photograph: RJ Sangosti/MediaNews Group/The Denver Post/Denver Post/Getty Images

blocks.text: Miller frequently confers with subordinates, daily at times, pressing them to maximize removals of immigrant children from the US, according to a number of sources familiar with the White House plans.

“The folks that have to do the implementation are told, ‘These instructions came directly from the White House,’ or ‘These instructions came directly from Stephen Miller,’ as a way of conveying, you know, the importance of implementing them in a timely fashion and doing it in the way that they were instructed to do it,” one source said.

Sources warned of the White House pushing each department to boost efforts individually and by working together in new ways to speed up and expand the deportation of undocumented children – especially by dismantling inter-agency communication safeguards designed to protect children, and hurrying them in vast numbers, without lawyers, in front of asylum officers and immigration judges who are either inclined or are under pressure to take a hard line and get them out of the US.
All departments involved, and the White House, were sent questions and asked for comment.
The White House did not deny that Miller is orchestrating a multi-agency effort to speed up the removal of undocumented children but claimed the effort was not new.
However, the White House and some other agencies that responded framed their endeavors as an anti-trafficking initiative instead of a means to enforcement.

“The Department of Homeland Security, the US Department of Health and Human Services, and the Homeland Security Council are working to locate and rescue these children. We are ensuring these children are reunited with their parents and families in their home countries,” said White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis.
The Homeland Security Council is a body which, under Trump, now answers directly to him within the executive office of the president of the United States and is led by Miller.

blocks.caption: Children arrive at Miami airport as they prepare to reunite with their recently deported parents in Guatemala. Photograph: Chandan Khanna/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: But there is no certainty that deported young people end up reunited with family and safe in their home countries, as many of them left in the first place because of threats to their wellbeing, including from their own family, or in order to reunite with parents in the US.

One source said: “This administration has shown time and again that it has no plan for children other than to disrupt their lives and endanger them … they have no credibility to claim that they are acting with children’s safety as their priority.”

Claire Trickler-McNulty, an immigration policy fellow at Hyphen, a nonprofit intermediary focused on racial equity, said: “A facade of trafficking is sort of a convenient, feel-good cover that has nothing to do with trafficking and everything to do with reducing the program [of federal care for undocumented children], getting rid of services, getting rid of things they don’t like, and then removing kids.” Trickler-McNulty was previously an assistant director at ICE and a senior counselor at USCIS during the Biden administration.

Another source said of the Trump administration: “They are weaponizing that narrative [trafficking] because it makes them out to be the good guys, and everything else makes it really clear that they’re not.”

Critics point out that while there are some genuine instances of exploitation within the US that were exposed during the Biden administration, including by the New York Times, the Trump administration and and other rightwing politicians and commentators are using extreme, and relatively rare, examples to justify their drastic intervention.

The sweeping inter-agency effort has also left more than 1,800 undocumented immigrant children stuck in the custody of federal health officials after often having previously experienced abuse, neglect, abandonment, trafficking or other harm in their countries of origin or on the way to the US. Sources believe many of those officials are collaborating with immigration enforcers while sharing children’s confidential files in an unparalleled and legally dubious dismantling of bureaucratic safety firewalls.

One consequence of this strand of the anti-immigration crackdown is the sharp acceleration in the DoJ’s immigration court orders to remove children from the US issued under the second Trump administration. This includes a rapid increase over this spring and summer. Removal orders rose from 7,366 a month in January 2025 to 16,200 in June, 16,750 in July and 14,744 in August, according to Mobile Pathways’ research.

Of the more than 200,000 children in total that have been ordered removed under the second Trump administration, 70% were under the age of 13. The percentage of hearings ending in a removal order also more than doubled over the 20 months.
“What is my biggest fear? A lot of it is [already] happening,” Trickler-McNulty said.

She is concerned by the administration gutting legal services and due process for children, closing down higher quality facilities, and having ICE officials take on senior roles in immigrant child welfare at HHS’s office of refugee resettlement (ORR).
“Stephen Miller is incredibly involved in the whole immigration side, he has his daily calls, he reaches down into the agencies,” she said.

Many unaccompanied children are facing the prospect of a forced return to dangerous situations in their countries of origin, particularly in Central America, including Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador, or even places as unstable as Afghanistan. Many have relatives in the US whom they could live with, who are vetted by the government and are known as sponsors. But the second Trump administration has severely restricted this from happening, either through new bureaucratic methods that keep children in custody until they can be deported, or by making prospective sponsors too scared of ICE to come forward.

Adults and families embroiled in the immigration system are subject to potential detention by DHS, while unaccompanied children are supposed to be quickly transferred from that department’s agencies into the custody of ORR.
This divide is by congressional design, in recognition that children in the country alone should not rely for care on the same agency that is trying to deport them, experts said.
Yet as in other policy areas, this White House is prepared to break norms.

blocks.caption: Viviana with her daughter Denise, three, at home in Arlington, Virginia. Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty Images

blocks.text: “The Trump administration has sacrificed every element of ORR’s child welfare mission on the altar of higher deportation numbers,” US senator Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, told the Guardian. “Instead of protecting kids from human trafficking or helping them reunite with family, Trump and officials at HHS and DHS are violating children’s rights [and] flouting federal law to hit quotas and satisfy their ideological crusade against immigrants. The result is significant harm and trauma to innocent children.”

ORR is responsible for providing the children with a safe place to live while ensuring they have access to legal information and thoroughly vetting their potential sponsors, usually family members, who apply for their release – serving a child welfare role that has historically been separate and apart from the nation’s immigration enforcement arm.
Yet “there was a rollback of that really important firewall, and there was a lot more information sharing” that kicked off in Trump’s second term, one source told the Guardian.

“It’s clear from who leadership is and Miller’s influence and the power dynamics of this administration that, you know, if DHS wants access to a child, they’re going to get access to a child,” another source said. “If ICE wants access to literally every single child’s identifiable information, mental health records, behavioral records, all of that, they have it. I mean, it’s not about sharing at this point. They just have access to it.”

blocks.caption: A woman and her child arrive at an immigration hearing in New York last year. Photograph: Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Half a dozen experts and government staff have detailed, as one put it, “an unprecedented level of collaboration between agencies like USCIS, ORR and ICE and the immigration courts”.

Two sources described being briefed on the White House putting together a group of officials, known as “a tiger team” in government parlance, to coordinate policy around unaccompanied children, involving DHS, ORR, the DoJ and the state department.

The result is “coercive measure after coercive measure in trying to get kids to relinquish their rights”. Experts interviewed for this article describe many measures and the extent to which they required inter-agency collaboration which have not been previously reported, including:

items: An influx of immigration and criminal enforcement officials joining ORR in key roles, with the likely effect of shifting the agency’s priorities further away from child welfare and toward mass deportations, given the expertise and point of view of its new leadership and their known closeness with Miller.

ORR having ICE officers present – and sometimes waiting to detain people – at new in-person appointments that are now part of the sponsorship process, and the two agencies appearing to share information so that prospective sponsors are detained just before or shortly after a child is set to be released from federal custody, which critics believe is not a coincidence.

ORR seemingly collaborating with USCIS to schedule and rush through asylum adjudications for the children in their custody, sometimes through unorthodox, virtual interviews, not giving the children enough time to truly prepare or consult with attorneys.

ORR receiving feedback from the White House that its policy ideas were not sufficiently punitive and Miller forcing the agency to implement new tactics with the express purpose of increasing deportations among children and their family members.

Immigration judges allegedly being told by supervisors to rubber-stamp some of the requests by ICE’s attorneys who are arguing to deport immigrants – including these children – in court, with the White House watching closely.
State department officials warning some countries of origin to expect increases in deported minors.
The Pentagon being asked by HHS to supply forensic auditors to scour for fraud among legal services organizations representing the children.

blocks.text: In a particularly dramatic case that a source suspects of involving inter-agency collusion, enforcement agents located and detained a small child’s parent just one day before the child was going to be released from ORR custody and reunited with the parent.

Then, the source said, USCIS quickly asked the child’s attorneys if they wanted to withdraw their client’s asylum application – given that the child no longer had a relative available to care for them.
If it was, indeed, a tactic, it was successful: that family agreed to be deported so they could finally be together and free again.
Sources said that federal rules prohibit ORR from sharing children’s welfare files with ICE and this wall had typically been effective but now was being routinely disregarded.

“They’re taking norms that no-one ever thought needed to be legislated … because there was at least a general understanding of how harmful it would be if they were undone. And this administration just doesn’t care about harm, right? The cruelty is the intent of this,” a source said.

A state department spokesperson said: “The United States expects every country to accept the return of its nationals expeditiously. The state department leads diplomatic efforts to ensure compliance with this basic responsibility.”

These practices are being implemented in tandem with other policies that are keeping children in foster homes, shelters or even secure lockups, away from family, for very long periods, where many lose hope and choose to self-deport. Hundreds of undocumented children are currently being sent to Texas, where it is easier to deport them.

Federal officials have also defunded over 20,000 unaccompanied children’s attorneys from nearly a hundred legal services organizations across the country, while approaching firms and anti-trafficking organizations with little immigration law experience but with ties to the administration or ICE to replace them.

Meanwhile, in a message shared with the Guardian, a Department of Defense (DoD) personnel manager sent out a recruiting request saying that the health department was urgently looking for lawyers to represent the children, seemingly from within DoD itself, which manages the nation’s military. The message encouraged recipients to pursue an encore career in government and continue serving their country, touting an expedited hiring process, a $10,000 signing bonus and a competitive benefits package.

blocks.caption: A child sits in the back of a border patrol vehicle after being apprehended by US agents in Arizona. Photograph: Brandon Bell/Getty Images

blocks.text: The message is unusual because it indicated the involvement of the Pentagon in child welfare and immigration matters, and its apparent attempt to recruit military personnel who may have only the most rudimentary understanding of immigration law and little training in trauma-informed legal representation.
“HHS considered recruiting and detailing military lawyers for temporary augmentation of capacity but is no longer pursuing this option,” an unnamed HHS spokesperson told the Guardian in a statement.
The Department of Defense referred questions to the White House and HHS.

“The erosion of due process, the dramatic attacks on both immigration courts and legal service providers, all of these feel like they are tools that are part of this larger project of essentially deporting these children by any means necessary,” said Azadeh Erfani, director of policy at the National Immigrant Justice Center (NIJC).

For some experts, Miller’s widely recognized leadership of the inter-agency effort is itself concerning because of his engagement with of white nationalist ideology. Miller’s rhetoric frequently echoes the “great replacement theory”, a racist notion that nonwhite immigrants will overrun western civilization.
For his part, Trump has said that immigrants in the US from around the world are “poisoning the blood of our country” – a line that drew comparisons to Nazism.
“There is little doubt that Stephen Miller’s influence on these anti-children policies comes with racial bias,” said Erfani.

Another source added: “There’s some real animus towards the kids coming from Miller and his acolytes. And I think that it’s also very connected to the same reason that he wants to get rid of birthright citizenship. It’s about demographics, right? And he sees the kids as, like, the future generation that will, you know, continue a multiracial, multicultural vision of this country.”

Miller’s departmental subordinates include a number of immigration enforcement veterans who have switched from ICE to immigrant child welfare in the health department, including Angie Salazar, now the acting director of ORR, John Fabbricatore, now a senior advisor at HHS, and Dawnisha Helland, the assistant principal deputy director of the unaccompanied alien children bureau at ORR.
Their roles at HHS give ICE a potential communication channel on issues involving unaccompanied children. “All these folks used to work together,” one source said.

The Trump administration repeatedly argues that its custody and enforcement policies for unaccompanied children protect them from trafficking and being taken in by relatives who pose as safe and loving while preying on or exploiting them.

“ORR is not involved in the enforcement of immigration law or in the removal process. ORR is, however, involved in an inter-agency effort to locate children that arrived at the border alone during the Biden administration, and who were then release[d] to poorly vetted sponsors. In some cases, these sponsors exploited the unaccompanied children in their care, including through trafficking,” the unnamed HHS spokesperson told the Guardian.

DHS echoed that sentiment, saying that its officials were dedicated to locating children “who came across the border unaccompanied [and] were placed with unvetted sponsors who were actually smugglers and sex traffickers”.
But critics reiterated their argument that this perspective is exaggerated to the point of being disingenuous.

At the same time, the administration has implemented changes to reporting child trafficking concerns that could make it harder for survivors to win asylum and other immigration relief, the Associated Press reported.

Meanwhile, one expert told the Guardian that they did not know how officials at ORR could ever again reassure a prospective sponsor that it was safe to apply for a child’s release, or tell a child that they were protected, with this administration’s track record.

That expert fears that families across the globe whose children are fleeing gang conscription, violence and persecution will no longer look to the US for survival. They will be too afraid of the chances of a child being swiftly detained and deported even in the typical case where the child aims to join other family members living and working in the US.
“If you’re that family and you have no option for your child to be safe except sending them to the United States, now that is off the table,” the source said. “And so what happens to those kids?”
Will Craft and Andrew Witherspoon contributed reporting and graphics

articles.title: Oktoberfest 2026: Everything you need to know
articles.summary: This year, AI will be used to manage overcrowded situations. Find all the numbers surrounding the fest — including the price of water!

image.caption: Oktoberfest attracts millions of visitors every yearImage: Wolfgang Maria Weber/IMAGO

blocks.text: On Saturday, September 19, at noon, Oktoberfest will once again open with the ceremonial tapping of the keg, during which the mayor of Munich drives a tap into the first wooden barrel of beer and calls out "O'zapft is," a Bavarian phrase that translates to "It's tapped."
His call will be followed by 12 gunshots, a signal that lets all festival tents know that they can start serving beer.
More than 6 million people are expected at the world's largest Volksfest, which runs this year through October 4.
Oktoberfest: What to know about 'the best party in Germany'
Expanded security measures to prevent overcrowding
The festival grounds are enormous: Oktoberfest takes place on Munich's Theresienwiese, a 34.5-hectare site roughly the size of 48 soccer fields.
But crowds can swell, especially on weekends — sometimes to dangerous levels.
Last year, officials had to temporarily close the entrances.

One reason is that nearly all 38 beer tents operate in two or three reservation shifts. When one group of guests leaves and the next arrives at the 14 large tents — which each accommodate several thousand people — huge numbers of visitors end up trying to enter and exit at the same time.
That's how, on one Saturday afternoon at last year's Oktoberfest, the crowds became so dense that movement temporarily came to a standstill. The crush caused some visitors to panic.
To prevent that from happening again, the city of Munich has overhauled its security plan for this year's festival.
Twenty-six new cameras, in addition to 56 police cameras, will monitor the grounds, while an AI system will analyze visitor flows and issue alerts if areas become overcrowded.

blocks.caption: Around 300,000 people were at Oktoberfest simultaneously on the second Saturday of the festival in 2025Image: Frank Hoermann/SVEN SIMON/picture alliance

blocks.text: A newly established coordination center is also intended to improve communication between security agencies and event organizers.
Organizers and police have drawn up a plan to defend against drones over the grounds, though no details have been disclosed.
In addition, 600 police officers will be deployed on site.
Oktoberfest is famous worldwide, but most visitors are local
Oktoberfest may be known around the world as an international tourist attraction, but most of its visitors don't travel very far to get there.
A study commissioned by the city of Munich last year found that the festival remains overwhelmingly regional.

blocks.caption: Statistically speaking, two international guests sit at every 10-person table in the festival tentsImage: Maryam Majd/REUTERS

blocks.text: In 2025, 41% of visitors came from Munich, another 25% from the surrounding area and 9% from elsewhere in the region. In all, three-quarters of Oktoberfest's roughly 6.5 million visitors came from Bavaria. Another 4% came from elsewhere in Germany.

About 21% of visitors — roughly 1.35 million people — traveled from abroad. Americans made up the largest group of international visitors, accounting for just under 20% of the total, or more than 270,000 people. Italians were next, at just over 13%.
Beer prices rise again
Cannabis is banned throughout the festival grounds.

Alcohol, on the other hand, is available in whatever quantities visitors are willing — and able — to pay for. A Mass, the traditional 1-liter mug of beer served at Oktoberfest, costs between €14.80 and €15.90 ($17-$18.25) this year, only slightly more than last year.
A liter of table water comes in at a hefty €11, although the grounds also have several free drinking water fountains.
Visitors planning to enjoy one of Oktoberfest's many rides would be wise to stay relatively sober. Tickets cost anywhere from just under €5 to €14.

Germany's traditional fairground culture was officially added to the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2026, and that tradition remains very much alive at the 191st Oktoberfest. According to organizers, about 90% of the festival's more than 130 fairground operators can trace their roots back to the 19th century.
The festival remains decidedly traditional when it comes to payment, too: Many vendors still accept cash only. Visitors caught without any can withdraw money from ATMs on the grounds.
Dirndl or lederhosen for Oktoberfest?
Then there's the question of what to wear.
Bavarians who take pride in doing things properly generally show up in local traditional dress.

blocks.caption: Traditional garb can be seen at the annual breweries' paradeImage: Felix Hörhager/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The dirndl is the traditional dress worn by women and girls, which consists of close-fitting bodice with a low neckline, a blouse worn under the bodice, a wide high-waisted skirt and an apron.
Men wear lederhosen, the traditional leather shorts or knee-length breeches with suspenders.

For those who are not Bavarian, lederhosen and dirndls are certainly an option, but they're by no means required. Munich's event marketing department, Simply Munich, advises first-time visitors to consider renting traditional garb rather than buying it.

Be aware that locals find cheap imitations of traditional dress off-putting, as Simply Munich points out: "If you want to avoid wry looks, steer clear of Seppl hats, 'leather pants' made of cloth and garish mini plastic dirndls. With jeans and a checkered shirt, you'll definitely be more suitably dressed."
This article was originally written in German.
