articles.title: Russia votes for new parliament in controlled elections
articles.summary: Russia is holding its first State Duma election since invading Ukraine, with voting also imposed in occupied Ukrainian regions. President Vladimir Putin's party is expected to dominate the tightly…

image.caption: The three-day election ends on Sunday eveningImage: Tatiana Meel/REUTERS

blocks.text: Russians were casting their ballots on Saturday to elect a new lower house of parliament, on the second day of a round of voting that President Vladimir Putin's party is all but guaranteed to win.
It is Russia's first parliamentary election since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Parties that support Putin's war in Ukraine are the only ones registered to run, and the opposition is barred from taking part.

blocks.caption: Russia's opposition party, Yabloko, was struck from the party list last monthImage: Pavel Bednyakov/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Despite expectations of an easy win for Putin, the elections are widely being viewed as a referendum on the continuation of his military campaign — now in its fifth year.

The polls are taking place at a time when public sentiment is starting to shift against the war over rising prices, internet crackdowns, fuel shortages and rumors of another mobilization drive following the elections.
More than 110 million Russians are eligible to vote for 450 members of the lower house of the Russian Parliament, known as the State Duma.
Putin's United Russia party currently controls over two-thirds of the seats and is expected to retain its dominance, allowing it to continue the military campaign despite ebbing public support.
Voting held in occupied Ukrainian regions
For the first time in a Russian parliamentary election, Moscow is conducting voting in occupied parts of the Ukrainian regions of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson.
Russia claimed to annex the four regions in September 2022, although it does not fully control any of them. The annexations are not internationally recognized.

Russian authorities say the occupied territories have more than 3.5 million eligible voters. Balloting began there and in some Russian border areas in late August, earlier than elsewhere, with officials citing security concerns.

blocks.caption: Ukraine has strongly condemned the voting in occupied eastern areasImage: Dmitry Yagodkin/TASS/picture alliance

blocks.text: Footage from a polling station in occupied Donetsk showed voters casting ballots while an armed Russian soldier stood nearby.
Ukrainian officials condemned the voting as illegal and urged foreign governments and international organizations not to recognize either the election or its results.
Kyiv also warned that helping organize the vote could result in criminal prosecution.

articles.title: Lacson flags Laguna Lake 'encroachment'; Cayetano slams 'malicious' intent
articles.summary: Senator Panfilo Lacson on Saturday flagged 170 hectares of alleged "unauthorized encroachment" in Laguna Lake in Taguig City, even as Senator Alan Peter Cayetano called out the former for selectively…

blocks.text: Published September 19, 2026 3:03pm

Senator Panfilo Lacson on Saturday flagged 170 hectares of alleged "unauthorized encroachment" in Laguna Lake in Taguig City, even as Senator Alan Peter Cayetano called out the former for selectively scrutinizing his political bailiwick.
In a statement, Lacson said Philippine Reclamation Authority (PRA) data showed the alleged encroachment in at least 13 titles covering the sprawling areas.

"There are titled areas that are still water. When the PRA vetted them using digital and satellite maps, they found the titles covered even water. These are 13 titles covering an area of 170 hectares on the Taguig side of Laguna Lake," Lacson said in a radio interview.

Lacson said this accounted for one-third of the 560 hectares of reclaimed land covering parts of Laguna Lake in Rizal and Laguna. He said he would continue to help the Office of the Ombudsman and other agencies to get to the bottom of the matter.
Lacson did not name Cayetano in his statement on Saturday, but has been trading barbs with him since July over alleged corruption involving infrastructure projects in the city.
'Pagtutok' sa Taguig
Meanwhile, at about the same time that Lacson released the statement to the media, Cayetano started a Facebook Live stream showing that he was at Laguna Lake.
He said he was engaging in an activity with children, but did not disclose what the activity was.
During the live stream, Cayetano slammed Lacson for what he claimed to be selective justice.

"So sabi ko, kung gaano kapino ang pagtutok niya sa siyudad ng Taguig na kung saan nagwo-work 'yung flood control, na kung saan, walang ghost, na kung saan napakaganda ng lakeshore at model sa buong Laguna Lake pero pine-paint niya in a very malicious way," Cayetano said.

(I said, if he is going to be so critical about the city of Taguig where the flood control works, where there is no ghost, where the lakeshore and model of the whole Laguna Lake is good, but he paints it in a malicious way.)

"Sabi ko for the sake of argument isantabi natin 'yan. Mayroon bang mga ibang lugar sa buong Pilipinas, mayroon nga iba napatunayan na may ghost pero tahimik walang investigation? So, ano po ang sagot nila? Sagot nila hindi dapat Taguig, hindi dapat kay Alan, hindi dapat ang mga Cayetano managot," Cayetano added.

(I said for the sake of argument, let us set that aside. Are there other places in the whole Philippines that were proven to have ghost projects, but this done quietly and without any investigation? What is their answer? They say that it should just be Taguig, it should just be Alan, it should just be the Cayetanos who are accountable.)
GMA News Online has also reached out to Cayetano's office for a response to Lacson's claims of alleged encroachment in Taguig, but it has yet to respond as of posting time. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: How Ubisoft Philippines helps bring game worlds to life
articles.summary: In helping build a blockbuster game like ’Assassins Creed Black Flag Resynced,’ Ubisoft brings the skills of talented Filipinos to the forefront

blocks.text: UBISOFT PHILIPPINES. The signage of Ubisoft Philippines in their Taguig studio.
Victor Barreiro Jr./Rappler
In helping build a blockbuster game like ’Assassins Creed Black Flag Resynced,’ Ubisoft brings the skills of talented Filipinos to the forefront

items: Ubisoft Philippines celebrated its 10th anniversary with a studio tour showcasing their contributions to 'Assassins Creed Black Flag Resynced'.
The Philippine team emphasized their pride in updating game mechanics and enhancing art assets while maintaining the game's original structure.
Studio leaders discussed the role of AI in game development, highlighting its potential as a tool for efficiency while stressing the importance of human creativity and teamwork.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Ubisoft Philippines celebrated its 10th year in the country by inviting members of the media and industry advocates to their office in Taguig for a tour of the studio on September 10.

The tour focused on introducing the office to newcomers like mysefl as well as imparting the contributions the Philippine studio made to Ubisoft’s latest blockbuster release, Assassins Creed Black Flag Resynced.

blocks.caption: UBISOFT PHILIPPINES. The front of office at Ubisoft Philippines.

blocks.text: Through the tour and a subsequent interview with studio manager Sashi Menon and studio art director JP Tan, I found myself enamored with the earnest pride the Philippine team had in their work.

Assassins Creed Black Flag Resynced is a modernized take on the 13-year-old Assassins Creed Black Flag, so its overall structure existed long before the creation of the Philippine studio. But it’s what comes from the Philippine side that makes it magical.

It’s taking the nuts and bolts of the older game and working on updating game mechanics like harpooning, improving on existing art assets like the weapons and clothing, rebuilding and reimagining the game world’s towns and forts, and ensuring the game world’s audio brings life and vibrance to the proceedings.

blocks.caption: HARPOONING MECHANICS. A Ubisoft programmer explains what they’ve done with harpooning in ‘Assassins Creed Black Flag Resynced’

blocks.text: My attention was drawn to watching the visuals through recorded gameplay and watching other members of the media try out the game, but it was in the studio tour where I felt that sense of pride coming through.
The team members in charge of specific aspects of the game themselves were on point, delivering presentations on what their teams were in charge of.
While some were nervous, they were still eager to put their best foot forward in showing off what they had achieved.

During my interview with Menon and Tan, I was curious about whether artificial intelligence (AI) plays a role now in helping to develop games, whether it’s in doing specific work or in adjusting workflow processes to help them do certain aspects at scale.

Tan said the game industry is in a kind of “figuring out stage” when it comes to using AI. He added that they were experimenting on use cases for AI but there hasn’t been anything yet that has grown into fruition.

blocks.caption: WORLD PRESENCE. Ubisoft Philippines is one of a number of studios the company has internationally.

blocks.text: When it comes to art, for example, Tan said, “We highly prioritize the skill of our artists, so that’s the most important thing. Being an art director, I am always on the lookout of developing the fundamental skills of each artist and their expression.”

“On the other hand,” Tan added, “it’s hard to ignore the benefits or the potential of AI-assisted workflows. Meaning any of the work, sometimes the tedious work, or the manual work that takes away from the creativity of things, that’s what we are on the lookout for.”

Menon added that AI use can and does happen but primarily as a tool to defeat busywork that eats up time. This could include helping in speeding up research by scraping the internet for needed information, but “the work remains the same” in that the human touch is needed.
Menon also said unlike some companies that use generative AI to ostensibly do everything, “we don’t see value in that.”

Tan, in closing remarks, noted that AI is “a tool meant to be understood and harnessed.” The realities of game development — and of artificial intelligence in the workplace — require human understanding.
“The future is coming fast, and it’s scary, but also at the same time, we need to keep our feet on the ground and teach the right values to our teams,” Tan said.

“Game development is essentially a problem-solving endeavor. It is essentially solving multiple constraints happening at the same time, whether it be artistic constraints. technical constraints, and production constraints. If you ask me if AI can solve all of that, not yet,” he added.

blocks.caption: A HUMAN TEAM. Ubisoft Philippines has a staff wall where they post photos from their work and play activities.

blocks.text: Ultimately, Ubisoft Philippines celebrating its 10th year of working in the country should be a cause for pride and celebration, as it brings triple-A games and the skills of talented Filipinos to the forefront of the games industry.

As Tan explained, “It always boils down to the person, the teamwork, their understanding of the game — what can be done for the game, what are the things that can be placed in the game and not in the game — that’s what makes it special.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Record fuel prices across EU prompt calls for bloc-wide windfall tax on firms
articles.summary:
German minister says companies are ‘exploiting situation’ in Middle East, as sky-high prices become major domestic issue for leaders

European governments have discussed imposing a bloc-wide…
articles.byline: Jon Henley Europe correspondent and Jillian Ambrose Energy correspondent

blocks.text: European governments have discussed imposing a bloc-wide windfall tax on energy companies, as near-record fuel and gas prices pile pressure on leaders desperate to contain mounting public discontent and the challenge of the far right.

With elections due next year in eight EU countries including France, Italy, Spain and Poland, leaders are scrambling to head off the potential fallout from what analysts have warned could be one of the continent’s biggest energy shocks in decades.

Germany’s finance minister, Lars Klingbeil, called on ‌the European Commission at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday to propose possible ways to tax what he described as the excessive profits of oil companies.

“Several member states have been calling for models for a long time,” Klingbeil said, demanding proposals by next month. “People can see how oil companies are exploiting the situation, overcharging and significantly increasing their profits.”

Oil futures have climbed back above $100 a ⁠barrel, about 50% higher than before the Iran war, as escalating attacks across the Middle East threaten more ​supply routes. Derivatives markets suggest traders do not ‌expect a near-term drop in ‌prices.

Pump prices have already reached all-time highs across Europe. In Germany, diesel prices surged to a record average of €2.45 a litre on Wednesday, while petrol hit a fresh high of €2.31 a litre, according to Europe’s largest motoring association, ADAC.

Prices are even higher in the Netherlands, where petrol eclipsed last week’s record high to reach €2.73 a litre on Wednesday, with diesel at an average €2.78 a litre. Prices have risen higher still for petrol in Denmark and for diesel in Finland.

Across the EU, petrol prices are 24% higher than a year earlier, while diesel is up 38% and jet fuel costs more than 100% more. Benchmark gas is trading at €81 a megawatt hour, up 150% on a year earlier, with analysts suggesting it could hit €100.

The EU’s economic commissioner, Valdis Dombrovskis, has said the commission has no plans “at this stage” for an ⁠EU-wide taxing mechanism, but stressed it was “ready to engage in discussion” and member states were free ​to impose their own taxes.

Sky-high fuel prices are already a major domestic political issue in France and Italy, both of which next year face crunch elections in which voters’ concerns are likely to be dominated by the soaring cost of living, driven largely by high energy prices.

In Italy, Giorgia Meloni’s ruling rightwing coalition, trailing rivals in the polls, said this week it would scrap road tax for 14.5m cars and motorbikes from next year at a cost of over €2bn, on top of a cut to diesel duty that has already cost €2.8bn.

“We have chosen to redirect a portion of the resources used to address rising fuel prices into a simple, structural measure designed especially for those who use cars and motorcycles every day to work, take their children, or get around,” Meloni said.

France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, told ministers he wanted the government’s “full mobilisation” on fuel supply and prices, including efforts to secure supplies internationally by working toward the “peaceful reopening” of the strait of Hormuz.

In the latest of a wave of protests, French fishers blocked access to two ports and a fuel depot in southern France on Thursday over soaring diesel prices that this week rose to €2.37 a litre, just below their record of €2.38.

The fisheries minister, Catherine Chabaud, said the fishers had agreed after six hours of talks to lift the blockades after a promise that those with ​cashflow issues would be granted zero-interest ⁠loans and support measures ​would ​to be ​tied ‌to ​fuel price changes.

The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, this week extended emergency fuel subsidies until the end of the year for the agriculture, fishing and construction sectors. But the government is reluctant to step in to cut fuel prices for all.

“Blanket measures that affect everyone – including those who don’t need them – are a false economy,” the country’s finance minister, Roland Lescure, told journalists earlier in the week. “Why? Because ultimately, we’ll have to fund them.”

In August, Spain doubled its diesel tax discount to €0.20 a litre from 1 September after diesel prices jumped by 15.7% in July, while in Germany, the embattled chancellor, Friedrich Merz, announced a fuel tax cut late on Friday.

Taxes on petrol and diesel ⁠would be cut by by €0.17 from 1 October until the end of the year, the government said, as well as holding talks with the oil industry with the aim of ​introducing a cap on fuel prices by 1 January 2027 ‌at the latest.

“Anyone who relies on their car every day is reaching breaking point,” Merz said in a statement. “We are ‌showing that we are resilient in the face of the crisis and are helping our citizens,” he added.

Merz’s centre-right CDU was this month heavily defeated in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt by the far-right AfD, and two more state elections this weekend are likely to bring further gains for the far-right party, which has campaigned on a platform of a return to the cheap Russian gas imports Europe largely abandoned after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

articles.title: Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania: SPD seeks to fend off AfD
articles.summary: For nearly three decades, the Social Democrats have governed Germany's northeastern state. If they can fend off the AfD, the result may boost the fortunes of the German government's junior coalition…

image.caption: Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania's state legislature is housed in Schwerin CastleImage: Jens Büttner/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Stretching along Germany's Baltic coast, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is known for the tourist draws of Rügen and Usedom, the quiet island of Hiddensee with the grave of playwright Gerhart Hauptmann, and the historic universities of Greifswald and Rostock, among the oldest in the country. The state is also shaped by its industrial heritage, including its shipyards and the vast nuclear power plant at Lubmin, built in former East Germany and closed in 1995.

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is Germany's most sparsely populated federal state, with a population of just 1.57 million at the end of 2025. The unemployment rate in the structurally weak state stands at 8%, above the national average. At roughly 6%, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania also has by far the lowest share of foreign nationals of any of Germany's 16 federal states.

For many former East Germans, the state is associated with long summers spent at campsites and holiday resorts along the Baltic coast. It is also home to 16 national parks, more than any other federal state in Germany, and to the Mecklenburg Lake District, centered on Lake Müritz.

Yet this federal state was also the scene of some of the earliest violent attacks on asylum-seeker accommodations following German reunification. Images of burning housing blocks in Rostock-Lichtenhagen in August 1992 were broadcast around the world. That year, the number of asylum seekers in Germany reached a provisional peak of 440,000, fueling heated debates across the country.

In August of that year, hundreds of far-right rioters attacked a residential building in Rostock that housed around 100 people from Vietnam. The building was set on fire as some 3,000 local residents applauded the attackers. Miraculously, no one was killed, though many people were injured. It was the worst outbreak of racist violence in Germany since the Second World War.
Incumbency advantage may help Manuela Schwesig

Former Chancellor Angela Merkel had her electoral district in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. For around 28 years, the state has been governed by the Social Democratic Party (SPD) in coalition with various partners.

Most recently, it has been led by the popular state premier and former federal minister Manuela Schwesig. The 52-year-old heads a coalition with the socialist Left Party. Schwesig stands a good chance of ensuring that this remains the case after the election on September 20.

Schwesig, who for a long time trailed the far-right populist Alternative for Germany party (AfD) by a wide margin in the polls, has been campaigning on the slogan "The woman against blue" — a reference to the AfD's party color.

In a televised debate with AfD lead candidate Leif-Erik Holm just over ten days before the election, the state premier described the AfD as "the most dangerous party for our country, for the economy, for social welfare, and also for us women." Addressing Holm directly, she added: "You are talking the country down."
Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is not an AfD stronghold
Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is the only eastern German state where the domestic intelligence agency has not classified the AfD as "confirmed right-wing extremist."

The center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, is polling at a historic low, the lowest in any German state. A poor showing in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania could further fuel debate over the increasingly unpopular chancellor. The environmentalist Greens are also fighting to remain in the state parliament, with support hovering around the 5% threshold for representation.

With a vote distribution like this, it is highly unlikely that a majority could be assembled to elect AfD lead candidate Leif-Erik Holm as state premier. After all, every party with a realistic chance of entering the state parliament has ruled out any cooperation with the AfD.

The party's lead candidate, Leif-Erik Holm, deliberately cultivates a down-to-earth image. At campaign events, he draws on his experience as a radio host, including with the public broadcaster NDR. A member of the Bundestag for the Alternative for Germany (AfD) since 2017, he repeatedly taps into widespread dissatisfaction with the government, the economic slowdown, and the comparatively difficult social conditions in the structurally weak and sparsely populated northeast.

Holm cannot match the popular SPD state premier, Schwesig, in head-to-head comparisons of the leading candidates. But the AfD's support in the polls, neck and neck with the SPD, underscores just how deeply divided Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania remains.
Governing the coastal state is unlikely to become any easier in the years to come.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: Over 15k cops to be deployed for 54th Martial Law commemoration
articles.summary: The National Capital Region Police Office said that around 15,227 police personnel are expected to be deployed at 11 p.m. on Saturday, September 19 in preparation for the upcoming 54th Martial Law…

blocks.text: The National Capital Region Police Office (NCRPO) said Saturday that around 15,227 police personnel are expected to be deployed at 11 p.m. on September 19 in preparation for the upcoming 54th Martial Law commemoration.

In an interview with Super Radyo dzBB, NCRPO spokesperson Police Lieutenant Colonel Hazel Asilo said that the full deployment on Saturday evening will be reinforced not only by NCRPO officers but also by police troops from nearby regions.

“Meron po tayo dito sa mga monitored areas natin, 'yung mga significant po gaya ng Ayala Bridge, Mendiola, C.M. Recto sa Maynila, siyempre ‘yung ating People Power Monument, ang EDSA Shrine, gano'n din po sa Luneta ay lalagyan natin,” Asilo said, detailing the police deployment.

(We will have deployments in our monitored areas, significant locations like Ayala Bridge, Mendiola, C.M. Recto in Manila, and of course our People Power Monument, the EDSA Shrine, as well as Luneta.)
Asilo noted that these areas are the primary convergence zones for mobilizations, based on historical events from previous years.
As of Saturday, Asilo said no groups have secured any rally permits yet for Monday's commemoration, but emphasized that they are monitoring online groups who might gather and stage a protest.
“Since wala pong nag-secure ng permit mula po sa mga grupo na posibleng mag-conduct, nagbe-base po tayo… doon po sa information na naga-gather po ng ating intel units,” Asilo said.
(Since no groups likely to conduct protests have secured permits, we are basing our plans on the information gathered by our intelligence units.)
Warrants of arrest on standby

Recalling the disturbances that occurred during last year's Martial Law protest, Asilo confirmed that authorities found the individuals, particularly minors, who caused trouble last year were not members of groups legitimately conducting mobilizations.
In preparation for possible renewed unrest, authorities are coordinating with other agencies and closely monitoring social media posts for any indications of incitement to cause trouble on Monday.

“Bilang paghahanda po, bukod po doon sa ating ginawang koordinasyon sa iba’t ibang agencies po natin nagmo-monitor po tayo sa ating mga social media posts para po sa mga posibleng mobilization nu'ng mga grupo na hindi po usually sumasama sa mga pagtitipon, or ‘yung mga grupo na hindi natin kilala na maaari pong mag-cause ng gulo,” Asilo said.

(As part of our preparation, aside from coordinating with various agencies, we are monitoring social media posts for possible mobilizations by groups that do not usually join assemblies, or unfamiliar groups that might cause trouble.)
She noted that these individuals or groups causing trouble use social media platforms to mobilize, unlike usual groups who officially coordinate with authorities.
Asilo emphasized that they have identified these groups and their leaders, stating that they are ready to serve warrants of arrest if these groups cause trouble again.
“May mga warrants of arrest po tayo na nakabinbin para po dito sa mga leaders nila. Kung kaya din po 'yung ating pagmo-monitor sa araw ng Lunes, September 21, ay nakataas,” Asilo said.
(We have pending warrants of arrest for their leaders. That is why our monitoring on Monday, September 21, is on high alert.)
“Para po kung sakali man po na itong mga leaders na ‘to or mga grupong ito ay muling lumutang… ay agad din pong mase-serve sa kanila ‘yung mga warrants nila,” she added.
(So that just in case these leaders or groups resurface... their warrants can be served to them immediately.)
While no groups have secured rally permits yet, the NCRPO anticipates around six groups to stage protests on Monday who regularly hold demonstrations.

Police personnel deployed at border control points will also monitor closely, according to Asilo, who reminded the public not to feel bad if their vehicles are flagged down for inspection or monitoring. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: House prosec wants Baste Duterte classified as 'hostile witness' in VP Sara impeach trial
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel will be seeking the Senate impeachment court to classify Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte as another hostile witness in the impeachment trial of his sister, Vice…

blocks.text: Published September 19, 2026 2:28pm

The House prosecution panel will be seeking the Senate impeachment court to classify Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte as another hostile witness in the impeachment trial of his sister, Vice President Sara Duterte.
“We will ask the court to declare him as a hostile witness,” said House prosecution panel spokesperson Benjamin Tolosa Jr. said at a news forum in Quezon City on Saturday.
Last Wednesday, the Senate impeachment court announced it issued a subpoena to the younger Duterte to appear at his sister’s impeachment trial.

“Tama po kasama siya sa mga witneses na naakalista sa issuance of subpoena na sinumite ng prosecution. Pinapatawag natin siya bilang testigo dahil main reason siya ang mayor ng City of Davao at nakita natin sa SALN (State of Assets Liabilities and Net Worth) ng bise merong iba-ibang kumpanya nakadeklara na meron siyang financial interest… [such as] Gencorp Industries. Gusto nating makita kung nagkaroon ng any dealings ang kumpanyang ito with the city government,” Tolosa said.

(It's true that he's one of the witnesses issued subpoena [by the court] which was submitted by the prosecution. We want him to testify because he is the mayor of Davao City and we found out from the SALN of the Vice President that there were different firms where she has financial interest such as Gencorp Industries. We want to see if there are dealings between this firm and the city government.)
The impeachment court is currently discussing Article II of the Articles of Impeachment, which involves the alleged unexplained wealth of the Vice President.

Tolosa said the prosecution will be asking the impeachment court to declare the Davao City mayor as hostile witness during the course of the trial, in which the panel will show that his interest is adverse to that of the prosecution.
Tolosa explained that once the younger Duterte is declared a hostile witness, the prosecution can ask him more “leading questions” which can be answered by “yes or no.”

Moreover, the prosecutor said that House panel also listed as witness an assistant commissioner of the Civil Service Commission to explain the guidelines on filing SALN, a representative of the Securities and Exchange to testify if the Vice President has financial interests in several companies, representative of PhilHealth Region XI office and representative of its bids and awards committee to check the agency’s dealings with alleged Duterte-linked companies.
A representative of the PNP firearms and explosives office was also listed to divulge information on the registered firearms under Duterte and her husband, Atty. Manases Carpio. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: IN DATA: How BARMM voted in its first-ever parliamentary elections
articles.summary: Local politics and key endorsements remained decisive in electing the Bangsamoro Parliament

blocks.text: Local politics and key endorsements remained decisive in electing the Bangsamoro Parliament

items: The BARMM election resulted in a mixed outcome with no single party achieving a majority, with the Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP) securing the most seats at 32, followed by the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) with 30 seats.

Local endorsements played a crucial role in the election results, with BFP dominating in four provinces due to support from local officials, while UBJP only won in the Special Geographic Area, its stronghold.
Despite attempts to reduce patronage and dynastic politics, the election results indicate that clan politics remain influential in the Bangsamoro region.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
The historic Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) election has concluded. How did the Bangsamoro people vote?
The results are mixed, with no single party getting a majority of the seats. But the parties that did successfully get seats are:

items: Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP) and its guest candidate from the Progresibong Bangsamoro Party – 32 seats
United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) – 30 seats
BARMM Grand Coalition (BGC) and its three member parties, the Bangsamoro Peoples Party, Serbisyong Inklusibo-Alyansang Progresibo (SIAP), and Al-Ittihad-Ungaya sa Kawagib Nu Bangsamoro – 15 seats
Bangsamoro Peoples Democratic Party (Raayat Democratic Party) – 1 seat
Non-Moro indigenous peoples representatives, who represent their tribes instead of parties – 2 seats

blocks.text: A look into where all the votes came from showed that local politics and key endorsements remained decisive in electing the BARMM Parliament. Here’s a breakdown of the numbers.
The top three regional parliamentary political parties (RPPPs) secured votes in different ways.

First placer BFP consistently got the most votes in four out of the BARMM’s six provinces: Basilan, Maguindanao del Norte, Maguindanao del Sur, and Tawi-Tawi. This could be due to the endorsements of local officials in these provinces.

The governors of Maguindanao del Norte, Maguindanao del Sur, and Tawi-Tawi had endorsed the BFP. Basilan Governor Mujiv Hataman had a hand in founding two other parties — the BGC and Bangsamoro Peoples Party — but his nephew and Vice Governor Jim Hataman-Salliman was a candidate of the BFP. Eleven Basilan mayors also endorsed the BFP.
Maguindanao del Norte is also the bailiwick of BARMM Interim Chief Minister and BFP president Abdulraof “Sammy Gambar” Macacua. He previously served as acting governor of Maguindanao del Norte.

Second placer UBJP — which had initially been seen as the front-runner in the election — won in only one province: the Special Geographic Area (SGA), which is where Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) and UBJP chair Ahod “Al Haj Murad” Ebrahim and his family reside. The party was a strong second placer in four other regions.

The UBJP, the official party of the MILF, was the majority party in the region’s transition government for the past seven years. Support from the former rebel group’s members across the region was also expected.
Third placer BGC’s voter base was more concentrated, getting 53.83% of the votes from Lanao del Sur alone. This province is the region’s most vote-rich, making up 30.4% of the voting population.

This large showing in a single region is not surprising given that the BGC and one of its individual parties were established by the Adiong family, one of Lanao del Sur’s most entrenched and long-standing political clans.

For the sectoral races, the UBJP swept all six seats up for election. But a look at the provincial breakdowns showed that voting patterns in the provinces were still largely affected by political dynamics.

Going deeper into the municipal and city levels showed roughly the same pattern of key endorsements and strongholds, save for some breakthrough areas. But these areas were where candidates had their own hyperlocal pockets of power.

For example, in BGC-dominated Lanao del Sur, some UBJP bets still managed to win in their own strongholds: one unopposed bet and two former mayors — former Kapai town mayor Hamza Gauraki and former Poona Bayabao mayor Lampa Pandi.

In BFP and Macacua’s Maguindanao del Norte, former Maguindanao del Norte vice governor Abdulnasser Abas of the UBJP captured his own district. A scion of the Midtimbang clan is the lone UBJP winner in Maguindanao del Sur, where three other BFP bets won.

While BFP bet Butch Malang lost the race, he was still able to capture one of the four towns in Ebrahim’s bailiwick of the SGA. Malang was administrator of the Special Geographic Area Development Authority until recently.

Across its seven-year transition, the BARMM’s interim government — the Bangsamoro Transition Authority — had attempted to pass laws that would make the regional government move away from patronage politics toward more genuinely representative governance. Anti-political dynasty and anti-turncoatism provisions were put in place with the goal of making politics more about principles rather than prominence.
Still, the results of the region’s first parliamentary elections showed that clan and dynastic politics continue to have a tight hold on the Bangsamoro people.
Can the BARMM’s incoming elected parliament change that? – Rappler.com

articles.title: South Cotabato school shooter used DepEd employee father’s gun
articles.summary: A Grade 9 student who opened fire at Banga National High School in South Cotabato used his father’s firearm, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said.

blocks.text: September 19, 2026 | 1:54pm
Police forensic experts sift through the scene of the deadly gun rampage on Sept. 18, 2026, inside a school campus in Banga, South Cotabato.
Philstar.com / John Unson
Content warning: School shooting
MANILA, Philippines — A Grade 9 student who opened fire at Banga National High School in South Cotabato used his father’s firearm, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said.
In a press briefing on Saturday, September 19, Remulla said the student’s father is a disaster risk mitigation officer of the Department of Education (DepEd).
The student accessed the firearm after opening a vault where his father kept three licensed guns.
“Mayroon siyang tatlong licensed firearms na hindi secured enough na nabuksan ng bata at kinuha 'yung baril,” Remulla said.
The DILG chief said the shooting happened at around 1 p.m. Friday, September 18.
Three people were killed in the incident, including the shooter, while eight others were injured. Two of those killed were students, according to Remulla.
One of the injured students remained in critical condition in an intensive care unit as of Saturday morning, according to a municipal disaster risk reduction official.

Authorities have previously said the student allegedly warned his classmates before the attack. He reportedly told them to go home after lunch because he would do something that could put them in danger, but his classmates thought he was joking.
The student later left his classroom and opened fire in an adjacent classroom before turning the gun on himself.
Remulla said the incident was the third case in which an improperly secured firearm was used.
Marcos orders probe, tighter school security
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Friday, September 18, expressed condolences to the families of those killed in the shooting.
“Muli tayong nahaharap sa isang trahedyang hindi dapat danasin ng sinumang magulang, paaralan, o komunidad,” Marcos said in a Facebook post.
(We are once again faced with a tragedy that no parent, school, or community should ever have to experience.)
He said the government would ensure that those injured receive the necessary treatment and assistance.
Marcos also said he had ordered government agencies to strengthen security in schools following previous shooting incidents in Tacloban and Zamboanga.
“Ito na ang ikatlong nakamamatay na pamamaril sa paaralan sa loob lamang ng tatlong buwan,” he said.
(This is now the third deadly school shooting in just three months.)
The president said he had ordered the Department of Education, DILG and Philippine National Police to report on the measures they had implemented following the previous incidents.
He also ordered an investigation into the shooting, including how the minor was able to obtain a firearm and bring it inside the school.
“Hindi natin maaaring tanggapin na maging bahagi na lamang ng buhay ng ating mga anak ang mga pamamaril sa paaralan,” the president said.
(We cannot accept school shootings becoming just another part of our children’s lives.)
The Department of Education condemned the shooting and said its officials were on site to assist the victims and coordinate with local authorities and law enforcement in the investigation.

blocks.text: The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao is holding its first parliamentary elections on September 14, 2026, after being postponed at least four times: first in May 2022, then in May 2025, October 2025, and again in March 2026.

The historic polls are seen as a pivotal moment in the decades-long peace process in a region that was mired in conflict and socioeconomic and political challenges. The upcoming elections are also a test for the Bangsamoro transition and the institutions and systems established in the last seven years.

articles.title: DILG's Remulla to delay trip to France amid Banga National High School shooting
articles.summary: Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said Saturday he will be delaying his planned trip to France for a follow up on an Interpol red notice request against former party-list lawmaker Zaldy Co, following…

blocks.text: Published September 19, 2026 1:04pm

Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said Saturday he will be delaying his planned trip to France for a follow up on an Interpol red notice request against former party-list lawmaker Zaldy Co, following the fatal shooting incident at Banga National High School in South Cotabato.

“In light of this and other documentary requirements by Interpol, I will have to delay my trip to France by two weeks or three weeks to finish this, to finish the legislation and to finish the documentary requirements asked of me,” Remulla said at a press conference.
Remulla added he will be working with the Department of Education to formulate guidelines to prevent shooting incidents in schools in the future.

“So ‘yung itatanong ‘yun, hunos-dili lang kayo, let me finish my work. The President asked me to report on Monday to give the guidelines again and then we will craft with the DepEd another set of rules kung paano natin maa-avoid ito.”

(For those who will be asking, calm down. Let me finish my work. The President asked me to report on Monday to give the guidelines again and then we will craft with the DepEd another set of rules on how to avoid these incidents.)
Remulla was supposed to go to France for the Philippine government’s follow up on its request for an Interpol red notice against Zaldy Co.
“We are filing a red notice for Zaldy Co again. Coincidentally, I will also be going to Lyon, France to follow up on his red notice with Interpol,” Remulla previously said.
According to Interpol, a red notice is a request to law enforcement authorities worldwide to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition, surrender, or similar legal action.
At the same press conference, Remulla said the shooter who was behind the deadly incident at the Banga National High School in South Cotabato was into the deep dark web.
Three children were confirmed to be dead, including the shooter, while eight were injured, according to the DILG chief.
Remulla advised parents to check on what their children are looking up on social media, and what websites they visit. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: From ovations in Venice to death threats in Israel: the extreme responses to NAZA documentary
articles.summary:
As Gaza documentary wins cinematic acclaim, its directors face vitriol in Israel amid a febrile election campaign

First there was a moment of stunned silence. Then, in the Sala Grande, the…

blocks.text: First there was a moment of stunned silence. Then, in the Sala Grande, the main screening hall of the Venice film festival within the Palazzo del Cinema, the audience stood almost as one and turned to applaud the film-makers for 25 minutes.
The film the audience had watched for 80 harrowing minutes was the Gaza documentary NAZA, which has been produced by the Guardian.
The film’s title comes from an Israeli military acronym used euphemistically to refer to the civilians expected to be killed in a military attack.

Unfolding against the background of Tel Aviv at night, the participants – intelligence officers and other soldiers – describe a series of systems, some powered by AI, that select the thousands who should die in strikes, often at night and surrounded by their families.
Perhaps most challenging for Israel’s political elite is that it is a story told exclusively in Hebrew by 24 anonymised Israeli military insiders, many of them from elite units.

The documentary depicts a wide variety of viewpoints that all lead to the same conclusion: participation in a programme of mass killing where there were few boundaries between combatant and civilian, in a war where more than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed. Some describe being shamed by their experience. Some are neutral. Others describe excitement, and a sense of “fun” as they justify their actions.

It will open in US cinemas from 30 September, with international distribution plans to be announced shortly. The ripples of ovation gathered in volume among the few who have seen the film before its New York premiere, but in Israel the film provoked a very different response.

Rightwing political figures have rushed to accuse its directors – the Oscar-winning Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor – of “treason”. The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who has long harboured an antipathy to critical media, declared on Wednesday he would seek new laws to strip citizenship from people who he said “smear” Israeli soldiers.

Demonstrators and members of far-right groups went further still, calling for violence against the pair and the demolition of their homes. Outside Szor’s parents’ house in central Israel, protesters called for the “death penalty for traitors”.

An editorial in the left-leaning newspaper Haaretz warned that their lives were credibly endangered. Dozens of human rights and peace organisations in Israel rallied to defend the film-makers, as did international press freedom organisations.

The whiplash ferocity of the response, even in the midst of a febrile election campaign where Israeli attitudes to the war in Gaza are a central issue, has surprised even those in the Israeli leftwing and human rights community who have long been on the receiving end of such denunciations.

The pushback to the documentary is both a testament to its power and evidence of how the Israeli right is exploiting a film, as yet unseen by most, to craft its own version of what it says it represents.
Critics in Israel seized on the longstanding idea that Israelis should not criticise their country in front of foreign audiences.

Ofer Winter, a controversial former rightwing army officer turned politician, told an election rally for his People of Israel in Rishon LeZion: “An Israeli citizen, a Jew, receives thunderous applause for going out and smearing and defaming his own people.

“I understand that you are afraid to return to Israel,” he taunted the directors. “You are right. You have nothing to return to. It is a disgrace and a shame to return after you spat in the faces of your own people.”

blocks.caption: A protest against the NAZA film-makers in Savyon, Israel. Photograph: Sharon Eilon/Sopa Images/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The rightwing journalist Yehuda Schlesinger of Channel 14, a station regarded as being a mouthpiece for Netanyahu, went further still, saying Abraham and Szor should be “pursued” and “hunted”, prevented from returning to Israel, and describing the ovation in Venice as “25 minutes of antisemitic applause”.
By Wednesday, Netanyahu had decided to weigh in, announcing he would promote two bills to legislate against the “defamation” of Israeli soldiers and the state of Israel.
“We will revoke citizenship for anyone who defames IDF soldiers around the world – he will be deeply hurt in his pocket.”
At points, the threats of violence have been realised.

On Wednesday, the journalist Haggai Matar, a director of the left-leaning independent +972 Magazine and Sicha Mekomit (Local Call), where Abraham’s first reporting on the allegations appeared in collaboration with the Guardian, said their offices had been broken into by rightwing activists who had filmed the intrusion.

“The discussion about NAZA has been a million times more prominent than the UK sanctions announcement,” said Dahlia Scheindlin, an Israeli political and polling expert who writes a column for Haaretz, adding that the right was exploiting the current inability of Israelis to see the film and make their own judgment.
“While it is unseen, it can be turned into something electorally potent that at present Israelis aren’t able to demystify.”

The film has also arrived in the midst of a markedly worsening atmosphere towards dissenting views, acute since Hamas’s deadly attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, with the film challenging a long-held expectation that Israel’s media self-censor in times of conflict.

As Israel has become increasingly isolated internationally over both Gaza, where an independent UN inquiry found Israel continues to commit genocide, and growing settler violence in the occupied West Bank, the film also appears to have touched a more complex nerve in Israel’s collective psyche.
Israel’s forthcoming elections in October have acted as an accelerant for the country’s rightwing parties, whose language has become more hardline and extreme under Netanyahu’s far-right coalition.

Human rights activists, critical journalists, the left more broadly and even the notion of an independent judiciary have long been presented as an enemy within by the far right, who appear to be seeking to weaponise the film against a wider community of critics of Israel and its military.
The extreme response from Netanyahu and his allies has itself been condemned.
The Yedioth Ahronoth columnist Nahum Barnea described the calls to strip the film-makers of their citizenship as “delusional”.

The former editor-in-chief of the Jerusalem Post, Yaakov Katz, wrote: “Not only does such a move not make Israel look stronger, but it creates the impression that we have something to hide and are afraid of criticism. It makes it seem like we fear to stand up for our truth and what we believe in.”
And for Haaretz’s Etan Nechin, who saw the film at a press screening in New York earlier this week, the reaction to NAZA is a symptom of a serious malaise.

“In a healthy democracy, NAZA would be shown on the evening news, its allegations would cause a public outrage and the state would promise a thorough investigation,” he wrote. “Instead, following the film’s Venice premiere, Abraham and Szor have effectively been pushed into exile.”

articles.title: This ‘hard to swallow’ Filipino film hopes to make Oscars history
articles.summary: ‘Filipiñana,’ the country’s official film entry to the Oscars, hopes the international audience sees something different — a ‘different side of the Philippines’ and a ‘different kind of Philippine…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines attempts to make history after selecting Filipiñana as the country’s official entry to the Best International Feature Film category of the 99th Academy Awards.
A 100-minute film showing the Philippines’ class divide, Filipiñana tells the story of 17-year-old Isabela, who works as a “tee girl” in an exclusive golf club.
“It’s hard to accept a formalist film that isn’t a narrative,” said film producer Bianca Balbuena in Filipino.
Initially a short film, the full-length feature directed by Rafael Manuel and co-produced by Bradley Liew has been praised for its visual storytelling, but has also drawn critique for its slow pace.

“As director Rafael said, how he thought of this is not script-based, it’s more on verses, like music: verses, chorus. So it’s hard to accept. Even us (producers), when we first saw the cut, we said, ‘This is hard to swallow.”

But it’s this unique approach that Filipiñana hopes to bank on when it tries to earn a nomination at the Oscars. Since the inception of the Best International Feature Film category in 1956, no entry submitted by the Philippines has even made the official shortlist of 15 films.

Filipiñana’s strong reception at the international festivals, including the Sundance Film Festival where it bagged the Special Jury Award for Creative Vision, has kept everyone behind the film hopeful.

“I think the international audience saw a different side of the Philippines, and saw a different kind of what Philippine cinema can be and is. They were excited to see something different,” Balbuena said.
Locally, Filipiñana premiered as the closing film of the Cinemalaya Independent Film Festival 2026

“Actually, Cinemalaya was our 22nd film festival,” Balbuena said. “Then now, we are in our 26th. It is going to Bangkok, going to Busan, Tokyo, Vienna, Hamburg, Singapore, and many more. It’s competing in Pingyao, China also.”
Jorrybell Agoto stars as Isabel, whose job as a tee girl includes setting up golf balls for elite patrons, including the country club’s president Dr. Palanca, played by Teroy Guzman.

Paolo Villaluna, the director general of the Film Academy of the Philippines (FAP), which announced Filipiñana’s Oscars selection last September 13, said the body will again support the country’s Oscars campaign.

“The film offers a visually distinct and controversial portrait of the Filipino experience,” said Villaluna. “The Film Academy will work closely with the Filipiñana team throughout the Oscars campaign, providing the support they need and make the most of this opportunity for Philippine cinema.”
Last year, the Philippines’ Oscars entry, Lav Diaz’s Magellan, made a strong push but still fell short of the Academy’s final cut.
But Filipiñana’s producers said they’ve been campaigning for the film internationally, even before it was selected as the country’s Oscars entry.

“Whether or not we get chosen, we already had a plan,” Balbuena shared. “It was [good timing] that we were at the North American release announcing [its selection]. So we can do an email blast to all the members to watch the North American theatrical run. We’ve also covered the biggest cities of the voters: US and UK. So we are ready since then.”
Aside from Filipiñana, FAP threw its support for the Oscars consideration of 58th (Best Documentary Feature Film) and Agapito (Best Live Action Short Film) in their respective categories.

blocks.caption: A still from the animated film ’58th, which rotoscopes and dramatizes the 2009 Maguindanao maasacre. Film still courtesy of FFR

blocks.text: 58th, directed by Carl Joseph Papa, is an animated docudrama film about the 2009 Maguindanao massacre, which claimed 58 innocent lives, but only 57 were officially recognized as the body of photojournalist Reynaldo “Bebot” Momay has yet to be found.

“We want the film to be a reminder and an eye-opener: this happened in 2009, and it’s still happening all around the world,” Papa said. “I hope it’s an eye-opener and people will remember, so the tragic events won’t happen again.”

“This is officially the deadliest single day for journalists in the whole history that has ever been counted: 32 journalists killed in one go,” added film producer Nessa Valdellon. “We’re hoping that people who cover…who write stories will be able to appreciate it and realize, ‘God, this is the importance of [our] jobs.’”

Agapito, co-directed by Arvin Belarmino and Kyla Danelle Romero, tells the story of manual pinsetters in a vintage duckpin alley and explores the themes of love, family, and patience in a working-class setting.

“Agapito is about a real person, actually. He’s my brother who’s in the autism spectrum, special child,” said Belarmino. “It’s my first time to produce because mostly the films I make before are subcultured, sociopolitical. It’s my first time to show vulnerability to tell about the story of a loved one.”

blocks.caption: A movie poster of ‘Agapito,’ a short film featuring pinsetters in a duckpin alley.

blocks.text: “Filipinos are still constantly telling their stories for the Filipinos. It’s just a matter of exposure to everybody,” said Jon Galvez, one of Agapito’s producers.

“My wish is: instead of trailers are shown outside cinemas, I hope it will be short films — to provide space for short filmmakers to show their films outside of festivals. Philippine cinema is worth it. Worth fighting for, worth watching.”

“Let’s just give it a chance,” Galvez added. “There are a lot of factors involved, that’s why it’s not supported all the time, but just give it a shot. The talent of Filipinos, the storytelling, it’s so different.”
The deadline for submission of films to the Academy Awards is on September 30, 2026, with the official shortlist of 15 films to be revealed on December 15, 2026.
In 2027, the five final nominees will be announced on January 21. The 99th Oscars ceremony is set on March 14, 2027 at the Dolby Theater in Los Angeles.
“I hope all eyes are on the Philippines now, all Hollywood eyes. I think we have a good chance with the three titles here,” Villaluna said.
“I hope the Filipinos support all our films. We are the masters of cinema, we are good storytellers.” – Rappler.com
Angel Camille Dio is a Rappler intern studying BA Journalism at Polytechnic University of the Philippines.

articles.title: Anthropic considers releasing new AI model ahead of IPO, sources say
articles.summary: Anthropic weighs new AI model launch amid OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra success, as CEO calls for industry slowdown and investors reassess competitive landscape ahead of IPO

blocks.text: ANTHROPIC. The Anthropic logo is seen in this illustration taken March 31, 2023.
Dado Ruvic/Reuters
Anthropic weighs new AI model launch amid OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra success, as CEO calls for industry slowdown and investors reassess competitive landscape ahead of IPO

items: Anthropic is considering launching a new AI model to compete with OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, following concerns about safety and competitive pressure.
CEO Dario Amodei has called for a slowdown in AI advancements, emphasizing safety, while investors are scrutinizing Anthropic's market position amid rising competition and interest rates.

Despite OpenAI's recent success with GPT-6 Astra, some investors believe Anthropic's established lead in enterprise AI tools will help it maintain its market position, although challenges from open-source models are emerging.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Anthropic is considering rolling out a new AI model to counter OpenAI’s momentum since its launch of GPT-6 Astra, according to three sources, ahead of an expected IPO and after its CEO called for an industrywide slowdown.

The timing of a potential launch aimed at addressing competitive pressure from a direct rival follows Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s call on the global AI community to slow down the pace of releasing new capabilities to address safety concerns, the sources said.
“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote in a 3,800-word essay on September 12.
The essay, which painted a bleak picture of swarms of AI agents taking over the internet and outpacing human control, drew support from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.

OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, released this month, has gained traction among businesses, prompting concerns among some investors who told Reuters they are re-evaluating Anthropic’s position as the leading provider of enterprise AI tools.
Anthropic is evaluating the safety of its next model as part of its deliberations over a release, one of the people familiar with the matter said.

Some of the discussions involve how to balance investment in releasing new models with efforts to strengthen the company’s profitability as rising interest rates make investors more focused on the timing of expected profits, said people familiar with the company’s thinking.

The debate over spending highlights the increasing pressure on the firms at the center of the AI boom to produce sustainable cash flows sooner, thanks both to rising rates and tough competition from open-source AI providers, especially in China.
Anthropic declined to comment for this story.
The potential launch would test how Anthropic can defend its enterprise market position against OpenAI while maintaining the safety-first identity that has distinguished it from competitors.

OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra on September 3, touting gains in computer use, software engineering, cybersecurity and professional work. The model has received a strong response from enterprise users and developers, prompting potential Anthropic IPO investors to scrutinize whether OpenAI could begin taking share from Anthropic, which has been viewed for months as the leader in enterprise AI.
Astra accounted for about 13% of enterprise AI spending tracked by corporate expense platform Ramp, compared with about 8% for Anthropic’s Claude Fable, according to the latest data.

Astra has also pulled ahead on OpenRouter, a widely used platform that routes developer traffic across AI models. OpenRouter said its users spent more on OpenAI models than on Anthropic models last week, the first time OpenAI has led on that measure in more than two and a half years.

Some existing investors and those who expect to invest in both Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s IPOs said they do not believe Astra poses a significant threat to Anthropic, given the size of its lead in the market for enterprise AI tools and the amount of time it takes to unseat incumbent vendors to large companies.

Anthropic’s annualized revenue run rate topped $65 billion by the end of July, up from about $9 ​billion at the end of 2025. It is also projecting a 2028 revenue of ‌roughly $190 billion to $200 billion, Reuters previously reported. OpenAI’s annualized revenue run rate passed $40 billion in July.

Investors also expect leadership among Anthropic, OpenAI, Alphabet’s Google and other major AI developers to shift repeatedly as companies release new generations of models, making any advantage potentially short-lived.

A potentially bigger challenge for Anthropic and other leading AI providers is the rise of open-source and open-weight models, which can lower token costs and allow companies to build more of their own AI infrastructure rather than rely on providers such as Anthropic and OpenAI, investors said.

The shift could put pressure on the economics of the AI industry as companies have more options to develop and run models outside the leading commercial providers, broadening the competitive threat beyond the race between Anthropic and OpenAI.

Meta Platforms has been among Anthropic’s largest customers, but is looking to reduce its use of Anthropic’s models as it develops more AI capabilities internally, people familiar with the matter said. Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

OpenAI, meanwhile, has taken some pressure off the race to public markets. Its CEO, Altman, confirmed on Saturday that the company would not go public in 2026, saying concerns around AI safety made this an ill-advised time for a listing.

Anthropic could push its IPO to after the November US midterm elections, with the elections not expected to have a major impact on the offering, according to two people familiar with the matter. The IPO has already been pushed back from earlier plans, with Reuters previously reporting that marketing was expected to begin in mid-October at the earliest. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Google's Gemini AI hacked three companies in security test
articles.summary: The AI model accessed the internet and guessed credentials to three websites, a Google official told the BBC.

blocks.text: Google's AI model Gemini autonomously hacked into three companies during a test of its cyber-security capabilities, the company has said, in what is thought to be the first known case of it carrying out such an act.
Gemini found "public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it thought were part of the test", a Google official told the BBC, noting that in each instance "the model stopped".
The affected companies have been informed about the breach.

It comes after renewed public scrutiny over the pace of AI development, with some tech firms calling for a slowdown as they raise concerns over its potential threat to humanity - though not all companies agree.
The hacks. first reported by the Wall Street Journal, occurred in May during a test conducted by an independent company that carries out cyber-security evaluations.

Heather Adkins, vice president of Security Engineering at Google, told the BBC in a statement: "We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they've now made to their testing processes."
She added: "These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly."
Other AI systems have recently reported similar instances of breaches.

In July, Anthropic's Claude escaped its test environment to hack three organisations on its own just days after OpenAI said its models had carried out cyber-attacks against several "publicly available services".
As public debate continues to grow over the safety of developing the tech, so too does conversation around regulation.

Both Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang and OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman are expected to attend a White House state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping next Friday. Altman will then brief the UN Security Council next week.
On Friday, Huang told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, "we should go as fast as we can" with AI development.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia issues first air raid alerts for Riyadh since Houthis escalated attacks
articles.summary: Residents later received the all-clear after explosions were reported in the capital.

blocks.text: Residents in Saudi Arabia's Riyadh have been given the all-clear after air raid alerts were issued and explosions were reported in the capital.
It was the first time alerts have been issued in Riyadh since the Houthis increased their attacks and declared a "maritime embargo" on the Saudis in July.

The Saudi Civil Defence sent alerts for the capital and several other regions late on Friday night and Saturday morning (local time) as the Kingdom's conflict with the Iran-backed Houthis continued to escalate.
Journalists from Reuters and AFP reported hearing explosions in the capital, but authorities have since said the danger has passed. Residents were urged to avoid gathering in crowds.
The Houthis recently seized control of the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island, a gateway to a key shipping route used by the Gulf state to export to Asia and Europe.
The Iran-backed group's military spokesman said the naval blockade was in retaliation for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled north-western Yemen.
Saudi vessels have relied on that stretch of the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.
Last week, the Houthis attacked several Saudi oil facilities with drones and missiles, causing fires which led to operations being temporarily halted.

The attacks on Saudi oil assets have directly impacted global energy markets and the price of petrol and diesel in many countries has sharply risen in recent weeks, compounding already elevated costs caused by the blockades of the Strait of Hormuz.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the country's de facto ruler, has personally asked US President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner.
Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, offering instead to assist with intelligence and targeting support, the sources said.
A senior Trump administration official told the BBC: "We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen government regarding regional stability."

Earlier this week, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said the Houthis had launched drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia in retaliation for more than 450 Saudi air strikes on their territory over the past week.

The United Nations Security Council held an emergency meeting on Tuesday, during which both Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia called for more decisive action against the Houthis, who they accused of choking the Bab al-Mandab Strait as a way of applying economic pressure.
Council members agreed that freedom of navigation in the Red Sea must be maintained to prevent disruption to global supply chains.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

The fighting has reportedly left more than 150,000 people dead and triggered one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with more than 22 million people in need of some form of aid, according to the UN.
Additional reporting by Tabby Wilson.

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — On September 14, the Bangsamoro people troop to polling precincts to elect their parliament after decades of armed struggle and historical injustices, years of painstaking negotiations with the Philippine government, and repeated electoral delays.

Election watchdogs report significant irregularities during the polls including reports of pre-shaded ballots, vote-buying, and armed individuals in voting centers. Commission on Elections Chairman George Garcia says election-related deaths rose to at least five before voting ended.

On September 16, four retired Supreme Court justices advised the impeachment court on the conviction threshold debate. Three of them took the position that the number of votes needed to remove the impeached official is not fixed at 16. Retired justice Adolfo Azcuna maintains that all 24 senators should be counted, arguing that a fixed supermajority is necessary to prevent impeachment from being misused for political purposes.

Meanwhile, former president Rodrigo Duterte appeared in person at the International Criminal Court (ICC) for the third status conference regarding his charges of crimes against humanity related to his drug war, on September 16. Duterte has been detained in The Hague since 2025, and his trial is set to begin on November 30, following the confirmation of three charges against him.

The ICC Trial Chamber III ordered the continued detention of Duterte: “The Chamber therefore finds no notable change in circumstances that warrant the release of the Accused, with or without conditions. For these reasons, the chamber hereby decides that the accused shall continue to be detained,” said the chamber’s decision.
