articles.title: US and Denmark reach security deal after Trump’s threats to take island
articles.summary:
The agreement would allow the US to expand its military presence, while Denmark and Greenland say it preserves their sovereignty and right to self-determination

Donald Trump announced on…

blocks.text: Donald Trump announced on Friday that the US had struck an Arctic security pact with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland, after threatening for months to take Greenland by force.

The US president cast the deal as a personal triumph, claiming in a post on Truth Social that the “very important, historic, and special” agreement “gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns”.

“We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland,” Trump added. The US already has a presence on the island, and the right to expand bases, through Nato.
Greenland is a self-governing territory of the Kingdom of Denmark, a fellow Nato member.

In his post, Trump said that the agreement means “no US adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval”.
The US and Denmark will formally sign the agreement next week, on the sidelines of the United Nations general assembly in New York City, according to the Danish government.

Statements from Denmark’s prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, and the leader of Greenland’s government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, posted online late Friday, emphasized that the agreement would fall far short of Trump’s stated desire for “the acquisition of Greenland by the United States”.
Frederiksen said that the agreement “recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination”.

Nielsen said the agreement “ensures and strengthens the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States and the Western alliance”, suggesting that the deal might possibly just reiterate the existing US rights through Nato to use the island as a security base.
Once agreed to, the pact will need to go through parliamentary procedures to be enacted, the statement said.

At a Nato summit in Ankara earlier this year, Trump renewed his bid for the US to acquire Greenland, threatening to pull all American armed forces out of Europe after the continent repeatedly pushed back.

articles.title: RCMP says relationships with allies 'strong' after report FBI stopped co-operation following CBC 9/11 memo
articles.summary: The head of the RCMP says the national law enforcement agency maintains "strong relationships" with its allies, seemingly downplaying reports that FBI Director Kash Patel sought to punish Canada for…

image.caption: Royal Canadian Mounted Police officers watch cadet badge presentations in 2017. The head of the federal police force said it maintains 'strong relationships' with allies. (Valerie Zink/Reuters)

blocks.text: Politics·New

The head of the RCMP says the national law enforcement agency maintains "strong relationships" with its allies, seemingly downplaying reports that FBI Director Kash Patel sought to punish Canada for a CBC memo regarding how to describe 9/11.
New York Times reported on a short-lived attempt to punish the Mounties

RCMP Commissioner Mike Duheme was responding to a report from the New York Times on Friday alleging Patel temporarily halted some co-operation with the Mounties in retaliation to a leaked CBC internal memo instructing reporters to not refer to the Sept. 11 attacks as terrorist attacks ahead of the 25th anniversary.
CBC has a longstanding policy to generally avoid labelling specific acts as terrorism without attribution.
In a statement, the RCMP said it cannot speak to the intelligence-sharing practices of other law enforcement agencies, but the commissioner stressed that the relationship continues.
"We value our relationship with our U.S. counterparts, as we work closely to respond to threats to national security and maintain situational awareness of emerging risks," said Duheme in a statement.
"We maintain strong relationships with Canada's security and intelligence community and work closely with domestic and international partners, including members of the Five Eyes community."

Following international outcry, Basem Boshra, CBC's senior director of journalistic standards and public trust, issued a clarification on Aug. 28 saying "direct attribution is not required for describing the historic events of 9/11 as terrorism."

However the damage seemed to have been done with the White House. Patel was very public in his anger, putting a statement out on X that "any agency in Canada that doesn't publicly reject this bastardization of history, and an insult to the souls lost during our largest terrorist attack in U.S. history will no longer have friend in this FBI."

According to the New York Times's sources, Patel sought to punish Canada and FBI officials cancelled meetings with their Canadian counterparts — telling them they would be out of touch for some time. The news outlet also reported that some collaboration between the two agencies stopped around the anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks, citing people with knowledge of the episode.
The allegations would mark a new chapter in the already disintegrating Canada-U.S. relationship, this time with public safety ramifications.

items: Republican Party revokes CBC/Radio-Canada media accreditation for upcoming midterm convention
The FBI’s controversial Kash Patel

blocks.text: Despite U.S. President Donald Trump's incessant jabs at his northern neighbour, including his 51st state rhetoric, security and intelligence officials in Canada have maintained that day-to-day operations continue largely unchanged.

Any substantial fallout with U.S. security agencies could be devastating for Canada. As a net importer of intelligence, Canada leans heavily on partnerships like the Fives Eyes — which includes the United States, United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand — to pass on information.
The RCMP and FBI have a longstanding partnership and collaborate on a range of issues from the shared border to terrorism and cybersecurity.
Canada grateful for deep co-operation with U.S: minister
A spokesperson for Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said the federal government "values its close and longstanding law enforcement and security partnerships with the United States."
"We remain grateful for the service of Canadian and American law enforcement personnel and for the deep co-operation between Canadian and U.S. agencies," said the spokesperson, Simon Lafortune.
"This collaboration is essential to keeping Canadians and Americans safe, and we will continue to engage with our American partners constructively and respectfully."

The FBI declined to comment. The White House did not respond to questions about the allegations in the New York Times's story but spokesperson Lauren Bis called the CBC guidance "disgusting and disrespectful to all the victims of the 9/11 terror attacks and their families."
"These terror attacks were pure acts of evil," said Bis.

articles.title: US and Denmark reach deal over Greenland's security
articles.summary: Trump said the agreement will give the US "permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland", though specifics haven't been confirmed by Danish officials.

blocks.text: The US and Denmark have announced a deal on Greenland's security and say the agreement will be signed next week.
US President Donald Trump said the agreement would grant the US "permanent control over security, and all other needs".
Denmark's Prime Minister said the deal "strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" but did not address specifics in the agreement that Trump mentioned in a social media post.
The deal comes after months of threats by Trump to "take" Greenland over national security concerns, citing its strategic location for defence purposes and its mineral wealth.

Trump, in a post on Truth Social, said the deal comes with "no cost to the United States" and will grant the US the ability to "to do what is necessary" to "secure and defend the security of Greenland".
He said the deal includes a rule that no US adversary can maintain a military presence in Greenland or "make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval".
Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen confirmed that the agreement will be signed at the United Nations General Assembly next week.

She said the agreement "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" while also "at the same time recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination".
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called it a "historic deal" and a "huge win for the United States and the American people".
"This deal permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns in Greenland," he told Fox News.

articles.title: Blumentritt descendants donate rare Rizal letter, other 19th-century items to National Museum
articles.summary: VIENNA, Austria - The National Museum of the Philippines has acquired three sets of 19th-century heirlooms kept by descendants of Austro-Hungarian ethnographer Ferdinand Blumentritt.

blocks.text: VIENNA, Austria - The National Museum of the Philippines has acquired three sets of 19th-century heirlooms kept by descendants of Austro-Hungarian ethnographer Ferdinand Blumentritt.

The items, long in the possession of Blumentritt’s great-great-granddaughter Elke Pickert, include an unpublished letter from Jose Rizal, a pair of watercolor paintings by Juan Luna, and a 19th-century Japanese parasol with an embroidered earlier version of the Philippine flag.
For over a century, these historical treasures remained tucked away in Kufstein, Austria, the ancestral home of Pickert’s grandmother, Dolores Blumentritt.

“The precious objects have been a part of our family history for many decades,” Pickert shared in a ceremonial turnover ceremony attended by officials from the National Museum of the Philippines and the Philippine Embassy in Vienna, as well as diplomats, academics, and local community members on Thursday.
Pickert told GMA News about her joy of having these items showcased in the Philippines. “I’m proud that it’s going to the Philippines, to the National Museum, and a lot of people can see it.”
Treasure trove
The heirlooms were discovered by Austrian anthropologist Dr. Johann Stockinger in 2017, upon visiting Pickert’s home in Kufstein for his previous research on Blumentritt.
Although Stockinger knew about Pickert’s lineage, he was unaware that the family had kept the historical items safe, including the portraits of Dolores.
“I saw the portraits hanging on the wall. I asked Elke, ‘Do you know who painted these?’ She said, ‘No’”, Stockinger told GMA News.

Stockinger quickly identified the artwork as original watercolor portraits of 25-year-old Dolores painted by Juan Luna in Leitmeritz (present-day Litomerice in the Czech Republic) in April 1899, signed “Recuerdos de LVNA”. The other portrait bore the sign, “LVNA 99”.
“I had to explain their significance to her. I was then allowed to rummage through a few boxes of old documents. In the process, I discovered Rizal’s letter to Blumentritt dated May 9, 1894.”

Stockinger was referring to the unpublished three-page letter Rizal wrote from his exile in Dapitan in May 1896. Here, the hero sent his greetings to Blumentritt and his daughter Dolores, whom he called “Loleng”.
The anthropologist also recalled a detail from Blumentritt’s old correspondence to German anthropologist Adolf Benhard Meyer about a wedding present sent from Kobe, Japan.

“I read in Blumentritt’s letter to A. B. Meyer dated April 29, 1900: ‘Loleng’s wedding will take place on May 17. She received a silk umbrella with the flag of the Philippine Republic embroidered on it from a Filipino living in Kobe.’ I then asked Elke if they still had this umbrella, and sure enough, she was able to find it in the basement.”
“She went down to her cellar, and she found it, after more than a century,” Stockinger said.

blocks.caption: During the turnover ceremony on September 17, 2026, National Museum Deputy Director-General for Museums Arvin Manuel Villalon offered a deeper insight into the artifacts and their contemporary relevance. Photo: Andy Peñafuerte III

blocks.text: During the turnover ceremony on September 17, 2026, National Museum Deputy Director-General for Museums Arvin Manuel Villalon offered a deeper insight into the artifacts and their contemporary relevance. Photo: Andy Peñafuerte III
A glimpse into Philippine-Austrian friendship

Rizal’s unpublished letter from Dapitan, written in Spanish and German and addressed to Blumentritt, describes his activities while in exile, including sending a collection of butterflies to Europe and treating indigenous patients.

The correspondence also reveals Rizal’s playful relationship with Loleng, which National Museum Deputy Director-General for Museums Arvin Manuel Villalon believes may have helped preserve the document through generations.

blocks.caption: This letter was written by Jose Rizal in Spanish and sent to Dr. Ferdinand Blumentritt on May 9, 1894. It was a letter greeting Blumentritt's daughter, Dolores, whom Rizal called Loleng. Photo: Andy Peñafuerte III.

blocks.text: This letter was written by Jose Rizal in Spanish and sent to Dr. Ferdinand Blumentritt on May 9, 1894. It was a letter greeting Blumentritt's daughter, Dolores, whom Rizal called Loleng. Photo: Andy Peñafuerte III

Teasing Loleng’s disinterest in mathematics, Rizal wrote: “Why learn quadratic equations and root extraction if you ultimately won’t have enough time to take care of your home and your children? I prefer that they learn about hygiene, hygiene, and hygiene. And later, a little bit more of domestic medicine, especially children's and women's diseases.”

Rizal closed his letter: “My mother and sister send their regards, especially to Frau Blumentritt and Loleng”, before sharing a German quote: “Tausend Grüße von Haus zu Haus, über Land und Meer” (A thousand greetings from house to house, across land and sea).

For the portraits, Luna and Felipe Agoncillo–serving then as diplomats of the First Philippine Republic–visited the Blumentritt family in Leitmeritz between April and May 1899. During this period, Luna painted several artworks, including portraits of Blumentritt and his daughter.

blocks.caption: These watercolor portraits of Loleng Blumentritt were painted by Juan Luna when he visited Leitmeritz (present-day Litomerice in the Czech Republic) in April 1899. Photo: Andy Peñafuerte III

blocks.text: These watercolor portraits of Loleng Blumentritt were painted by Juan Luna when he visited Leitmeritz (present-day Litomerice in the Czech Republic) in April 1899. Photo: Andy Peñafuerte III

Loleng’s watercolor portraits show the fashion at the time: she wears puffy sleeves known as gigot and what looks like a Victorian velvet choker. Her hair is neatly arranged in a high chignon, with soft curls in the front.

“All in all, she was likely quite fashionable as befits the daughter of a prominent gentleman scholar. And we regard these portraits as small artistic treasures that tell us so much of this important circle of relationships,” Villalon said.
The third item is a traditional Japanese silk umbrella embroidered with wisteria, chrysanthemums, and a hoisted Philippine flag.
It was sent from Japan by diplomat Mariano Ponce as a wedding gift to Dolores, who would marry Karl Pickert in 1900.

Ponce, chosen by Emilio Aguinaldo to represent the Philippine Republic, procured the umbrella made of white silk called habutai. It was embroidered with chrysanthemum, wisteria, butterfly motifs, and an embroidery of a Philippine flag hoisted on a bamboo pole.

blocks.caption: This Japanese parasol, made of white silk and decorated with embroidery of chrysanthemum, wisteria, and the then-Philippine flag, was a wedding gift from the Aguinaldo government to Loleng Blumentritt and Karl Pickert. Photo: Andy Peñafuerte III

blocks.text: This Japanese parasol, made of white silk and decorated with embroidery of chrysanthemum, wisteria, and the then-Philippine flag, was a wedding gift from the Aguinaldo government to Loleng Blumentritt and Karl Pickert. Photo: Andy Peñafuerte III
The gesture was part of a larger tribute where Aguinaldo’s revolutionary government covered Dolores's entire wedding expenses, according to Villalon.

“The letter, the portraits, and the umbrella also show the endearing qualities of Filipino values, such as utang na loob or reciprocity, familial ties, and, of course, cherished friendships, the friendship between the Blumentritts and, of course, our hero, Dr. Jose Rizal,” Villalon added.
Older than the Philippines and Austria
Some of these historical objects are older than the republics of the Philippines and Austria, Philippine Ambassador to Austria Evangelina Lourdes Bernas noted.
So, most Filipino and Austrian guests at the turnover ceremony stood in awe to see these heirlooms in person.
Bernas said that the objects stand as “a testament to the ties of friendship between our countries that are much older than our formal bilateral diplomatic relations”.
National Museum Director-General Jeremy Barns described the acquisition as “super nakakataba ng puso (heartwarming)”, stressing how it shows family connections and friendships.

“It’s like a window into the time of Rizal and his friendship with Blumentritt. Here’s another opportunity to dive a bit deeper and ask, ‘Who is Blumentritt and what is his importance? What is his relationship with Jose Rizal?’ We’re enriched by stories like this, and these objects prove that these stories really happened,” Barns told GMA News.
National Museum Board of Trustees Chairman Andoni Aboitiz added that the items symbolize the Philippines today: “an international, cosmopolitan, and very reflective people”.

“My wish is that the people realize that this is a symbol of who we are today, not just of what happened in the past, but who we are today: open, free, and people who are always looking for new ideas and not resistant to change," he said.
For anthropologist Dr. Hermann Muckler from the Austro-Philippine Society, the pieces symbolize “a very close and very relaxed and even very productive relationship”.

“This brings us here in Austria closer to the Philippines. And thanks to Johan Stockinger, who was for a long time the president of the Austro-Philippine Society. He is still on the board, in a very important function where he is digging into the history of this personal relationship between Rizal and Blumentritt. So, it’s quite likely that new findings will surface in the near future," Muckler said.
According to Barns, the items are set to be presented in an upgraded gallery at the National Museum in Manila next year. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: The 9 best of a TIFF grappling with a world coming apart
articles.summary: Like every year, the Toronto International Film Festival’s 51st iteration boasted a basket of incredible, now-buzzy titles for the coming year. This year, many were about people — overwhelmingly…

image.caption: Jordan Firstman's first-time feature Club Kid feels anything but amateurish. (A24)

blocks.text: Entertainment

Like every year, the Toronto International Film Festival’s 51st iteration boasted a basket of incredible, now-buzzy titles for the coming year. This year, many were about people — overwhelmingly young people — grappling with a confusing and fracturing world and the feeling they weren't made for it.
The Debut, Club Kid and more land as decisive triumphs at the Toronto International Film Festival
Like every year, the Toronto International Film Festival's 51st iteration boasted a basket of incredible, now-buzzy titles for the coming year.

And like most years, the best of those films seemed to fit a theme. This year, it was characters in a sort of psychic crisis: people — overwhelmingly young people — grappling with a confusing and fracturing world and the feeling they weren't made for it.
To navigate those stories of crying and comedy, we've put together a list of some of the best.
The Debut
A kaleidoscopic carnival of comedy and grotesquerie. An unpleasant and fascinating story of self-improvement and self-immolation. Taxi Driver for theatre kids.

In short, Jesse Eisenberg's The Debut is a sure-to-be-divisive, sure-to-entertain work of art. Showcasing Julianne Moore as a terrifyingly terrible community theatre actress and Paul Giamatti as her Whiplash meets Dead Poets Society mentor, its offbeat narrative style is paired with Moore's transformative performance of a lifetime. You might love it. You might hate it. But either way, you shouldn't miss it.
Club Kid

Writer/director/star Jordan Firstman's first-time feature feels anything but amateurish. The familiar story it tells, that of a disaffected young man (Peter) suddenly tasked with taking care of a son (Arlo) he never knew he had, would be enough for a good movie. But as soon as the sentimental comedy/drama steamrolls through the normal "reluctant mentor" story beats, it flips and crashes into something more.
The result is a star turn for just about everyone you see on screen (including Peter's odd roommate Nicky, played by Debut supporting actor Eldar Isgandarov). It also just might make you cry.

items: The Debut is totally going to win an Oscar
Club Kid is one of TIFF's best. It might make you cry

blocks.text: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother

Bassam Tariq's singular vision — both in terms of the movie's religious themes and gorgeously stylized cinematography — makes Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother something special. On top of that, star Mahershala Ali as Latif and his co-stars make it something incredible.

But it is Latif himself, a reluctant hitman who's lost his wife, nearly lost his faith, and is soon sent on a whirlwind mission to help a lost rich brat survive the week, that propels the story forward. It's a near-indefinable collage of styles and genres — birthdays, broken glass, smiles and tears — but one that is nearly impossible to look away from.
Julián

As he's dropped off at his grandma's house in Brooklyn for the summer, the star of hand-drawn Canadian co-production Julián (Knyght Darius Jack) is already off-balance. But a niggling sense of unease sets everything on edge: there is something pushing back against the person whom Julián wants to be, how he wants to act and what he's allowed to care about. That confusing, bigger-than-him battle pitches into a higher gear when he tries to join the local girls in making glamorous mermaid costumes for an upcoming parade.
For some reason he can't fathom, the world keeps telling him the person he wants to be is wrong. And as the movie proceeds to show, the world is better when we fix that.
Iron Boy

From Pixar animator Louis Clichy (and starring his own son, Gary, in the lead role) Iron Boy is another animated tale of fitting in. A French farm boy with a pernicious case of scoliosis, Christophe, 10, can't seem to keep things straight. He's fighting with his overbearing father, getting into trouble at school — and literally falling over at every opportunity. Our young hero is soon fitted with an iron back brace to keep things from tumbling into chaos.

Unsurprisingly, things don't go exactly to plan. Iron Boy's resultant charting of failure to meet expectations, first loves and redemptive self-acceptance is as much grounded character study as it is magical realism. Its entirely hand-drawn animation style is also a rare and beautiful sight to behold.
Toy Gun Bandit
Like if the infamously over-the-top "Montana Meth Project" anti-drug ads from the early 2000s had made a feature film, Toy Gun Bandit says "not even once" to robbing your local gas station.

Unfortunately, our star apparently never saw those ads. Instead, French-Canadian teen Félix makes bad choice after bad choice, sending his legal situation spiralling from bad to astronomically worse in a cautionary tale that reads like a modern day Reefer Madness.

What keeps the eclectic, almost incidental plot from fraying into nothingness is Felix himself: first-time actor Félix Munger — a true revelation — plays the desperate-for-attention eponymous protagonist with an electric, vulnerable and mesmerizing charisma. The film pairs wonderfully with TIFF's other Canadian teen-on-the-run film, In Alaska, as both are character studies grounded by powerhouse young performances. With Munger in front of the camera of Toy Gun Bandit, you cannot help but root — and mourn — for the bright future he constructs, then inevitably destroys.
Sunburn

Like street photography in motion, Sunburn makes the everyday fascinating — with serious thanks owed to François Truffaut's Small Change. The plot is as subtle as it is personal: a group of young people try to make sense of themselves, and each other, in Toronto's St. James Town neighbourhood during a heat wave.

And like TIFF's other teen-ensemble triumph La Gradiva, the true story is under the surface — though in Sunburn, that truth isn't quite so heart-rendingly tragic. What lifts Serville Poblete's coming-of-age hodgepodge to the next level despite its conversely light tone is the serious talent he displays for capturing and evoking senses and sensations.

The visceral capturing of dripping ice cream on a sweltering day. Of open mouths and dripping sweat. Of bursting pimples and bursting waterballoons and the general exuberance of real life. Every joyfully real aspect of the world he clearly knows so well is delivered in a dreamlike package.
Eklipse

"What did I do to you?" asks Tomy of his friend Chris — or the boy who used to be his friend. As Eklipse drifts from Tree of Life-esque shots of the trees, cattle and mountains of its Tyrolean Alps setting, the two drift further and further apart. And Tomy has no idea why.

However, we know it is because Tomy's father has contracted AIDS, a terrifying and misunderstood death sentence in this rural and remote 1990s setting — though no one has told Tomy. The tender and withholding, riddle-like feature from Manuel Wetscher is the kind many will hate: "Nothing even happens" will likely be a common critique.
But if you like solving a riddle, there's a wealth of painful, twist-the-knife messages just waiting to break your heart.
The Smell of Apples

Speaking of heartbreaking, that's something The Smell of Apples can deliver in spades. A view of apartheid South Africa told from the perspective of a white child reckoning with the sins of his father, you could call it Zone of Interest refracted through a psychically destructive coming-of-age story.

Or you could call it a serious Academy Award best international film contender, one made with such power and aplomb it would be an indictment to ignore. Or you could just call it what it is: incredible.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Latvia’s president warns that Europe is not up to date with drone and aerial warfare in Ukraine
articles.summary:
Edgars Rinkēvičs reveals that drone warfare in Ukraine is moving at ‘lightning speed’ and current efforts to prepare for an aerial war could be obsolete by next year

Latvia’s president has…

blocks.text: Latvia’s president has warned that Europe is not keeping up with developments of drone and aerial warfare in Ukraine and that most countries in Nato could not repulse an attack by Russian missiles if the conflict expands.

The remarks came during a Guardian interview in Washington DC in which Edgars Rinkēvičs said that the technological developments in drone warfare in Ukraine are moving at “lightning speed” and that current efforts to prepare for an aerial war could be obsolete by the middle of next year.
“What we see is that air defense, drone defense, anti-ballistic defense has serious problems,” he said. “And let’s be frank. Ukraine has it. The whole of Europe and Nato has it.
“Because if Russia decides to use a couple of missiles in that territory, I think that would be a serious challenge today for many countries to cope with that,” he added.

Ukraine and European allies are now facing a delay in supplies of crucial Patriot and other air-defense missiles. The US has expended nearly two-thirds of its stocks of critical interceptors in the war in Iran, according to analysis of a Congressional Budget Office assessment, and it could take at least five years to replenish stocks.
The US has considered outsourcing Patriot production to Ukraine and Europe but so far an agreement has not been made.

“It’s up to the United States government, it’s up to the company,” Rinkēvičs said, noting that discussions were ongoing and acknowledging the difficulties of some technical issues with licensing. “We have some capacities in Europe, but let’s face it: Patriots are still one of the best, if not the best, to tackle this.”

The remarks come ahead of the United Nations general assembly in New York City, where Donald Trump is expected to hold meetings with senior European leaders, and as Nato allies have stepped up their warnings about the risk of Russia escalating the war in Ukraine.

Poland’s prime minister Donald Tusk warned in a speech on Thursday that Russia could launch drone or missile strikes against Nato countries supporting Ukraine in the coming months in an effort to test the alliance’s commitment to collective defense under article 5 of its charter.
Tusk said that Russia would seek to “weaken Nato’s integrity” and show that “article 5 is more theoretical than practical,” adding that Russia would seek to play off the incidents as accidents.

The Baltic nations, which are also on Russia’s eastern flank, have tempered their warnings, saying that there was no indication that Moscow sought to launch a conventional war to retake territory that it once held under the Soviet Union.

But Russia would increase mobilisation in the coming months after local elections, Rinkēvičs said, then use the winter to “push” in Ukraine, and also to “do whatever it takes to dissuade nations that are supportive of Ukraine to continue”.
Acts of sabotage, cyber-attacks and drone and missile incidents all indicated Russia testing European resolve to support Ukraine, he said.
“I would rule out a conventional military incursion but we should be very vigilant when it comes to all kinds of other possibilities,” he said.
A Nato jet shot down a Russian drone over Lithuania on Tuesday. Poland scrambled fighter jets and closed Lublin and Rzeszów-Jasionka airports on Thursday due to a Russian strike on western Ukraine.

Rinkēvičs also expressed concern about whether European allies were on track to hit a goal of spending five per cent of GDP on defense that has become a White House benchmark for the Trump administration’s continued support for Nato.
He also said that discussions over Europe bearing a great burden for its own defense were growing “more constructive”, but added that when it comes to “real capabilities … you need time”.
“Our message is also to do that, we need time,” he said. “It cannot happen in a month, or in a year.”

articles.title: Trump signs sweeping Russia sanctions bill
articles.summary: The bill is named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a staunch advocate of aid for Ukraine.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has signed a sweeping sanctions bill, taking aim at Russia's economy by punishing major purchasers of its oil and gas.

The bill, passed by the US House of Representatives earlier this week, gives Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas – most significantly China and India.
At Trump's behest, the bill also extends to Iran's energy and weapons sectors.
The bill is named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, one of Ukraine's staunchest defenders in Washington before his death on 11 July.

The 48-page bill, formally titled the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, includes exceptions for countries that import less than 15% of their natural gas from Russia and are working to lessen their dependency.

Additionally, the bill includes sanctions against Russian President Vladimir Putin, senior figures within the Russian government as well as banks and other financial institutions and Russia's "shadow fleet" of tankers used to circumvent existing sanctions.
Senator Richard Blumenthal, a New York Democrat, previously described the legislation as "scorching sanctions" which would "throttle Putin's war machine".
Data from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, or CREA, shows that China accounted for 50% of Russian crude exports between December 2022 and August 2026, followed by India at 37%.
Turkey and the European Union each accounted for 5% during the same time period, although Russian energy exports to the EU have been decreasing.
Senator Graham had long sought to push the Trump administration to do more to punish Russia for the war that followed its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The bill also had the support of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who praised its passage by the House of Representatives earlier this week.

"It is symbolic that the US House of Representatives' passage of Lindsey Graham's sanctions bill took place on the night of yet another Russian attack on Ukraine involving ballistic missiles, other missiles, and drones," Zelensky wrote on Telegram on 17 September.
Graham, 71, died on 11 July of an "aortic dissection" caused by cardiovascular disease shortly after returning from a trip to Kyiv.
"He died doing the work he was born to do," Trump said at the time.

Prior to his death, he was widely considered one of Ukraine's fiercest allies on Capitol Hill, at a time when Republicans were bitterly divided over the extent of US involvement abroad and the amount of aid being given to Ukraine.

articles.title: Men deported from US bound and beaten in Equatorial Guinea detention hotel, lawyers say
articles.summary:
Group trapped at Hotel Bamy after US removal as rights groups sound alarm over poor conditions and violence

Two men that the Trump administration expelled to Equatorial Guinea were…

blocks.text: Two men that the Trump administration expelled to Equatorial Guinea were bound, fitted with bags over their heads, beaten and pushed down a flight of stairs, all in plain view of other US deportees, according to witnesses and human rights lawyers.

The men – one from Egypt and one from Eritrea – were then taken to a prison. About 30 detainees from the US remain trapped at a hotel in the outskirts of the coastal city of Malabo after being deported from the US. Detainees have said they believe the men were beaten for telling the press and human rights advocates about the poor conditions and violence inside the hotel, and that they are haunted by flashbacks and terrified they will be retaliated against next.
Human rights advocates and experts have warned for months that conditions at the Hotel Bamy – a run-down establishment that has served as a detention center for US deportees – are dangerous.

The US has sent at least 66 people from different African countries, Cuba and Brazil to Equatorial Guinea, which has received $7.5m as part of a deal to cooperate with the US deportation program. The Trump administration has pursued dozens of similar deals with countries to take in immigrants that the US cannot deport directly to their home countries, where judges have deemed they would face torture or persecution. In the past, the US government allowed those people to live and work in the US indefinitely.
The Trump administration, however, has sought instead to expel them to third countries where they have no ties, do not speak the local language and have no legal status – trapping them in limbo.

Advocates have been especially concerned for deportees sent to Equatorial Guinea, where the authoritarian government is notorious for human rights abuses, including torture, according to the US state department. Detainees held at Hotel Bamy have told the Guardian that armed guards keep watch over them 24/7, and that they have not been provided any medical care or even fresh clothes since arriving there. One of the detainees, who has a severe stomach hernia that requires visits to the hospital to drain his stomach due excessive fluid build-up, said he has been unable to see a doctor since arriving at Hotel Bamy.
Other detainees have managed to obtain medication for HIV, diabetes and other conditions via human rights lawyers, but remain fearful that access to medications will be arbitrarily cut off.

The two men who were tortured – Ahmed Soliman, 31, of Egypt, and Samson Birhane, 47, of Eritrea – have since been transferred to a prison in Malabo. Multiple witnesses recounted that the police officers shouted, “Where is the phone? Where is the phone!” as they beat the men, who had initially been accused of breaking a mirror at the hotel before they were pulled aside and arrested.

The beating, which occurred on 11 September, followed the release of a video first reported by Reuters showing conditions at the hotel and the violent behavior of the guards. The detainees had been using cellphones to communicate with lawyers and the media about the conditions they were facing.

blocks.caption: Equatorial Guinea police point gun at migrants deported by Trump administration - loop

blocks.text: In the video taken by Soliman, which lawyers shared with the Guardian, authorities are seen pointing guns at the deportees. A Cuban man asked the officer for the return of his confiscated mobile phone ​so he could contact relatives and a ​lawyer, but was ignored. When officers noticed Soliman filming the exchange with his mobile phone, multiple officers rushed at him and others standing nearby, pointed their guns, and told Soliman to remain on his knees with his hands up for 10-15 minutes.

In another video, Soliman was able to film authorities forcibly sending US deportees to Ethiopia, where they are likely to face torture. When deportees resisted going with authorities, officials gave them the option to “go back to their home country” or “go to prison”. At least 12 people have been returned by Equatorial Guinea to their home country, where they face persecution.

In May, human rights experts at the United Nations issued a rare public appeal asking Equatorial Guinea to halt plans to return deportees to their home countries and to comply with international human rights standards and avoid refoulement, or the expulsion of people to countries where they face persecution.

“This is a human rights catastrophe,” said Bella Mosselmans, director of the Global Strategic Litigation Council, who represents several of the deportees at Hotel Bamy. The US and Equatorial Guinea “must be held accountable for the atrocities they are committing”, she added.

In the week since Soliman and Birhane were beaten, police have also been searching the other detainees’ hotel rooms for cellphones, and have confiscated them. They have also barred lawyers from seeing the deportees. Authorities have told the 29 US deportees who remain at Hotel Bamy that they may never see Soliman or Birhane again, according to lawyers. One detainee who witnessed the beating said authorities treat them as if they are “blanks” who “don’t even exist”. Another detainee said an officer told her: “You will disappear from the earth. I am the law.”
Witnesses said they feared for the lives of Soliman and Birhane, who came to the US as children.

Soliman is a gay man from Egypt who had lived in Phoenix for most of his life. He had a green card, but lost status after he was convicted of drug possession. He served time for his crimes, and in October, a judge had determined he would face persecution and torture if he were to return to Egypt due to his sexuality.

Birhane had come to the US as a refugee when he was 13, but lost status after a conviction for robbery when he was in high school, in 1988. He was allowed to remain in the US after a judge ruled he faced torture in Eritrea, and had been regularly checking in with Immigration and Customs Enforcement as required.

Lawyers for the deportees shared copies of multiple emails they had sent to the US embassy in Equatorial Guinea alerting them to threats and violence against those detained at Hotel Bamy, but those messages have gone unanswered, they said. In July, amid a lawsuit challenging conditions for deportees, the African Commission issued an urgent interim order instructing the government of Equatorial Guinea to refrain from deporting, transferring, or relocating deportees against their will.
The US Department of Homeland Security did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.
A spokesperson for the state department said: “The US government will use all legal means to remove those with no right to remain in our country.”
The agency did not respond to questions about whether it was aware of how Equatorial Guinea was treating US deportees, nor would it acknowledge whether any measures have been taken to intervene.
“As a general matter, we do not comment on the details of our private diplomatic communications with other governments,” the spokesperson said.

articles.title: Canada to play Cuba for 2028 Olympic berth in men's volleyball
articles.summary: Canada is inching closer to a 2028 Olympic berth in men’s indoor volleyball following a three-set semifinal sweep of Mexico on Friday at a qualifying tournament in Moncton, N.B.

image.caption: Canada, the world's 13th-ranked men's indoor volleyball team, celebrates its second three-set sweep of Mexico in five days in Moncton, N.B. The Canadians are one win away from qualifying for the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles. (Ron Ward/Volleyball Canada)

blocks.text: Recap
Canada is inching closer to a 2028 Olympic berth in men’s indoor volleyball following a three-set semifinal sweep of Mexico on Friday at a qualifying tournament in Moncton, N.B.
13th-ranked Canadians post 3-set sweep over No. 23 Mexico in Moncton, N.B.
Canada is inching closer to a 2028 Olympic berth in men’s indoor volleyball.
The world’s 13th-ranked team can secure its spot for Los Angeles on Saturday with a victory over No. 16 Cuba in the NORCECA qualification final at 6 p.m. ET in Moncton, N.B.
For the second time this week, Canada’s 14-member outfit swept Mexico 3-0 in sets, by scores of 25-21, 25-18, 25-13 in the first of Friday's semifinals.

The Canadians, fresh off Wednesday's five-set defeat to the United States in the gold-medal match of the NORCECA Continental Championship, also in Moncton, outscored Mexico in attack points (42-31), blocks (8-0) and aces (8-2) at Avenir Centre.

"This was the last step before our final goal," Canada head coach Dan Lewis told Volleyball Canada. "[Our players have] executed everything they’ve needed to do up until this point. Now they need to rest and prepare for the final."
On Tuesday in Moncton, Canada swept Cuba in the continental semifinals to clinch its spot at the World Cup in Poland next Sept. 10-26.

The Canadians boasted the top four scorers in Friday's match, led by captain Eric Loeppky, who was named best spiker at the continental championship. The 28-year-old outside hitter from Winnipeg had 17 points, followed by Sharone Vernon-Evans (13) and Jackson Howe and Stephen Maar (10 each).
Fynn McCarthy of Kelowna, B.C., added seven points, following up his best server award with a match-high four aces.

items: Canadian men lose gold-medal match to U.S. at NORCECA tourney

blocks.text: Canadian player Xander Ketrzynski reminded he and his teammates need only to stick to what got them to the final.

“Just keep playing like ourselves. It’s just another volleyball game," the 26-year-old Toronto native said. "Sometimes at these big moments you can get a little bit ahead of yourself but at the end of the day, you got here for a reason, you’ve got to keep performing that way.”

items: Canadian men clinch 2027 World Cup berth, beating Cuba

blocks.text: Mauro Fuentes Rascón and Diego González, the top scorer in the continental championship, shared the scoring lead for Mexico with eight. Jesus Izaguirre contributed nine digs.

“Mexico fought hard, but our guys showed up to play," added Ketrzynski. "They battled, they executed and we played the way we’re supposed to, the way we practised all summer. Our hard work showed today."
Canadians didn't panic after slow start

Lewis noted it was important for his charges to understand there would be an initial storm of aggressive serving by the Mexicans and if they built momentum, the Canadians would need to stay cool and return pressure on serves.
Canada fell behind 14-9 in the first set but took eight of the next 10 points, capped by a Maar ace, for a 17-16 advantage and didn't relinquish the lead.
Neither team led by more than four points in the second set until Canada went ahead 23-17.

"Continue to identify the opportunities to take points," Lewis said. "After that, we switched and had more service pressure on them. We started to dig balls and that really put them at a big disadvantage."

items: Things are looking up for Canada's volleyball teams
Canadian women's volleyball team qualifies for Olympics for 1st time since 1996

blocks.text: The Canadians held leads of 8-4 and 15-7 on the way to a convincing third-set victory.
Canada's squad has competed at six Summer Games, achieving its best result with a fourth-place finish in 1984, also in L.A.
Canada also swept the Mexicans in 2024 Olympic qualifying and placed 10th in Paris.
In 2016, Mexico finished 11th in Rio after ending a 48-year Olympic absence.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Doug Harrison has covered the professional and amateur scene as a senior writer for CBC Sports since 2003. Previously, the Burlington, Ont., native covered the NHL and other leagues for Faceoff.com. Follow the award-winning journalist @harrisoncbc

articles.title: Trump claims deal struck with Denmark to give U.S. security control over Greenland
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump said on Friday that Washington has entered an agreement ‌with Denmark and Greenland that gives ‌the U.S. permanent ​control over security, and all other ​needs, in…

image.caption: A demonstrator displays a Greenland flag during a protest outside the U.S. consulate in Nuuk, Greenland, on Jan. 22. (Marko Djurica/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·Breaking

U.S. President Donald Trump said on Friday that Washington has entered an agreement ‌with Denmark and Greenland that gives ‌the U.S. permanent ​control over security, and all other ​needs, in ​Greenland.
Agreement could see significant U.S. military presence on the island

The United States, Denmark and Greenland ‌have entered into an agreement that will see the US develop a significant military presence on the island, while prohibiting U.S. adversaries from ​building their own bases there, Donald Trump ​said on Friday.

In a Truth Social post, the U.S. president wrote that no ​U.S. enemies would be able to make sensitive ⁠investments on the island ⁠without the approval ‌of the United States and that the agreement had no expiry date.

"At my direction, we worked with representatives of Denmark and Greenland to guarantee that ⁠the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure ‌and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America," Trump wrote.

"Additionally, from now on, no U.S. adversary can EVER have a base ​in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive ⁠investments in Greenland, without our express written approval."

Earlier on Friday, ⁠Reuters exclusively reported that the U.S. and Greenland were ⁠closing ⁠in on a ​deal for the island that would result in an increased U.S. ​military presence, ⁠but would stop well short of Trump's long-held dream of acquiring the island for the United States.

articles.title: UP students stage walkout over 2027 budget cuts, Pax Silica
articles.summary: Around 6,000 students, teachers, and officials from the University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB) joined a walkout on Friday to protest issues including education budget cuts and the proposed…

blocks.text: Published September 19, 2026 5:20am

Around 6,000 students, teachers, and officials from the University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB) joined a walkout on Friday to protest issues including education budget cuts and the proposed Pax Silica initiative.

In a video posted online by UPLB Perspective, students from various UPLB departments were seen joining the protest and chanting calls for accountability over corruption and the defense of people’s rights.
In a statement, the UPLB Student Council said the walkout drew thousands of participants despite heavy rainfall.
The student body reiterated its call to hold accountable those behind billions of pesos in anomalous flood control projects.

“Kung matatandaan natin, noong nakaraang taon ay 7,000 na indibidwal ang nakiisa sa walkout na ginanap hinggil sa bilyon-bilyong pisong halagang pondo na ninakaw mula sa mga mamamayan para sa mga ghost flood control projects,” the UPLB Student Council said.
(If we recall, 7,000 individuals participated in last year’s walkout over the billions of pesos in public funds stolen from the people for ghost flood control projects.)

“Ngunit magpahanggang ngayon ay hindi pa rin nakukulong ang lahat ng mga sangkot, at patuloy pa rin na nagpapakasasa sa pera ng mamamayang ninakawan nila ang mga korakot habang ang sambayanang Pilipino ay patuloy pa rin na lumulusong sa baha, nawawalan ng tahanan, naaantala ang kabuhayan, at nasasawi ang mga buhay,” it added.

(Yet up to now, not all those involved have been jailed, and corrupt officials continue to feast on the people’s stolen money while Filipinos continue to wade through floods, lose their homes, suffer disruptions to their livelihoods, and lose their lives.)
Students from the University of the Philippines Diliman (UPD) likewise staged a demonstration, raising similar concerns.
The UPD Student Council said around 3,000 students joined the walkout.
In a statement, the UPD student body cited reports of farmers and Indigenous Peoples in Tarlac being displaced to clear land for the proposed Pax Silica project.
“Huwad ang development na ito dahil alam nating lahat na ang proyektong ito ay para lamang sa gahamang interes ng mga nasa tuktok,” it said.
(This development is a lie because we all know that this project is solely for the greedy interests of those at the top.)
The UPD Student Council also cited a potential P2.95 billion reduction in funding for the UP System under the proposed 2027 national budget.
UPLB and UPD are set to hold protests on September 21, marking the 54th anniversary of the declaration of martial law under former President Ferdinand Marcos Sr. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Carney rallies Liberal MPs as 'crucial session' of Parliament set to resume
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Friday his government is focused on bringing down costs for Canadians and defending the country's sovereignty, though he acknowledged that some of those efforts are…

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney gives a speech to his caucus on Friday in Ottawa. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Friday his government is focused on bringing down costs for Canadians and defending the country's sovereignty, though he acknowledged that some of those efforts are in their early stages.
House of Commons returns next week after summer recess
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Sep 18, 2026 5:18 PM EDT | Last Updated: 12 minutes ago

Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government is focused on bringing down costs for Canadians and defending the country's sovereignty, though he acknowledged that some of those efforts are in their early stages.

"As we build Canada strong, we remain laser focused on bringing down costs for Canadians and keeping Canadians safe. Because we know that the full benefits of our plan will take some time," he said on Friday to a room full of Liberal MPs.
Speaking to the Liberal caucus as MPs prepared to return to the House of Commons next week, Carney welcomed three new members who won byelections in August.

The Opposition Conservatives have been sharpening their lines of attack on the government. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre asked at a news conference this week whether Canadians feel their lives have improved since Carney took office.

items: As Carney's popularity soars, Conservatives weigh what to do
Carney is 'fast-tracking corporate Canada's wish list' in trade war: NDP leader
6 more byelections on horizon will test Liberal momentum

blocks.text: Carney, who just wrapped a busy week that included an investment summit in Toronto and a speech to the European Parliament in France, told MPs that "was just the warm-up."
"This is a crucial session of the House of Commons," he told the caucus. "We are going to introduce some of the most consequential legislation not just of this government, but in decades."
He said the government will introduce a bill this fall to streamline project reviews, to be known as the Building Canada Strong Act.
"For projects and supply chains, our standard will be simple: one project, one review, one year," he said.
"If we're going to say no, say no quickly. If we are going to say yes, say yes on time. When Canada decides a project should go ahead, that project will go ahead."
Carney: 'High standards do not mean decisions have to be slow'
Canada can maintain its high standards for projects while moving quickly, he said.
The prime minister said the government will also push ahead with its social media and AI regulation bill this fall.
"We've been hearing the concerns of families and educators, medical practitioners in our community, children falling victims of sexual abuse, cyberbullying and extreme violence online," he said.
"The status quo is failing our kids. The tech companies won't fix it. We will not stand by."
The government is also set to release a new budget during this fall sitting, which is expected to run until December.
Carney said the government will "manage spending and optimize our balance sheet" with its fiscal plan.
He said the government is in a financial position now to add new support for social programs and expand child care, but did not share specifics.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
David Baxter is a reporter with The Canadian Press
With files from Sarah Ritchie

The Traitors is back with a new lineup of stars ready for their murder mystery moment. The cast of the award-winning reality competition series' fifth season was announced Friday, bringing together a new slate of celebs and reality TV stars into the castle with the same frame of mind: trust no one.
Alan Cummings to return as host of the Emmy Award-winning show
The Traitors is back with a new lineup of stars ready for their murder mystery moment.

articles.title: Israel moving ahead with settlement plans that would split West Bank in two, rights group says
articles.summary: Rights groups say the Israeli government is forging ahead with a contentious settlement expansion plan that would effectively divide the occupied West Bank, long criticized as a threat to the…

image.caption: A Palestinian man reacts as Israeli forces stand guard during the demolition of a Palestinian building near Hebron in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on Wednesday. (Mussa Qawasma/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Rights groups say the Israeli government is forging ahead with a contentious settlement expansion plan that would effectively divide the occupied West Bank, long criticized as a threat to the viability of a future Palestinian state.
Netanyahu government accelerated, intensified 'elimination' in West Bank: B'Tselem report

A rights groups says the Israeli government is forging ahead with a contentious settlement expansion plan that would effectively divide the occupied West Bank, a plan long criticized as a threat to the viability of a future Palestinian state.
On Wednesday, Israeli rights group Ir Amim said Israel's government will open the bidding for an additional 2,167 units in a settlement project that would effectively cut the West Bank in two.

The tender for 2,167 units is in addition to a tender for 1,234 units announced at the end of August, tripling the amount of housing units and bringing the total number of housing units to 3,401, the group said in a statement.

Settlement development in this open tract of land east of Jerusalem known as E1 is especially contentious because it runs from the outskirts of Jerusalem deep into the occupied West Bank. It would bisect the West Bank and cut it off from East Jerusalem — fragmenting the land Palestinians hope will form the heart of a state.

The United Nations and most countries deem the settlements illegal under Article 49 of the Fourth Geneva Convention pertaining to military occupations. Israel rejects this, calling the area "disputed" rather than occupied.
The E1 project has been under consideration for more than two decades, but was frozen due to U.S. pressure during previous administrations.

items: U.S. ambassador visits Palestinian town amid rise in occupied West Bank settler violence
Canada, U.K., France to ban trade of goods from Israeli settlements in occupied West Bank

blocks.text: A spokesperson for Palestinian President Mahmoud ​Abbas condemned the new units as a violation of international law.
Israel has not officially confirmed the bids are out to tender. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office did not respond to a request for comment.

Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, an ultra-nationalist in the governing right-wing coalition, has said the plan would "bury" a Palestinian state. Smotrich, who is accused of pushing "extremist rhetoric," is sanctioned by Canada and several other countries for "inciting violence against Palestinians in the West Bank," by calling for their displacement for expanded Israeli settlements.
Controversial West Bank settlement project gets final approval
Bidding to open days before elections
The tender is scheduled to open for bidding on Oct. 25, two days before Israel is due to hold a parliamentary election.
Israel's right-wing coalition government has approved a massive expansion of settlements in the West Bank.
Ir Amim said the bidding date reflected the government's resolve to push ahead with the settlement project and "create an increasingly irreversible reality on the ground ahead of the elections."
It comes days after Canada, Britain and France banned exports from Israeli settlements in the West Bank last week.
Netanyahu's actions around the time of the Palestinian militant group Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023 attack are a key issue in the campaign.

There has been mounting criticism of the prime minister, who has rejected calls for an official government inquiry into the events surrounding the Oct. 7 attacks. Last week, Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported that Netanyahu was directly warned by the U.A.E. that Hamas was planning a major offensive just days before the attack. Haaretz reported Netanyahu's office called the report an "absolute lie."

Peace Now, an organization that tracks settlement expansion in the West Bank, called the project "deadly for the future of Israel and for any chance of achieving a peaceful two-state solution" which is "guaranteeing many more years of bloodshed."
Last month, British Foreign ​Secretary Ed Miliband condemned Israel's launch of a tender for the E1 project.

"The impact of settler violence and terrorism has been catastrophic for Palestinian communities. Settlement expansion and attempts to create irreversible divisions on the ground threaten peace, security and the prospects for a viable Palestinian state," Miliband said.
Some 700,000 Israelis live in the occupied West Bank and east Jerusalem, territories captured by Israel in 1967.
Report accuses Israel of 'mechanism of elimination'
On Monday, Israeli human rights group B’Tselem accused Israel's government of "rapidly and systematically dismantling all the foundations of Palestinian existence."

A new report by the organization points out five main areas that it says prove that Israel's actions in the West Bank are part of a "comprehensive mechanism of elimination," which include: violence and intimidation; movement restrictions; economic strangulation; social and political disruption; and territorial takeover and displacement of Palestinians.
It alleges that Israeli authorities use policies across the five areas to expand permanent Israeli control over the territory while weakening Palestinian communities.
B'Tselem said the use of those mechanisms has "accelerated and intensified" since the current Netanyahu government took office in 2022, but particularly following the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks.
B'Tselem said the policies are being conducted "more openly, directly and violently" than before.

Israeli authorities have generally claimed that violent settlers are a small extremist minority acting outside government policy, not representatives of the broader settler movement or the state, though the report said that settler militias are not a "rogue external force" but an "operational arm of the mechanism of territorial control."
"Official state bodies do not have to expel every community themselves. They create conditions in which armed settlers, with state backing, make Palestinian life impossible," it said.
United Nations data shows settler violence in the West Bank has reached record levels.

items: Israeli settler blockades part of escalating violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank
Prosecutors charge Israeli settler for killing Palestinian activist in West Bank

blocks.text: More than 1,260 attacks causing casualties or property damage were recorded in the first half of 2026 — about six incidents per day — while 18 Palestinians were killed in settler-related incidents by late July, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.
"The current reality in the West Bank is neither a temporary crisis nor a collection of random human rights violations," the B'Tselem report notes.

"It is an accelerated and explicit phase in an ongoing project of elimination that operates within the Israeli apartheid regime and is driven by a settler-colonial logic of dispossession, displacement, and the establishment of Jewish-Israeli sovereignty."
Israel's government did not respond to a request for comment on the report.

Officials have rejected accusations by B'Tselem and other rights groups that characterize Israeli rule as apartheid or as a systematic effort to dispossess Palestinians, arguing that Israeli policies are driven by security concerns and historical claims to the territory.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Sara Jabakhanji is a Toronto-based senior writer assigned to cover news developments in the Middle East. She has worked in CBC bureaus in Ottawa, London and Toronto. You can reach her at sara.jabakhanji@cbc.ca.
With files from Reuters
