articles.title: Ronaldo named in first Portugal squad since World Cup - at age of 41
articles.summary: Cristiano Ronaldo is named in the first squad selected by new Portugal coach Jorge Jesus for their upcoming Nations League games.

blocks.text: Cristiano Ronaldo has been named in the first squad selected by new Portugal coach Jorge Jesus, ending speculation the 41-year-old could retire from international football.
Ronaldo refused to confirm whether he would continue to play for his country after Portugal's World Cup round-of-16 defeat by eventual winners Spain in July.
But the Al-Nassr forward is part of a 25-man group chosen for Portugal's four Nations League games between 24 September and 4 October.
Jesus has replaced Roberto Martinez, who stepped down as Portugal coach after their World Cup exit.
The 72-year-old was Ronaldo's club boss last season, when the pair helped Al-Nassr win the Saudi Pro League for the first time in seven years.
The former Manchester United Real Madrid forward, who announced that this summer's World Cup would be his last, was in tears after Portugal's World Cup exit.
When asked if he would keep playing for his country, he said: "I will meet the family and take decisions with a calm head."
This sparked speculation he could follow his great rival Lionel Messi and retire from international football.
Ronaldo will turn 42 before next summer's Nations League finals and will be 43 by Euro 2028.
The oldest player in the history of the Euros is Ronaldo's former Portugal team-mate Pepe, who was 41 and 130 days for his last game at Euro 2024.
Manchester United pair Diogo Dalot and Bruno Fernandes are also in the squad, along with Ruben Dias (Manchester City) and Pedro Neto (Chelsea).
Portugal are at home to Wales on 24 September (19:45 BST) and away to Norway three days later. They then play in Denmark on 1 October and return home to host Norway on 4 October.

articles.title: Police begin operation to move migrants from Ceuta beaches
articles.summary: Police reportedly fired into the air on Friday morning as they struggled to contain crowds jostling to secure a place at the tented site.

blocks.text: Police have begun moving hundreds of migrants in Ceuta to a new tented site in the port area of the Spanish territory in north Africa.
Officers struggled to contain crowds of people jostling to secure a place at the site after weeks of living on the beaches. Shots could be heard, with reports that police fired into the air.
Several hundred migrants have now reached the camp, which has a capacity for 1,700 people.
Most of the 72,000 migrants who breached the border from Morocco in July have returned, but it is believed that more than 13,000 remain in the enclave.
The operation began at about 07:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Friday, with more than 3,000 migrants being transferred, according to the Spanish government-owned news agency Efe.
During the process, some migrants broke through the cordon along the designated 2km (1.2 mile) route to the port. Video shows young men running in the darkness as police tried to maintain control.

More than 170 police officers have been deployed, including drone technicians, Efe reported. It added that the situation was later "brought under control quickly", and the operation was able to continue.
The operation is part of the government's attempt to concentrate the migrants in facilities where they can be identified and cared for while their administrative status is individually determined.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy holdout juror had no doubt she deliberately killed her children
articles.summary: It is the first time the juror, who refused to side with the others and acquit Clancy, has spoken publicly about his decision.

blocks.text: The lone holdout juror in the trial of Lindsay Clancy has said he "didn't have any doubts" that she was criminally responsible for killing her three children.

"Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she knew exactly what she was doing and planned it," Michael Desronvil said in a statement to CBS News, the BBC's US partner.
The judge declared a mistrial on 4 September after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict following nearly 40 hours of deliberating.
Clancy admitted to the killings but her lawyers argued she had been suffering from postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors said the killings were calculated.
Warning: This article contains distressing details

The 36-year-old was charged with three counts of first-degree murder after strangling Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months, at the family's Massachusetts home before jumping out of the second-floor window.

To find Clancy guilty, jurors had to be unanimously convinced beyond reasonable doubt that she intentionally killed her children and that she did not do so as a result of postpartum psychosis, a rare and serious condition.
The jury - nine women and three men - considered a range of options including not guilty by reason of insanity, manslaughter and first-degree murder.
Several jurors have said following the mistrial being declared that the panel was ultimately divided 11-1 in favour of finding Clancy not criminally responsible.
Desronvil said he believed the evidence presented in court showed she had planned the killings.
"I didn't have any doubts," he said in a statement to CBS on Thursday.
"As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented."
Paula Devlin, one of the other jurors, told CBS Mornings that the panel had spent several days trying to convince Desronvil to change his mind.
"We all worked together to convince ourselves once we got to that point where it was 10 to 2," she said.
The jury foreperson, a retired fifth-grade teacher, described not being able to reach a verdict as "awful" and an "emotional rollercoaster".

She told NBC that Desronvil had "admitted he had reasonable doubt", but as she started filling out the verdict sheets, he apparently said: "But I'm still not going to say that she's not guilty by reason of insanity."

Another juror told local CBS station WBZ-TV that most of the jurors had been "very firm in their stance" from the start and "the stand-alone juror was not the only one that was unwilling to see things from the other side".
But they added that because Desronvil would not "follow" his reasonable doubt nor offer logical reasoning for his position, they felt Clancy had not received a fair trial.
The identities of all 11 jurors have not been officially disclosed but in the US, once a case is over, any juror can choose to speak publicly about a case and their deliberations.
Patrick Clancy, the children's father and Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband, is due to speak publicly about the case in an interview with the CBS programme 60 Minutes on Sunday.
In it, he is expected to discuss his grief, his memories of his children and the conspiracy theories that have flooded social media since the trial began.
He said he still speaks to his children "all the time", describing it as "a way I stay connected to them".

During the trial, Clancy's defence team had attempted to use her being put on more than a dozen medications in the lead-up to the killings, as well as seeking help from a suicide hotline and an emergency room, as evidence of her psychosis.
Postpartum psychosis can involve hallucinations and delusions, and her lawyers argued that she was unable to understand the nature of her actions or distinguish right from wrong.
A forensic psychiatrist who testified for the defence said Clancy experienced a "command hallucination" and a "delusion of influence" when she killed her children.

However, her psychiatrist testified for the prosecution that Clancy did not show signs of psychosis during their sessions, while another psychiatrist noted that the condition was not currently recognised by the American Psychiatric Association.

Under Massachusetts law, prosecutors had to prove beyond any reasonable doubt that Clancy was criminally responsible for the jury to find her guilty. The defence did not have to prove her mental illness or lack of criminal responsibility.
The mistrial leaves the case unresolved. Prosecutors have not said whether they will seek a retrial.
Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, has said he hopes to reach an agreement with prosecutors to avoid a second trial.
He told ABC's Good Morning America that he was upset that the lone juror would not acquit Clancy.
He said the holdout "would not apply the law of reasonable doubt" as instructed by the judge, adding: "That's not right. And that's why I was upset."
The next court hearing is scheduled for 29 September at Plymouth Superior Court in Massachusetts.

articles.title: New cat species identified for the 1st time in a century
articles.summary: A diminutive wild cat that inhabits Bolivia's cloud forest has been identified as a previously unknown species, marking the first time a new living cat species has been formally named and described…

image.caption: A Leopardus tilcayo cat, a newly identified species through research led by National Geographic explorer Paola Nogales Ascarrunz, walks at the Senda Verde animal refuge in Bolivia's Yungas region on Sept. 1, 2026. (Fernando Faciole/National Geographic via Reuters)

blocks.text: Science·New

A diminutive wild cat that inhabits Bolivia's cloud forest has been identified as a previously unknown species, marking the first time a new living cat species has been formally named and described in more than a century.
Leopardus tilcayo is a tiger cat identified as a new species through genetic testing
The cat, called Tilcayo by local communities, is ‌part of a group called tiger cats found across much of South America.

It was found in Bolivia's lush Yungas forest, a mountainous region where forests are often covered by clouds and surrounded by high humidity, according to researchers. It measures about 46 centimetres (18 inches) long and weighs around three pounds, making it smaller than the average domestic cat.
Researchers used genetic data to confirm that the cat is a new species, ​and gave it the scientific name Leopardus tilcayo, retaining its local name.

"Its fur is ​light brown … with irregularly shaped rosettes across its body," said Paola Nogales Ascarrunz, a National Geographic explorer and one of the authors of the study describing the newly identified species published on Thursday in the journal Current Biology.

Little is yet known about the cat's biology and ​lifestyle. Remains of small rodents in scat samples suggest they may form part of its diet, while camera-trap evidence indicates it could be ⁠more active at night, Nogales Ascarrunz said.

Tiger ⁠cats are so-called cryptic species, meaning they cannot easily be distinguished merely by appearance, ‌said evolutionary biologist and study co-lead author Jonas Lescroart, of the University of Antwerp in Belgium.
Tiger cats previously had been considered a single species, but genetic studies decades ago suggested the existence of multiple species.
Only 2 live individuals found so far
Referring to the new species, Lescroart said, "Our information at this moment is limited to the two live individuals that we examined, and a small number of camera-trap records."
One of the live cats is a 10-year-old male that now lives ⁠in Senda Verde Wildlife Sanctuary after being kept by a local family in their home.

Observing the Bolivian cat drew interest because "its characteristics did not match the descriptions, most of them based on Brazilian cats," Nogales Ascarrunz said. "This made us wonder: What tiger cat do we actually have in Bolivia?"
The team analyzed DNA from 38 cats sampled across ‌several South American countries, including eight museum specimens. The study found that tiger cats are in fact five genetically distinct species.
"We never expected this Bolivian tiger cat to be a separate species, and no one had ever proposed it as a different animal — subspecies or otherwise," Lescroart said.
Genetic analysis suggested that the Tilcayo lineage separated from other tiger cats about 1.4 million years ago.

"The more differences in their DNA, the longer the time that we ​estimate those lineages to have been physically separated," Lescroart said, adding that such a gap is generally considered a species-level divide in cats.

The research team also described a new tiger cat subspecies in Peru's Yungas, naming it Leopardus ⁠tigrinus antisuyo after Antisuyu, the region of the old Inca Empire that included the area it inhabits.
See some of the new species discovered in 2025
New species may be listed as endangered
The International Union for Conservation of Nature's red list, ⁠tracking the status of species, currently treats tiger cats as two "vulnerable" species with declining populations.

The researchers have shared their findings with the IUCN, whose upcoming review ⁠will assess ⁠the five lineages separately. That could give a more accurate picture ​of risk, Lescroart said, and species such as the Tilcayo could potentially be considered endangered when assessed on their own.
The need for a clearer assessment is particularly acute ​in the Yungas, one of the region's most ⁠threatened ecosystems.

The mountain forests face growing pressure from deforestation, agricultural expansion, human-caused fires and mining, Nogales Ascarrunz said. Restoring forest patches damaged by fires, protecting remaining native forest and maintaining connections between habitats are urgent priorities, Nogales Ascarrunz added.

"Showing the general public that even in a flagship group such as cats … there are still new species to be discovered may transmit an important message," said Eduardo Eizirik, an evolutionary biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil and senior author of the study.
"There are many undiscovered species out there ⁠in the world, and they are at risk of ‌disappearing before we even discover them."

articles.title: At least 16 killed after vehicle loaded with explosives rams into Pakistan mosque
articles.summary: A vehicle loaded with explosives rammed into a mosque building during Friday prayers, a senior police official says.

blocks.text: At least 16 people, including five police officers, have been killed after a vehicle loaded with explosives rammed into a mosque in north-western Pakistan, according to a senior police official in Peshawar.
A gun battle is still ongoing between attackers and security forces at the mosque, near police headquarters, in the Kohat district of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
One of the assailants has reportedly been killed, an officer says, and a rescue operation is under way.
In a statement, Pakistan's President Asif Ali Zardari expressed "his best wishes for the swift recovery of those injured in the explosion."
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa police chief inspector general Zulfikar Hameed described the attack as a "suicide attack" to Reuters news agency.
There has been no immediate claim of responsibility.
Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif also condemned the blast.
Militancy in Pakistan's border areas has risen sharply in recent months, targeting the military and police.
Islamabad says the militants use safe haven in Afghanistan to train and plan attacks in Pakistan.
Afghanistan's Taliban government has denied the accusation and said militancy is Pakistan's domestic problem.

articles.title: British woman who was kidnapped in Malawi rescued by police after shootout
articles.summary:
Four of Nurat Osman’s alleged abductors were killed during rescue after she was taken from outside her home last week

A British woman kidnapped in Malawi last week has been rescued by police…

blocks.text: A British woman kidnapped in Malawi last week has been rescued by police after a shootout in which four of her alleged abductors were killed.

Nusrat Osman was abducted outside her home in the southern city of Blantyre on 11 September at about 12.30pm. Police had offered a reward of 30m Malawi kwacha (£12,950) for information leading to her rescue and the arrest of the perpetrators.

Malawian police announced Osman’s rescue late on Thursday in a statement. “There was an exchange of fire between police and kidnappers, who were armed with [an] AK47 rifle and a Girsan Regard MC pistol. In the process, the criminals got shot and were taken to hospital where they succumbed to their injuries.” it read.

A police officer, deputy inspector general Mlowoka Noel Kayira, was also shot during the operation. “He is currently receiving medical attention at the hospital and is in a stable condition,” police said.
Osman, a 47-year-old auditor and mother of two, was safe and “not too shaken” after her ordeal, her brother Shobi Jiwa told the Sun, expressing his gratitude to Malawi’s police.

Jiwa reserved special thanks for Kayira. “He is the hero of our family. He’s the hero of the country,” he said. “He’s the hero of the world, actually, for putting his life at risk and taking a bullet into himself for my sister.”
Kidnappings are rare in Malawi, which has experienced a rise in pickpocketing and house burglaries by often armed men in recent years amid unstable, crisis-ridden economic conditions.
The landlocked southern African country is one of the world’s poorest nations, with a population of about 22 million and an average annual income of just $672, according to the World Bank.

In 2024, a country report by the US state department’s diplomatic security service said: “Kidnappings are not a widespread concern in Malawi, and there have been no recent high-profile incidents involving westerners.

“Historically, expatriates have not been significant targets for kidnappings in the country. When kidnappings do occur, they often involve members of the Asian business community rather than foreign travellers or residents.”

Osman, who is originally from Leicester, worked for a local audit firm and had lived in Malawi with her husband and children for several years. Before her rescue, her family said they had not had any news of her, including any contact from the kidnappers demanding a ransom.
Her husband, Nazil Osman, told the local news outlet Nyasa Times: “I don’t know where she is or how she is. My wife is an auditor, and I have no issues with anyone.”
Her brother told the Sun on Tuesday: “My sister has been missing for five days with no trace or call,” adding that the family could not think of a motive for her kidnapping.
Police did not say whether information received in response to the offered reward had led to Osman’s rescue, adding that investigations were ongoing and more details would be shared “in due course”.

articles.title: Early voting begins in midterms as campaign shifts focus to cost of living and Iran war – US politics live
articles.summary:
Campaigning or control of Congress is expected to ramp up as some states open early voting

Good morning, and welcome to our US politics live blog. The midterm elections are less than…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 18s agoTrump officials sending undocumented children to Texas sparks fears of mass deportation
20m agoEarly voting begins in midterms as cost of living and Iran war loom large

blocks.text: Trump officials sending undocumented children to Texas sparks fears of mass deportation
Alexandra Villarreal

The Trump administration has started sending a majority of undocumented children who came to the US alone and have new immigration court cases to Texas, where government facilities for them are unlicensed, their chances of getting a lawyer are low and advocates fear that “a deportation churn-out factory” awaits them, the Guardian has learned.

blocks.caption: Unaccompanied minors wait in Texas to be transported by the US Border Patrol after crossing the Rio Grande River from Mexico. Photograph: Go Nakamura/Reuters

blocks.text: Almost 80% of children in federal custody who arrived unaccompanied by a parent or legal guardian and who were placed in immigration court proceedings in July – and over 90% in August – have been funneled into shelter networks somewhere in Texas, a dramatic upswing from the months prior, according to analysis shared exclusively with the Guardian from researchers at the immigration data insights platform bklg.org.

This is understood to amount to a total of 925 children in the care of the Health and Human Services (HHS) department’s office of refugee resettlement (ORR) and in open immigration court proceedings based in Texas, with 651 sent there in July and August alone.
Early voting begins in midterms as cost of living and Iran war loom large

Good morning, and welcome to our US politics live blog. The midterm elections are less than two months away, but some states begin early voting today, marking the start of a crucial stretch of campaigning for control of Congress.

Virginia begins early in-person voting, while voters in Minnesota, Idaho and South Dakota can cast absentee ballots in person, as the campaign turns increasingly on the cost of living and the continuing war in Iran.

blocks.caption: The start of early voting comes at a time of deep angst among many US citizens about issues including rising gas. Photograph: Nam Y Huh/AP

blocks.text: High gas prices and low approval ratings are adding to the challenges facing president Donald Trump as Republicans head into the 3 November elections with their control of the House and Senate at risk. In its analysis of the US economy, the Wall Street Journal reports that mortgage rates are nearing 7%, consumer prices rose 3.4% in the year to August and gas prices are close to their highest levels since 2022.

“We are seeing what happens when a president launches a war of choice without anticipating the unintended consequences,” Aaron David Miller, a former adviser on Middle East policy to Republican and Democratic administrations, told Reuters.

Trump will take his case to the UN on Tuesday, where he is likely to present the Iran war as a victory despite having initially promised the military campaign would be over within weeks. The conflict has instead entered its seventh month, with Iran still able to disrupt regional shipping and the war putting further pressure on global energy prices.
In other developments:

items: The Trump administration has approved a potential sale of 48 advanced F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, worth an estimated $24.3b. The Department of State said the propose sale “will improve Saudi Arabia’s capability to deter current and future threats by strengthening its homeland defense”. The move comes despite concerns from intelligence agencies that China could potentially gain access to, or steal, sensitive F-35 technology through Saudi Arabia, according to the New York Times. The newspaper reported:

blocks.text: double quotation markOne detailed report, issued months ago by the Pentagon’s Defense Intelligence Agency, raised questions about whether the Americans and Saudis would be able to secure sites with F-35 technology. It also raised concerns about the access that Chinese military personnel have to Saudi bases and the prevalent use by Saudi Arabia of Chinese technology in telecommunications infrastructure and defense installations.

items: Former staff members of the US Institute of Peace have asked a federal appeals court to prevent the Trump administration from carving the president’s name into the facade of its headquarters in Washington, which was renamed the ‘“Donald J. Trump United States Institute of Peace” last year. Lawyers for the institute’s ousted board members argued that engraving Trump’s name on the building would cause “irreparable harm” by undermining the organization’s independent mission.

The USIP dispute comes as another Washington cultural institution faces a court battle over changes under Trump. A federal judge has ordered the Kennedy Center to give 30 days’ notice before making any major physical changes to the building, including demolition as Trump has threatened. The president said the centre could be “ripped down” amid a dispute over plans to put his name on the building and a proposed $257m renovation. The center is currently closed due to what its Trump-backed leadership described as safety issues caused by age and structural deficiencies.

blocks.caption: Traffic cones keep cars from entering the driveway at the Kennedy Center in Washington, which was ordered to be closed for repairs by its board. Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/Reuters

articles.title: Dozens of suspected illegal miners die in Nigerian custody
articles.summary: Authorities linked the deaths to disease, but this has been disputed by intelligence reports and relatives of the accused.
articles.byline: Makuochi Okafor, Harry Sekulich, Wycliffe Muia

blocks.text: Thirty-seven people accused of illegal mining in north-central Nigeria have died in custody, local officials said.
Police have set up an investigation into the deaths, which the Nigerian Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) blamed on an apparent disease outbreak.
However, an intelligence report shared with AFP news agency suggested the group died because of overcrowding and poor ventilation inside the detention facility in Niger state.
"We believe they suffocated because there was no ventilation," the father of one of those detained told the BBC.
Abdullahi Dalhatu said his son had survived because he was near a small window.
"His friend slumped and fainted, and many others also collapsed."
His son described how detainees began collapsing in the heat of the overcrowded and poorly ventilated cell, his father said.
He said the detainees repeatedly knocked on the door for help but nobody opened it.
State governor Mohammed Umaru Bago called the deaths "sad and tragic" during a press conference on Thursday.
An NSCDC commander has been detained following the deaths, Bago added.
He declared three days of mourning and postponed the start of campaigning for elections scheduled for January.
Officials had arrested the group of young men on Tuesday for suspected illegal mining near Borgu, in the mineral-rich state of Niger. The region is known for small-scale gold mining.

Two days later, 37 people detained as part of the suspected unlawful operation were found dead inside the detention centre run by the NSCDC, a paramilitary agency responsible for protecting critical infrastructure and tackling crimes including illegal mining. It also assists police with internal security operations.
The NSCDC told the BBC that illegal mining was widespread in Niger state, where artisanal miners often operate in open fields.

Its spokesperson, Babawale Afolabi, said more than 50 people were arrested during an operation earlier this week. They had not been charged because profiling and documentation were still under way before the deaths, he said.
"Illegal mining in Niger is serious," Afolabi said.
The NSCDC had earlier said the detainees were possibly victims of a diphtheria outbreak, a serious bacterial infection that can be fatal.
But the agency's national headquarters later said the cause had not been established and would require medical and laboratory tests.
"The NSCDC wishes to clarify that reports attributing the deaths to any specific disease remain subject to medical and laboratory confirmation," it added in a statement.
Dalhatu told the BBC that security officers had been pursuing suspected illegal miners in the community for several days before making arrests.
He said relatives went to the NSCDC office seeking their release but were repeatedly told to return later. "Unfortunately, the following day we got the news that our children had died," he added.
One father told Nigerian media that his son had appeared healthy when relatives took him food the day before his death and called for an independent post-mortem examination.

Another relative, whose 17-year-old brother was among those who died, said the family had visited him during his detention and questioned how a disease could have killed so many detainees without apparently affecting their guards.
Post-mortem examinations are expected to help establish what happened.

Niger's police chief ordered an immediate investigation into "the unfortunate death of suspected illegal miners while in the detention facility of the NSCDC", spokesman Wasiu Abiodun wrote in a statement.
The victim's bodies have since been taken to the general hospital in nearby Minna for examination.
It is not clear yet whether any of the suspects had been charged.

Nigeria's constitution requires anyone detained on suspicion of a criminal offence to be brought before a court within a "reasonable time" - generally within a day where a court is available within 40km (25 miles), or two days in other cases, unless a longer period is considered reasonable.
The scramble for gold reserves dug up in illegal mines in Niger state has been blamed for fuelling criminal gang violence, according to officials and experts.
Much of the gold in the region is trafficked through global supply chains, a 2024 SwissAid report found.

articles.title: Australian man accused of murdering Thai teenager and putting body in suitcase pleads not guilty
articles.summary:
Simon Peter Carman appeared in a Pattaya court on Friday charged with killing Tunchanok Donhomla

An Australian man accused of murdering a Thai teenager and putting her body in a suitcase…

blocks.text: An Australian man accused of murdering a Thai teenager and putting her body in a suitcase pleaded not guilty on Friday in a hearing in the seaside resort city of Pattaya, a court official said.

Simon Peter Carman, 45, was arrested in June after 17-year-old Tunchanok Donhomla was reported missing in Pattaya City, about 150km south-east of Bangkok. A suitcase containing her body was found shortly after.
Police said she died of suffocation.
Carman appeared on Friday at Pattaya provincial court, where he pleaded not guilty to all charges, a court spokesperson said.
He had been charged with murder, concealing a body and taking a minor for indecent purposes. The next court date was set for 12 October.
Police previously said CCTV footage showed him entering a condominium in Pattaya with the girl in the early hours of 25 June, and leaving that evening carrying a large black suitcase.
In a police interrogation video shared online by Thai media, Carman has said he was acting in self-defence because the girl was threatening him with a knife.
The case put the spotlight on Pattaya, which is popular with foreign tourists for its beaches and nightlife, but also has a reputation for sex tourism.

articles.title: Louisiana firefighters find feline native to sub-Saharan Africa while responding to house fire
articles.summary:
The African serval, illegally enclosed in the back yard, was subdued and transferred to an animal welfare facility

Louisiana…

blocks.text: Louisiana firefighters responding to a small house blaze found a wildcat native to sub-Saharan Africa illegally enclosed in the back yard, and an animal welfare agency is now seeking to place the creature in an appropriate environment, according to officials.

Firefighters investigating a report of a minor fire at a home in the suburban New Orleans community of Marrero on Tuesday spotted the cat in question – an African serval – behind the residence in a chain-linked enclosure resembling a cramped baseball batting cage, a spokesperson for the local animal protection services said.

A statement from Jefferson protection and animal welfare services (JPaws) said its director, Michelle Brignac, and humane department supervisor, Victoria Clark, joined firefighters at the scene after they were summoned there. Local laws require an exotic animal permit to legally keep a serval as a pet, and the owner of the home at the center of the case did not have such a document, JPaws spokesperson John McCusker told the Guardian on Thursday.

blocks.caption: An African serval cat being transported after being found in an enclosure in the back yard a of a home. Photograph: John McCusker, JPaws

blocks.text: The statement said Brignac and Clark therefore “subdued the hissing serval and wrangled it” into a transport carrier from its 9ft-by-9ft (7.53-sq-meter) cage that McCusker likened to “a dog kennel”. Brignac and Clark then brought the serval to the JPaws facility in the nearby community of Harvey, according to the statement from the agency, which also shared vivid photographs of the wildcat.

Beside their black spots, svelte physiques and striking facial features, servals are known for their ability to leap as high as about 7ft (2 meters) in the air. So McCusker said JPaws gave the serval an entire room to itself while the agency sought an appropriate refuge for the wildcat, which was born in captivity but whose natural habitat is African grasslands.
Servals share some similarities with domesticated cats that make them immensely popular as pets, including their affinities for grooming themselves, purring, yowling and stalking potential prey.

Nonetheless, they are not easily sustained pets, JPaws’ statement maintained. Servals in captivity do not have the physical space and stimulation needed to engage in normal, healthy behaviors, and they endure chronic stress as a result, the agency’s statement said.

They mark their territory, become aggressive as they mature, cannot be fully house-trained and destroy furniture, and they have been known to barge through walls and doors, according to JPaws. Experts also say servals require a diet and specialized care beyond what house cats need, making them a major responsibility.

JPaws’ statement said the agency would explore having the serval held temporarily at New Orleans’ Audubon zoo. A zoo spokesperson, however, said the institution did not plan to take the serval in and understood JPaws was looking into another arrangement, the details of which were not immediately available on Thursday.
The Marrero serval was the latest of several indicators of the wildcats’ growing popularity, a boom driven in part by social media content creators showing them in videos online.

blocks.caption: Servals mark their territory, become aggressive as they mature and cannot be fully house-trained. Photograph: John Mccusker/John McCusker, JPaws

blocks.text: Cases involving servals have also tended to generate widely read news headlines in North America.
That happened in Ohio in 2023, when officials in the Cincinnati area captured an African serval named Amiry that was spotted in a Cincinnati neighborhood tree and later tested positive for cocaine.

In late 2025, a search for an African serval that escaped a Pennsylvania wildlife center culminated in heartbreak after a motorist fatally struck the wildcat, as Philadelphia’s NBC News affiliated reported.

blocks.caption: The Marrero serval was the latest of several indicators of the wildcats’ growing popularity. Photograph: John Mccusker/John McCusker, JPaws

blocks.text: And the news outlet People reported on authorities in the Canadian city of Vancouver returning an African serval to its owners after it escaped and nestled under a neighbor’s porch in June.

The British Columbia province to which Vancouver belongs had just banned keeping exotic cats such as African servals as pets. But, People reported, the owners of such cats were given until the beginning of May 2027 to apply for permits to legally possess them.

articles.title: Iranian actor Laheh Marzban faces severe threats after Venice film festival speech
articles.summary: Marzban, who won a best actress award for her portrayal of a woman held hostage by her father in Falling House, has received condemnations from authorities after dedicating her prize to ‘the women…

blocks.text: An Iranian actress who won the best newcomer award at the Venice film festival has come under severe attack from the country’s authorities and state media after highlighting the plight of women in Iran in her acceptance speech.

Laleh Marzban last Saturday won the best actress award in the Orizzonti sidebar competition for emerging talent, for her role in Mohsen Gharaei’s Falling House, a film revolving around three generations of women who are incarcerated in their own home by the family’s father.

At the awards gala, Marzban dedicated her prize to “the women of my country who have paid the highest price for even the smallest measure of freedom”. Speaking in Farsi, she added that Iranians were experiencing some of the most difficult days of their lives but should not lose hope.

On Thursday, the Supreme Council of the Cultural Revolution, a conservative-dominated government body appointed by Iran’s supreme leader, issued a statement condemning Marzban’s speech as “presenting a one-sided narrative of Iran’s proud society”.

Referring only to “recent statements and behaviour made at the Venice film festival”, it said reducing Iranian women to “the stereotypes desired by western circles […] is not in line with the awareness-raising mission and social commitment of art”.
The statement has come on the back of a raft of similarly worded attacks in state-affiliated Iranian media, some of which called for the actress to be disciplined by the regime.

Zahra Chekhmaghi, a journalist and presenter associated with the Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB), called Marzban “a two-faced person, […] self-interested, hypocritical, despicable and miserable”, while another IRIB-affiliated media personality, actress Zhila Sadeghi, criticised Marzban for not dedicating her speech instead to the children killed in a US missile strike on an elementary school in Minab on 28 February.

On state TV IRIB, a Qu’ran expert said the actress had been “deceived by the enemy” and called on the government to not let her work in Iran. Another news agency, Student News Network (SNN), urged the ministry of culture to not let Marzban back into the country.

The Iranian reaction to Gharaei’s film and Marzban’s speech appears to mirror the pushback against another film that premiered on the Lido this year, Guardian-produced documentary NAZA, about Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza.

Prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu said this week he would seek new laws allowing Israel to strip citizenship from people who “smear” Israeli soldiers, escalating a campaign against NAZA’s directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.

Gharaei’s Falling House thematises the collapse of traditional patriarchal family structures in Iran, and men’s efforts to keep them in place by force. Marzban plays twentysomething Ensi, who announces to her family her plans to leave the country and pursue a modelling career in Turkey. In a desperate effort to assert his authority, her father Rashid (Farhad Aslani) locks Ensi and the other female members of the household in their rooms.

Asked after Falling House’s Venice premiere how the film would be received in Iran, Marzban said: “This question is very important for me as an actress, and as all other women in Iran, whether they be doctors, artists, whatever profession women can perform, we can only make one step at the time, one step towards our objective,” she said.
“I have made my small part. I have given my contribution. I really hope many other people can make small steps towards our common objective.”

articles.title: Andrew Hastie says AI advised him to reply ‘congratulations!’ to man who planned to end life with assisted dying
articles.summary:
Liberal MP speaks of AI’s shortcomings as cyber chief tells inquiry the tech is needed to fend off ‘highly capable malicious cyber actors’

  • Get our

blocks.text: When a man with a terminal illness wrote to his local MP Andrew Hastie, telling him he planned on ending his own life with voluntary assisted dying, Microsoft Copilot suggested Hastie reply with “congratulations!”, “great to hear from you” or “that is wonderful news!”.
Hastie shared the episode at a parliamentary inquiry on Friday to underline the shortcomings of the American-run software as he called for AI run by Australians.
The hearing offered the some of the most detailed explanations of the Albanese government’s desire to bring Anthropic and OpenAI to Australia, in the face of calls to slow them down or shut them out.
The defence establishment told the inquiry that cutting the companies out could be catastrophic.
Abigail Bradshaw, the director general of the Australian Signals Directorate, said her agents needed advanced AI every day to fend off “highly capable malicious cyber actors”.

“If a digital adversary has access to newer, more capable models than we do, they may be able to identify and exploit vulnerabilities in systems and networks before we can identify them,” Bradshaw said.
But Australia’s top cyber-intelligence agency is “entirely reliant” on US-housed processing and would “dramatically” lose capability if cut off in a conflict, Bradshaw said.

The defence department’s chief AI officer, Chris Crozier, said the government was already trying to keep its tech needs local, contracting Google to build a series of interlinked datacentres spread across the country and disconnected from the US.
“Somebody can’t wake up and have a bad day and decide they’re going to turn it off,” Crozier said.
“We do not want to be using AI tool sets that are located offshore … we want the compute, we want the application, we want the data, we want the decision making, all based in Australia.”
Bringing big tech into the country would make the job much easier, he said, and not just by allowing the army to protect and maintain its datacentres.
The Office of AI, set up in the prime minister’s department, said bringing firms under Australian law would make it easier for local law enforcement to combat threats on the platforms.
Tight conditions on access could also materially improve Australia’s chances of using and defending itself with the best AI tools in the world, the inquiry heard.
“We will get more assured access, earlier access, more detailed technical access, and better integration with technical experts at the frontier,” Bradshaw said.
These would be assured by strict requirements on any top developers looking to train models in Australia, such as demanding government oversight and early access to advanced models, she suggested.

blocks.caption: The Australian Signals Directorate chief Abigail Bradshaw. Photograph: Mike Bowers/The Guardian

blocks.text: The government is already planning to set the rules for companies that come here. It is consulting on standards that would force AI companies to report issues and breaches and potentially reserve some computational power for local research.
Large datacentres will have to engage with communities, build away from schools and homes, and underwrite new renewables in most states.
after newsletter promotion
Another pillar of the standards – copyright law – is yet to be settled, with AI developers refusing to train models here without law reform.

A proposal to give the companies access to everything Australians create online by default sparked a wave of backlash from creatives, who say the companies could pay for local licensing deals to access Australian content.

But Jenna Priestly, the assistant secretary at the attorney general’s department, on Friday confirmed looser copyright laws would also affect AI access to foreign-made content distributed in Australia.
She said the companies wanted to train models on “maybe billions” of pieces of information and claimed it was practically “impossible” to make deals with every rights holder.

“As Australia’s copyright framework protects not only copyright material that’s Australian in origin, but worldwide, I think it is a fairly large number that [companies] would need to go and strike deals with,” Priestly said.

The Greens senator David Shoebridge, who is among those fighting calls for copyright reform and demanding a pause on AI development, on Friday said Labor had refused him a seat on the inquiry committee.

Labor ministers have spent the week meeting with OpenAI’s vice-president, and Anthropic’s special envoy Jeff Bleich, who this week suggested Australia had just months to bring in effective regulation.

The attorney general’s department told Friday’s hearing the shape and timing of any copyright reform was yet to be decided. But the prime minister’s department said Anthony Albanese wanted draft laws on the broader AI standards by the end of 2026.
Australia’s chance for influence on and special access to the models could be at risk by a delay, Bradshaw said.
“Decisions around training are a matter of urgency,” she said. “I think it is inevitable that those providers will look at other places to locate.”

articles.title: Weather tracker: Thunderstorms hit Spain as Japan braces for typhoon
articles.summary:
At least one person dead as stormy weather causes severe flooding in Barcelona and Valencia

Intense and slow-moving thunderstorms broke out on Wednesday afternoon across parts of eastern…

blocks.text: Intense and slow-moving thunderstorms broke out on Wednesday afternoon across parts of eastern Spain, bringing some severe flooding and killing at least one person.

Storms first struck over the Castilla-La Mancha regionduring the afternoon before passing over Spain’s east coast, becoming very slow-moving and continuing overnight. Torrential rainfall, strong winds and large hail were reported in Valencia and Barcelona, causing widespread flooding in both cities. Weather stations west of Barcelona recorded some of the highest totals with more than 100mm (4in) of rain falling in the space of a few hours, and locally 70mm in just 30 minutes in the early hours of Thursday morning. Cars and roads were submerged, and flights were cancelled across the region.

Wednesday’s La Liga fixture between Levante and Athletic Club had to be postponed due to flooding at the Estadio Ciudad de Valencia. On Thursday rescuers found the body of a man near Olivella, west of Barcelona, after his car was swept away in the waters. Spain’s east coast is susceptible to extreme rainfall during the autumn months, as experienced in 2024, when devastating flash floods killed more than 200 people in Valencia. With the Mediterranean Sea reaching record temperatures, this is providing extra fuel and moisture to thunderstorms, making flooding more likely.

In New Jersey in the US on Sunday, the Racefaster half marathon was disrupted due to extreme rainfall and a partly submerged course. Runners had to wade through chest-deep waters at times as 50mm-100mm of rain fell. Despite the flooding, 250 people managed to finish the race. Flooding was also reported to the north-east in Connecticut and Rhode Island, where up to 190mm of rain was recorded in a 36-hour period.

Tropical Storm Dujuan, currently over the open west Pacific Ocean, will move north-west on a track towards Japan over the coming days. It is forecast to intensify into a category one typhoon on Friday. The joint typhoon warning centre is forecasting that Dujuan will skirt past the southeast coast of Japan, potentially affecting Tokyo and the surrounding areas.

articles.title: ‘We have something that will kill Elliott’: Icac questions former Labor councillor over message
articles.summary: Sharangan Maheswaran denies message he received about NSW minister was related to work for fugitive property developer

blocks.text: A former Labor councillor says he had a “common interest” with a conservative Liberal operative, but denied that a message he received about damaging the reputation of NSW Liberal minister David Elliott was related to political work for a fugitive property developer, an inquiry has heard.

Sharangan Maheswaran told the Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Friday that a message sent to him by lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood claiming “We have something that will kill Elliott” did not relate to work by Greenwood’s company Beckington for Jean Nassif.
Maheswaran, who is no longer a councillor, was a lawyer to property developer Nassif and became an executive at his company, Toplace, in September 2020.

Icac is examining whether Liberal figures Greenwood, Charles Perrottet and Christian Ellis anticipated receiving $2m in prohibited donations from Nassif in exchange for political outcomes, including damage to the career of former NSW Liberal minister and centre-right faction member David Elliott, who had opposed Toplace developments. Greenwood, Perrottet and Nassif have denied that Nassif paid for political outcomes.
On Friday, Dwyer took Maheswaran to a message Greenwood wrote to him in February 2020 in which he said: “We have something that will kill Elliot.”

Maheswaran replied: “Your ears must be ringing. I just picked up the phone to let you know that I’ve got something decent, and the SMH [Sydney Morning Herald] is going to fire up re [centre-right Liberal MP Alex] Hawke this week off the back of an ALP bill to ban developers.”
Dwyer put it to Maheswaran that the messages showed he shared “a common interest with Beckington in terms of damaging the reputation of David Elliott”.
Maheswaran said he “had a common interest with Mr Greenwood in relation to the Hawke faction of the Liberal party”, but rejected the suggestion the messages related to work by Beckington for Nassif.
When he was asked if Nassif had told him that Elliott had objected to Toplace proposals, Maheswaran said “this is a new invention by Mr Nassif”.

Dwyer asked him if he “seriously contend[ed] to the commission that Jean Nassif never told you that David Elliott was objecting to his proposals”, asking if Maheswaran was suggesting that Nassif had lied to the commission.

Maheswaran said: “His complaint, up to 2025, as I understood it, was that Mr Elliott was backgrounding against him to the media and to various public officials and government officials, but it wasn’t specifically related to any planning process.”

Asked again if Nassif had lied, Maheswaran said “absolutely”. He was shown a draft statutory declaration he sent to a lawyer in 2022 in which he wrote that Nassif had spoken to Elliott about his opposition to a Toplace developments.
Dwyer put it to Maheswaran that he was “happy to assist him [Nassif] with the political outcome he was seeking, which was to get rid of Mr Elliott”.
“I don’t think that was an objective that Mr Nassif was seeking at that point in time,” he responded.

The inquiry heard that Maheswaran came to know Nassif through his daughter Ashlyn Nassif, who was sentenced to a six-month community corrections order earlier this month after pleading guilty to providing false or misleading information to obtain a $150m construction loan from Westpac.
Maheswaran said he was subcontracted to do work for Toplace through Ashlyn Nassif and her sister Evelyn Helou’s law firm EA Legal in late 2019, through another company, Anwalt Pty Ltd.
after newsletter promotion
But he took issue with Dwyer’s suggestion that he and Anwalt were one and the same.

He said: “That’s nonsensical from a corporation’s perspective, from a commercial perspective, from any sort of understanding of contractual law, I’m sorry, Dr Dwyer, I’m speaking in terms of as I understand the world.”
“No problem,” replied Dwyer. Under questioning, Maheswaran accepted that he was the only shareholder and employee of Anwalt at the time.
Dwyer said: “So the only person doing any actual work was you, correct?”
“At that point in time, yes,” said Maheswaran.

Maheswaran told the commission he was paid $1.4m by Toplace between 2020 and 2023, but said he had not disclosed that he was a close associate of a property developer when he nominated for council in 2021, which Dwyer said was required by law.

Icac is investigating whether Maheswaran and fellow Labor Strathfield councillor Karen Pensabene engaged in conduct towards former mayor Matthew Blackmore in a way “that involves the dishonest or partial exercise of their official functions and/or a breach of public trust, including conduct which could involve blackmail” and possible breaches of the Surveillance Devices Act.

When Icac announced its public hearings, Maheswaran told Guardian Australia: “I have every confidence that my actions will be regarded by the public and by any fair tribunal to be lawful and entirely in the public interest.”
On Friday, the inquiry heard that Pensabene had been excused from her summons for medical reasons.
The inquiry continues.

articles.title: ‘We demand the truth’: Olga Tokarczuk and JM Coetzee lead calls for proof of life of disappeared Eritrean writers
articles.summary:
More than 180 writers sign letter renewing calls for information on 12 authors detained incommunicado since 2001 crackdown on free speech by Isaias Afwerki

More than 180 writers have signed…

blocks.text: More than 180 writers have signed a letter to Eritrean president Isaias Afwerki calling for proof of life for 12 writers arrested in 2001.

Nobel laureates Olga Tokarczuk and JM Coetzee join prominent writers including Colm Tóibín, Elif Shafak, Isabel Allende, Ben Okri, Yann Martel, Kamila Shamsie and Tsitsi Dangarembga in signing the letter dated 18 September, marking 25 years since a government crackdown on the independent press. “Within days, Eritrea’s free press and the nation’s independent voices were systematically crushed,” opens the letter.
It lists 12 writers who have been held incommunicado since 2001, including the poet Amanuel Asrat and playwright and journalist Dawit Isaak.

“The families of these writers, the Eritrean people and the global literary community have been met with a painful and unlawful silence,” continues the statement. “To withhold all information regarding their health, location, and survival is a violation of international law and an act of cruelty.”

Along with Asrat and Isaak, the other writers named in the letter are Dawit Habtemichael, Fessehaye “Joshua” Yohannes, Mattewos Habteab, Medhanie Haile, Sahle “Wedi-ltay” Tsegazeab, Said Abdelkadir, Said Idris “Abu Are”, Seyoum Tsehaye, Temesgen Ghebreyesus and Yousif Mohammed Ali. Six of the writers were profiled in the Guardian in 2015.
The letter, signed by 188 writers in total, calls for “immediate, verified proof of life for all arbitrarily detained Eritrean writers and critics”.

Other signatories include Andrei Kurkov, Anthony Doerr, Chloe Aridjis, Lauren Groff, Lemn Sissay, Maaza Mengiste, Madeleine Thien, Margaret Busby, Max Porter, Philippe Sands, Preti Taneja, Tice Cin and Viv Groskop.

“Mr President, Eritrea’s future must be built with its brightest minds, not based on their suppression,” the letter adds. “No writer or journalist should be disappeared for peacefully expressing their views.”
Eritrea operates as a repressive dictatorship under Afwerki, with no national elections held since independence in 1993.
“We remain in solidarity with our missing colleagues, and we will not cease our efforts until they are free,” the letter concludes.

PEN International will attempt delivery of the letter at the Eritrean embassy in London at 10am on Friday. Earlier this year, the organisation launched a petition, open to the public, which also calls for proof of life.

“Twenty-five years is an unbearable length of time for any family to live without knowing whether a loved one is alive,”, said Burhan Sönmez, president of PEN International. “These writers have not disappeared from our memory. We will continue to speak their names, and we will continue to demand the truth about what happened to them.”

articles.title: At least one dead and multiple injured in Philippines school shooting
articles.summary: At least one person is believed to have died and several injured after the shooting in Banga in Mindanao province.

blocks.text: A shooting at a high school in southern Philippines has left at least one person dead and several injured.
The incident happened on Friday afternoon at Banga National High School in South Cotabato, in Mindanao province.
Local media and officials have reporting conflicting casualty figures. The identities of the shooter and the victims have not been confirmed.
The Department of Education said in a statement that it was "deeply concerned by the reported shooting incident".

"Our immediate priority is the safety and well-being of our learners, teachers and school personnel," the statement said, adding it was coordinating with authorities to verify the incident and provide necessary support.
"We urge everyone to remain calm and refrain from sharing unverified information as authorities continue their investigation."

South Cotabato Governor Reynaldo Tamayo told reporters earlier that one person died and four people had been hospitalised. He did not give details on the identity of the shooter, nor did he indicate the shooter was among the dead or injured.
Local media have been reporting much higher casualty figures, citing other Philippine authorities.
Classes have been suspended "in all levels in the entire municipality of Banga" due to the shooting, the Banga disaster management authorities said in a statement.
The Philippine Red Cross said it has deployed medical teams to help out in the aftermath of the shooting.
Police are at the site investigating the shooting, local media reported.
Gun crime is not uncommon in the Philippines, which has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in the region - though school shootings remain rare.

In June, three students were killed and more were injured after their peers opened fire at a high school in central Philippines. Investigators believed the deadly shooting had been motivated by a "grudge" over bullying.

articles.title: Japan raises interest rates to 31-year high to curb impact of rising prices
articles.summary: Increase from 1% to 1.25% follows US Federal Reserve and European Central Bank tightening monetary policy

blocks.text: Japan’s central bank has increased interest rates to a fresh 31-year high as it attempts to combat high global inflation linked to the war in Iran.
The Bank of Japan voted to raise its target interest rate from 1% to 1.25%, the highest level since 1995.

The move meant the BoJ joined the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank in tightening monetary policy this month, as central banks attempt to curb the impact of rising prices, linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
The Bank of England on Thursday voted to leave UK interest rates on hold at 3.75% but warned they could soon rise amid the fallout from the Iran war.

The BoJ has been raising rates since 2024, when it lifted its base rate out of negative territory. It has been under pressure to raise borrowing costs as the yen weakened steadily against the dollar this year, to levels that prompted policymakers to intervene to stabilise the currency. The Japanese currency weakened about 0.7% against the dollar on Friday.
The vote to raise rates was not unanimous – with two board members dissenting to the increase.

“The tone of the statement, along with two dissenters for the decision to raise rates, leaves lingering doubts that Japan’s central bank will be cautious in tightening monetary policy further,” ⁠Fred Neumann, the chief Asia economist at HSBC, said.
“While back-to-back hikes appear unlikely, investors will look for clues as to whether officials are prepared to raise interest rates again in December.”

The drop in ​the yen helped the Nikkei stock market index to rise nearly 2%, while the Japanese two-year government ‌bond yields, which are most sensitive to ‌monetary policy expectations, fell four basis points to 1.82%.
European stock futures slipped 0.35%, indicating a lower open.
after newsletter promotion

Prashant Newnaha, a senior rates strategist at TD Securities, said the BOJ reiterated its concerns that underlying inflation could deviate upwards from its 2% target, but “we don’t see a smoking gun supporting a back-to-back hike ‌in October”.
He said: “We stick with our call for rate hikes roughly every quarter with the next 25 basis points hike in December.”

Hopes of ​alternative ways for oil supply from the Middle East to ​reach markets pushed Brent crude futures down as much as 1.5% to $103.29 a barrel even as concerns about strikes between Saudi Arabia and ​Yemen’s Houthis lingered.

articles.title: South Korea will not send military to support US war on Iran, defying Trump pressure
articles.summary:
Seoul resolves recent speculation over sending military to strait of Hormuz, saying ‘there won’t be deployment that would involve or enter war’

South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, has…

blocks.text: South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, has said he will ⁠not deploy the military to the ⁠Middle East in a way ​that could draw the country into conflict, resisting calls from Donald Trump to support his war in Iran.
“There won’t be deployment that would involve or enter war. I can tell you that very clearly,” Lee said at a ⁠news conference on Friday. “We won’t deploy military assets in any form to that end.”

However, Lee added that he was reviewing whether to play a greater role in safeguarding navigation in the region. South Korea maintains a naval presence off the coast of Somalia as part of an anti-piracy mission.
“[It] is also clear that we must do the minimum as other countries do to ​protect our commercial shipping and crude shipments, and also the safety of ‌our people,” he said.

Trump has criticised Seoul for what he called insufficient support for the Iran war ‌and scaled back major joint military drills by the two countries’ armed forces this summer, a move that unsettled the US ally.
South Korea’s government has been reviewing a ‌possible military deployment to the Strait of Hormuz, although the idea is proving unpopular domestically.

Asked about progress in reaching an agreement with the US on Seoul’s US investment commitments under its trade deal with Washington, Lee said concern over the commercial viability of the package was the main sticking point.
Lee said there were elements that were difficult for Seoul to accept, but that the two sides were nearing an agreement.
South Korea committed last year to invest $350bn in US manufacturing in return for Washington lowering tariffs on Korean imports to 15%.
Seoul this week postponed ‌a parliamentary briefing on the investment plans, which is expected to take place next week instead.

The South Korean president also said it was possible that a meeting could take place in the coming months between Trump and the North Korean leader, Kim Jong-un, but many factors needed ​to align for that to happen.
“What’s clear is that President Trump wants talks, and I want him to as well, and we’re continuing coordination to make dialogue between the North and the US possible,” he said.

North Korean state media has so far remained largely silent on the repeated calls from Trump for such a meeting. Trump has been pushing aides for a meeting with Kim as soon as the autumn, the Wall Street Journal has reported.

articles.title: Indonesia gets its first aircraft carrier amid debate over cost and military ambitions
articles.summary:
The gift from Italy has sparked fierce debate among defence analysts and opposition politicians who question its true cost and purpose

Indonesia has received its first aircraft carrier, a…

blocks.text: Indonesia has received its first aircraft carrier, a former Italian warship that the government says will strengthen the archipelagic nation’s maritime security and disaster response capabilities.

The 41-year-old former ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi, with capacity for short takeoff and vertical landing aircraft and helicopters, arrived Friday morning at a naval base in North Jakarta’s Tanjung Priok port, where it was welcomed with a military ceremony.

Italy in March agreed to give the carrier, which was retired in 2024, to Indonesia in a move aimed at boosting Italy’s broader defence engagement with the south-east Asian country. Italy is seeking deals on submarines and aircraft, and gifting the carrier to Indonesia also saves it the cost of decommissioning the ship.

blocks.caption: Indonesia’s first aircraft carrier, the ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi (C), arrives at Tanjung Priok port in Jakarta. Photograph: Mast Irham/EPA

blocks.text: The transfer would make Indonesia only the second country in south-east Asia with a carrier in its fleet. The first was Thailand’s HTMS Chakri Naruebet, which was commissioned in 1997 after being procured from Spain along with carrier-capable AV-8S Matador jump-jets.

The carrier will be formally commissioned into the Indonesian Navy next week as the KRI Gajah Mada, named after the famed 14th-century Majapahit-era military leader, whose campaigns and vision of a unified archipelago have made him one of Indonesia’s most celebrated historical figures.

Defence development was one of the top priorities for president Prabowo Subianto’s administration, as he has advocated an expansion of the military through the purchase of submarines, frigates, fighter jets, missiles and pushed for more defence cooperation with various countries.

But the Garibaldi acquisition has sparked a fierce debate among defence analysts, economists and opposition politicians who question whether Indonesia needs an aircraft carrier at all and whether the government should be spending millions of dollars to refurbish and operate an ageing warship while facing mounting fiscal pressures at home.

Indonesia’s finance ministry approved $450m in financing for the aircraft carrier program in 2025. However, some lawmakers have warned the overall bill could be far higher. TB Hasanuddin, a member of parliament’s Commission I, said the cost of retrofitting the carrier alone could reach 16tn rupiah (about $900m).

blocks.caption: The aircraft carrier ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi sailing near Bangka Belitung island.  Photograph: Indonesian Navy 2nd Fleet Command Public Relations Office/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Unlike major naval powers that use aircraft carriers to launch fighter jets far from home shores, Indonesia views the vessel as a mobile command centre and support hub for helicopters, drones and maritime operations across its thousands of islands.

Speaking during a disaster management meeting early this month, Prabowo said the vessel would help authorities combat forest and peatland fires that regularly blanket parts of south-east Asia with hazardous haze.

Prabowo said the carrier could accommodate up to 10 medium-sized helicopters, including aircraft with capabilities comparable to the Black Hawk and Mi-17, and could carry large quantities of water and be deployed to areas with large numbers of fire hotspots.

He also outlined plans to operate drones from the ship and use it as a mobile platform that could be rapidly deployed to help in the event of natural disasters, which are common in Indonesia, a nation that sits in the Pacific “Ring of Fire.”

blocks.caption: The through-deck aviation cruiser class ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi docks in Indonesia. Photograph: Mast Irham/EPA

blocks.text: Operating a carrier is extremely costly, however, and experts have questioned whether Indonesia’s leadership has thought through whether one is necessary for the country’s defence or disaster-relief needs.

The acquisition comes as Indonesia’s economy faces growing fiscal pressures. Prabowo’s government has been funding a free nutritious meals program – which has been tainted by multiple food poisoning incidents – and other costly initiatives while economists have warned about slowing growth, weaker state revenues and widening budget constraints, prompting closer scrutiny of major government spending projects.

blocks.caption: Experts have warned that operating a carrier is extremely costly. Photograph: Indonesian Navy 2nd Fleet Command Public Relations Office/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “The plan to acquire the Garibaldi must be based on genuine operational needs and our ability to operate it, rather than being driven by pride or other considerations,” said Muhammad Fauzan Malufti, of the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

He said policymakers must weigh not only the vessel’s acquisition and modernisation costs, but also the Navy’s ability to sustain its operations, including personnel, maintenance, fuel, weapons systems and supporting infrastructure.

Fauzan said the government should be transparent about those considerations, particularly given the vessel’s age. He cited Thailand’s carrier as a cautionary example, saying it has spent much of its service life in port because of operational and budget constraints.

“The bottom line is that this should not be forced. Otherwise, the benefits could be outweighed by the costs,” Fauzan said. “The money might be better spent on other priorities, such as increasing the number of frigates in the fleet.”

blocks.caption: Indonesian defence minister Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin on the ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi. Photograph: Mast Irham/EPA

blocks.text: Military analyst Khairul Fahmi of the Institute for Security and Strategic Studies said aircraft carriers are not a priority for Indonesia, which is focused on preventing adversaries from operating freely in the country’s territorial waters.
“Indonesia has a greater need for submarines, frigates and asymmetric weapons systems to protect its maritime sovereignty,” he said.

But he added that if Indonesia is seeking to position itself as a major maritime nation, “an aircraft carrier can be both a symbol of national power and a multifunctional platform capable of supporting a wide range of military and non-military missions.”

articles.title: Why US plan to sell F-35 warplanes to Saudi Arabia is controversial
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia has lobbied the US for years to buy F35s, the world's most advanced fighter jet.

blocks.text: Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois, a Democrat, opposed the sale on Thursday.
He warned "it could put the crown jewels of American military technology within reach of the Chinese Communist Party".
Other Democratic lawmakers and some American defence officials have raised similar concerns about giving F-35s to Saudi Arabia.
They said Riyadh might share the sensitive technology with China under a security partnership between the two countries.
The state department said in announcing the deal on Thursday that it would support US "foreign policy and national security objectives".
It said the deal would improve "the security of a major non-Nato ally that is a force for political stability and economic progress in the Gulf region".
"The proposed ⁠sale of this equipment and support will not alter the military ⁠balance in the region," the state department added.
Trump has a close relationship with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited the White House last November.
The two also met in May last year in Riyadh, where a $142bn arms sale was sealed – described by the White House as the "largest defence sales agreement in history".
The latest proposed sale announced to Saudi Arabia would include 48 F-35s, which are built by the arms company Lockheed Martin.
This would place the country on a level with Israel, which currently has a fleet of 50 jets.
However, Israel's ministry of foreign affairs announced in May, external that it would procure another F-35 squadron.
This deal would double the size of Israel's F-35 fleet to 100, according to the Jerusalem Post, external.
Just one of Lockheed Martin's F-35A jets costs about $82.5m.
Congress has previously questioned arms deals with Riyadh after the murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi in 2018.
Former US President Joe Biden's administration considered supplying F-35s to Saudi Arabia if Riyadh would normalise its ⁠relations with Israel, but that diplomatic effort faltered.
The proposed sale comes as the Saudis are engaged in fighting with the Houthis, an Iran-backed armed group that controls much of western Yemen.
The Houthis have recently seized control of swathes of Yemen's Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed pro-government forces.
The Saudi crown prince has personally pressed Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner.
But Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, the sources said.
Additional reporting by Sareen Habeshian
